Conductive contact creation with graphene and carbon nanotubes faces a major challenge due to their compatibility issues with traditional metals. The migration of metal atoms during the bonding process can greatly impact the final electrical connection made at the atomic level. In this lab experiment, we record the Local Density of States (LDOS) near the vacuum level for three materials: gold, graphite, and silicon. Our results show that silicon exhibits the highest Local Density of States, followed by graphite with gold having the lowest. By using high-resolution photoelectron spectroscopy, we were able to obtain extremely precise energy resolution, roughly equivalent to one millielectronvolt. Our experiment utilized a fixed exposure regime, lasting about one second, at 5 keV kinetic energy electron beam intensity. Our findings suggest that using graphene or carbon nanotubes may not sufficiently protect carbon surfaces from being contaminated by metals. Therefore, alternative methods, such as chemical bonding or van der Waals union, should be considered for carbon collaboration with metals.

As the size of formal proof libraries continues to grow, managing and finding specific proofs becomes increasingly challenging. To address this issue, we focus on the organization of formal proof archives by examining their structural patterns in a dependency graph, where nodes represent individual proof steps and edges indicate the used premises. Drawing on the theory of complex networks, we initially discovered that the dependency graph of Isabelle/ML exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, with a significant disparity between the majority of nodes having low in-degrees and a smaller group having high in-degrees. Furthermore, nodes with high in-degrees within the range of 11 to 25 inclusive make up approximately 0.8% of the total archive, corresponding to a fraction consistent with that of influential scientists during the period of natural selection. Similar findings apply to the Scalable Bella project, suggesting the universal nature of the observed pattern. Additionally, we have developed an unsupervised clustering method to group proof methods in Isabelle/ML, which can also be applied to other formal systems, offering a tool for organizing and understanding their underlying proof structures.

The objective of this research is to assess the effectiveness of time-scale modifying an algorithm on the wave detection algorithm B4 by examining its performance in recognizing and analyzing ULF waves in the Magnetosphere. By investigating the accuracy of the time-scale modified B4 on simulated and real data, the study shows that the method is functional on actual spacecraft data. The findings also indicate that time-scale modifying the B4 algorithm without scale dependence enhances its ULF wave detection capabilities on the ULF frequency band. Consequently, the study suggests integrating the time-scale modifying technique into B4 to enhance the algorithm's performance in recognizing frequency-dependent patterns in Magnetosphere ULF waves and to make its results more applicable to various scientific investigations.

The counterterm method developed in $d\ge 4$ charged rotating black brane solutions is subject to a misunderstanding, specifically when angular momentum and mass are defined, potentially misleading inexperienced researchers. Nevertheless, when properly employed, this method, initially intended for asymptotically de Sitter spacetime, can be adapted for anti-de Sitter spacetime as well. Furthermore, a review will be provided of counterterms in different dimensions and their application to black brane solutions.

We've developed a Thai word sense disambiguation system utilizing the Thai Red Rubies dataset and our own Thai wordnet resource, which we also developed as a basis for improving the country's English to Thai machine translation capabilities. Our Thai wordnet is structured in the Senseval-2 format and incorporates 10,000 word senses with their corresponding glosses. Our system employs the Lesk algorithm to determine the most appropriate sense of a word given a sentence context. During testing, our system achieved an accuracy of 62.43% for words within the Red Rubies dataset and 50.17% for words outside of it. Additionally, we applied the PageRank algorithm to the Red Rubies dataset to enhance the system's performance by establishing relevance among word senses, which resulted in a 65.11% accuracy for word senses within the Red Rubies dataset and a 62.56% accuracy for word senses outside of it.

The quantized Weyl algebras for each integer q have been studied extensively on specific types of topological spaces. Research reveals that the universal Weyl algebras developed from these quantization exhibit isomorphism with certain classical algebras under specific conditions, involving q. Furthermore, findings indicate that the algebra isomorphism is also valid at the level of $C^*$-algebras, established through an in-depth analysis of the universal enveloping $C^*$-algebras, including detailed proximities and topological spaces considerations. Importantly, this breakdown of the quantized Weyl algebras has significant implications for understanding the well-known Kaparzanov-Vinogradov involutions.

The original semantics of GP 2, a graph language, ensured consistency between local and global states by blocking potentially conflicting local choices, resulting in a semi-nondeterministic computation model. In contrast, the revised GP 2 semantics removes the blocking mechanism, replacing it with a last-in-first-out (LILO) order for multiple local updates at a site, and introduces a new fairness condition that ensures equal treatment of site and edge priorities in a program, resulting in a fully nondeterministic model. Notably, the revised semantics discards local consistency, but achieves global consistency, and it is demonstrated that the global state can be reconstructed from individual site states, and thus it is possible to bypass the blocking mechanism to achieve consistency without it.

We have developed a new two-component model for the emission spectra of disks surrounding X-ray-emitting stars, where we combine the standard grain-free-free grain model with the puffed-up inner disk model proposed by D'A\-ges et al. The new model features two distinct free-free emission components, one generated by the outer disk and another by the puffed-up inner disk region. Our model has been successfully applied to the disks of FU Ori-type stars, which include the FU Ori system, its counterparts FUV Ori and CC Mir, with consistent results. The model has accurately reproduced the 1-30 $\rm{\mu m}$ spectral energy distributions for these sources. The obtained stellar and disk parameters match previous findings and provide further insights into the puffed-up inner disk region. The model offers a general approach for analyzing the spectral properties of sources featuring X-ray-emitting star cores. It has the potential to make significant contributions to understanding various phenomena associated with extremely optically thick matter in very close proximity to the core.

We arrive at the conclusion that there are no factorizations of the Chebyshev polynomials of the fifth and sixth kinds using the minimal polynomials of specific cosine values into products of two binomial expressions.

Highly distributed intelligent systems face complex fault diagnosis challenges. Deep learning's strong feature extraction capabilities make it suitable for fault detection and classification. In this study, we focus on incipient internal faults in mixed signal flows in smart grid systems, investigating both normal and faulty energy pulse signal patterns. We introduce a new classification approach based on deep learning, which utilizes a deep neural network to distinguish between internal fault signals. The proposed method has achieved a balanced accuracy rate of 94% for fault detection and 91% for fault type identification within three pulse periods.

In mmWave multicasting with on-off-on mapping, we investigate sum-rate optimization with receiver multi-antennas, limited bandwidth, and blockage. Initially, we demonstrate the tightness of a constructed lower-bound for the on-off-on mapping sum-rate. Then, we transform the optimization problem into a more tractable form, converting it into a Max-Min Fairness Optimization problem with constraints. Utilizing these properties, we design an algorithm that achieves near-optimal performance and has efficient computational complexity. Simulation results show that deploying multiple receiver antennas can greatly improve system performance, with up to 10-fold increase in lowest achievable user-rate in the presence of severe blockage. Furthermore, this algorithm's computational complexity remains relatively low, at just 0.11% and 0.33% of the complexity required for an optimal but intractable solution under moderate and severe blockage, respectively.

We show that certain groups have near exponential residual finiteness growth patterns. Specifically, we find that all finitely presented groups that satisfy torsion conditions have near exponential residual finiteness growth patterns. This group category includes surface groups and 3-dimensional hyperbolic groups, particularly those associated with arbitrary cat(0) spaces. Notably, it encompasses groups that act freely on a tree graph, satisfying torsion conditions, such as atoroidal Kleinian groups. Furthermore, we identify a duality relationship between near exponential and sublinear residual finiteness growth patterns, illustrating that many groups indeed exhibit near exponential residual finiteness growth patterns.

The paper explores the behavior of a one-dimensional elastic network comprised of
N+1 particles situated on a N-pronged graph with a central hub. Each connection lacks
bendability (actuation) and is characterized by varying masses attached to the
graph. We investigate the long-term behavior of this network using Dirichlet boundary
conditions at the hub, and in cases where the edges have no bendability, we examine
exponential stability within a certain interval. We establish that without bendability
on the edges, the network becomes unstable. We extend our findings to a more complex
scenario where the masses are variable, a feature previously examined in existing
studies. The study provides a connection between the theoretical boundaries of the
M\"obius transformation, resulting in a determinate spectrum, and the stability analysis,
a concept previously established by Avila and Munoz-Lec. We demonstrate that without
bendability on the edges, the network becomes unstable.

By employing a cutting-edge Bayesian neural networks approach, researchers have revised our understanding of the single-neutron 2hu1g resonance, leading to predictions of novel nuclear shell effects in unexplored regions. These predictions were then used as a foundation to develop new energy parametrizations for the shell model, allowing for the analysis of unknown nuclear regions. Employing the Bayesian approach to determine uncertainties in shell model calculations has yielded more precise estimates of magic angles and ground-state energies compared to traditional methods. Moreover, by integrating the newly established shell model with a density-dependent relativistic mean field framework, researchers have obtained novel insights into the density-dependent two-nucleon interaction, including its behavior as density increases or decreases. Finally, by combining the shell model with microscopic effective field theory, researchers have made significant predictions regarding the two-nucleon interaction, nuclear force range and other properties.

We've developed a new series O-mode HEMEX sapphire wafer process tailored for microwave resonators found within transmon qubits. We've examined the physical properties of the developed HEMEX sapphire, comparing its dielectric properties to those of Electronic-Grade Fusion (EFG) sapphire using various measurement techniques such as couplings with quartz dielectric resonators, microwave resonators, and laser-based surface profiling. One key discovery was that HEMEX sapphire exhibited an order of magnitude lower loss tangent tangent ($tan\delta\sim5\times10^{-6}$) at 4-6 K in comparison to EFG sapphire. This is a crucial advantage since lower loss tangent allows for a dielectric constant that is less influenced by external factors, ultimately resulting in more optimal transmon qubit performance. Furthermore, the HEMEX process enables a more efficient production workflow, including a larger range of oxide thicknesses that can be precisely tailored to match the desired characteristics of the qubit resonators. In comparison to EFG, HEMEX also allows for a more controlled and uniform oxide thickness at the nanoscale, ultimately providing the capability to etch and pattern quartz oxide for microfluidic applications. We have combined the HEMEX process with a series O-mode process on the Oxford Superconducting Microcircuits (OSMC) platform to develop a wide range of millimeter-sized sapphire wafers, each containing multiple resonators and other essential components

The anomalous optical drag phenomenon, observed when light interacts with matter, has historically understood to pull on the light itself, thus far explaining phenomena such as optical trapping and drag in the same direction as the light's displacement. However, when considering the Kramers-Kronig relations, which link the real and imaginary parts of a material's optical conductivity, researchers found that an alternate interpretation of the drag effect exists, where the actual effect is the matter being pulled by the light, resulting in scenarios where the light's displacement and effect are opposite and potentially accounting for observed reversals of optical trapping.

This study presents an efficient Lagrangian dual method for solving a broad class of robust optimization problems with binary or categorical uncertain data. A new type of nonconvex Lagrangian is constructed by introducing two sets of continuous relaxation variables for the binary and categorical data, which facilitates the incorporation of these variables into the dual function. It is proven that the proposed Lagrangian dual method can solve the original problem in a computationally efficient manner. Unlike traditional Lagrangian dual methods, which become computationally infeasible for large-scale problems, the proposed method scales linearly with the size of the problem. Furthermore, our numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method outperforms common packing and separation algorithms for solving robust optimization problems with binary and categorical data.

The rapid advancement of social media platforms has significantly transformed the way we communicate with each other and access information about our communities. To enhance our city-dwelling experience, researchers are utilizing data analysis as a key tool to gain insights into the social dynamics of urban areas. This analysis measures citizens' sentiment towards city-related topics such as transportation, government services, and local events by detecting recurring patterns in social media data. By identifying these topics and trends, urban planners and policymakers can make more informed decisions, while city-dwellers can stay informed about their environment through engaging and informative content.

This paper presents an approach to detecting and analyzing sentiment in social media data, focusing on topics relevant to urban living. Our methodology consists of two primary components:

1. A topic model that determines which topics are discussed within a particular context (e.g., bike-sharing programs in Chicago).
2. A sentiment detection model that assigns positive, negative, or neutral sentiment to individual tweets, allowing us to study collective sentiment across topics.

We implemented this approach using 32,000 tweets related to urban mobility in five cities, spanning a period of 6 months. Our research reveals both global and local trends in urban social media data, showcasing the value of this approach in evaluating urban sentiment over time and across multiple topics.

This work has significant practical implications. By providing decision-makers with actionable insights, it can aid urban planners and policymakers in designing better services and infrastructure. Furthermore, organizations can leverage this research to create engaging and informative content that

Our primary strategy against data's explosive growth in complexity is not traditional supervision, but rather unsupervised learning that enables us to discover new patterns within data. In the past, similar situations led to significant breakthroughs in science, but this time, vast amounts of data and high-performance computing have created a vastly more extensive exploration potential. We aim to bring order to the unorganized mass of scientific information by identifying interconnected concepts and highlighting the dynamic relationships between them, ultimately facilitating easier knowledge acquisition and allowing us to navigate the endless expanse of pattern-based data.

GNNs exhibit relatively low transferability compared to other learning methods, but there's been limited investigation into the factors influencing GNN transferability.
This study takes a graph-based transfer learning approach, focusing on mutual information as a measure for measuring the similarity in graph properties between source and target tasks.
Through experiments on 11 real-world tasks, we found that the community structure in graph representations strongly governs the similarity between source and target tasks, which in turn affects the transferability of GNNs.
Additionally, we discovered that the performance of transfer learning is optimal or near-optimal when the community structure similarity is high, but it falls short when the community structure similarity is low, regardless of other similarities or differences.
This finding has motivated the development of search algorithms to find suitable source tasks for transfer learning and has inspired a new graph augmentation approach to improve the transferability of GNNs.

Recommender systems relying on positive point bias have gained great success by taking a multi-view approach on user, item, and feature levels. To address various user and item representations, a model combining hierarchical Poisson distribution and Indian buffet process is proposed. By integrating IPDs and IBPs, the model establishes correlations among users, items, features, and provides k most relevant features to each user based on their shared hidden item similarities. Additionally, it allows item similarity matrices to be learned as an intermediate layer and builds item similarity by sharing hidden user representations. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to the Higgs dataset and Netflix Prize dataset.

This research investigates the complexity of solving mostly set disjointness, where two entities from a given collection are identified as disjoint except when they share a unique item, which must appear in both sets. In contrast, the conventional set disjointness problem involves determining if any pair of sets contains only distinct items. A key aspect of mostly set disjointness is that all known complete problems arise from instances where the sharing element is present, in contrast to the standard case where such instances are relatively rare. Additionally, the complexity of mostly set disjointness has been found to encompass a broader range of reducible cases compared to set disjointness, with such reductions having been proved relative to various incomplete circuits.

We present a precise field-fluctuation calculation for the critical properties of a two-dimensional Ising model with Fisher-like exponents, where we derive and verify the relationship between critical exponents $\nu$ and $\beta$ for the paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. Furthermore, by employing the $\epsilon$ expansion, we assess the validity of Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation in the context of nonlinear $\sigma$ models. A comparison of our computations with previous research reveals that the transformations produce two distinct classes of models: those with Hubbard-Stratonovich and those without, displaying contrasting magnetic and Gaussian properties. We predict that the model without the transformation will demonstrate more reliable results and more substantial quantum renormalization of critical exponents and transition temperatures in the two-dimensional and three-dimensional scenarios.

We suggest utilizing Dove prism deviced to create a new form of optical tweezers that can be used to trap and maneuver individual atoms. By orienting the prism so that its axis is perpendicular to the direction of the light source and its facets aligned at a 60-degree angle to the beam's path, we can take advantage of the light's lateral gradient to affect the behavior of atoms in the beam. When an atom in the beam diffracts into a spatial frequency corresponding to a particular internal angle determined by the prism's orientation, it will experience maximum interaction solely with that particular internal angle, allowing for selectivity in atomic interactions with the tweezers. When tested using simulated data, our method proves capable of delivering comparable levels of control over atomic positions as the standard laser trap technique, but with improved capabilities for precision in manipulating and separating atoms. This method has the potential for use in a wide range of quantum technology applications involving single atoms.

Many-electron velocity, resulting from anomalous Hall effect, generates Hall conductivities when coupled with an in-plane magnetic field. Researchers initially observed this phenomenon in systems with triangular lattices, and more recent studies have uncovered its presence in systems based on the Breit-Rosenfeld model. This model, and the related pentagonal and honeycomb lattice models, demonstrate Hall responses both within the plane and out of proportion to them, resulting in disparate scaling between transverse and longitudinal responses. By examining how an electron's local spin and orbital motion interact within these systems, researchers have been able to understand the origin of these effects, which arise from the unique geometry of the underlying lattices.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a significant shortage of ventilators, leading to the need for innovative point-of-care solutions. This problem can be resolved by developing an open-circuit ventilator sharing system that enables patients to breathe naturally while being on the same ventilator. This shared ventilator design is similar to an anaerobic tank and uses a precise control algorithm to deliver the correct tidal volume to each patient. Our proposed method employs a silencer to mix the patient's breaths with the remaining patients' demands in real-time, ensuring the desired tidal volume is met for each individual. A theoretical model was developed to analyze the system dynamics, which suggested minimal influence from the ventilator's baseline flow and pressure drop on the shared ventilator's performance. Furthermore, simulations based on various patients and ventilators demonstrated the feasibility of this shared system, with performance comparable to separate ventilators. Two implementations were also developed using the Arduino and Python frameworks to verify the design's efficacy. These outcomes demonstrate that this shared system has the potential to alleviate the scarcity of ventilators in clinical settings.

For certain types of rational maps with two critical points, we investigate the properties of the deck transformation group when the map is raised to a power. When the map has a superattracting point, this group has been previously studied by other mathematicians. Our research reveals groups can be more complex when the point isn't superattracting. Even in cases where the map is fully hyperbolic, this complexity can arise. We provide examples to demonstrate the diverse structures that can occur. Furthermore, we examine how these structures relate to the map's conjugacy with another simple type of rational map. This leads us to ask additional questions about these deck transformation groups, opening avenues for further investigation. Some properties of these groups are likely to depend on a specific, complex quantity related to the map. Research is needed to clarify how this influence arises.

Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are among the most promising materials for the emerging field of two-dimensional atomic-scale heterojunctions. They possess a distinct characteristic of having a work function that can be modulated by varying the thickness of the bulk-like monolayer. Our investigation, which is based on state-of-the-art many-body calculations, reveals that the work function, ionization energy, and electron affinity of these materials are sensitive to the thickness of the monolayer. Specifically, our results show that the ionization energy and electron affinity are several times greater than the work function, and the work function exhibits substantial variation between 3.1 eV (for few atomic layers) and 2.2 eV (for a full monolayer) when formed from materials like MoS$_{3}$, WS$_{3}$, and their Wo and Mo counterparts. These findings are highly applicable to the study of charge transfer and electron interactions at the interface of atomic layers, and highlight the potential for modulating the work function through controlled layer-by-layer deposition. Furthermore, our predictive findings will facilitate the development of efficient charge-tunneling devices that exploit the work function, ionization energy, and electron affinity of these materials.

A defined approach in data manipulation, learning delta lenses, enables the incorporation of data toations. An asymmetrical learning delta lens has the property of preserving essential data characteristics, albeit allowing modifications to the input. The foundation of this paper is a mathematical structure that unifies and sketches the variety of asymmetric learning delta lenses, including applications in feature reduction, knowledge extraction, and knowledge refinement. The research further demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed framework by showcasing its compatibility with popular data preprocessing techniques, such as feature drop and feature fuse. The study provides evidence for the potential of the proposed framework in solving complex data problems by answering open questions in existing research and extending the concepts of feature drop and feature fuse to higher levels.

This paper focuses on estimating oscillatory integrals resulting from the convolution of functions f and g with kernels p, pertaining to a specific class where functions are defined as being from L^2 to L^2. The integrals in question are given by the expression: (p * fg)(x). The integrals are typically known to be well-defined, provided functions f and g, as well as the phase and amplitude functions, are smooth, though this requirement is relaxed in the text to permit functions with minimal regularity. The analysis proceeds by categorizing phase and amplitude functions into two groups: those with uniform (L^infty) regularity and those with uniform (L^p) regularity respectively. The latter group requires a different set of assumptions and analysis techniques. The estimates derived are found to be valid in a wide range of contexts, encompassing not only the given convolution class, but also general Fourier multipliers.

This paper introduces and analyzes a novel iterative strategy rooted in analytic continuation, which addresses rarefied gas flow solutions. Building upon a first-order numerical solution, the approach develops an analytical representation of the exact solution using a series expansion, followed by an iterative scheme to enhance accuracy. A synthetic iteration strategy is utilized to improve convergence rates, where the first-order numerical solution serves as a starting point. Numerical experiments with various applications, including Bessel functions and gas flow simulations, demonstrate the iterative scheme's effectiveness in achieving precise solutions with improved convergence rates when applied to flat target problems and rarefied gas flow with a plane and spherical surface, where the conventional solution often fails due to ill-posedness. Furthermore, the approach successfully yields accurate results for rarefied gas flow with a spherical surface by analytically representing singular boundary layers associated with a Maxwell surface scattering model.

If dark matter behaved the same as visible matter, the axion quark nugget model could provide an explanation, it is argued that including Higgs fields is essential in this framework, as this would account for the dynamic relationship between dark and visible sectors. The proposed scenario involves replacing baryons with more stable dark matter compounds, referred to as dark-baryons, while nuggets consisting of axions and dark-quarks would explain the observed dark matter abundance. The model further suggests that certain structures, such as dwarf galaxies, could be made entirely of dark matter compounds, as an alternative to the standard cold dark matter CDM model.

Data from nearly 36.1 fb^-1 of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions collected by the CMS detector in 2016 has been used to investigate the properties of a 125 GeV Higgs-like boson when decayed into ZZ. This study focused on ZZ final states containing electrons and muons, enabling detection of the ZZ minimum-charge states. A near-statistical resonance was identified at 125.6 GeV, with an uncertainty of 1.2 GeV, using events that fit expected models and account for background. This resonance was in alignment with both shape and rate predictions based on standard model Higgs annotations, with a likelihood ratio indicating approximately 3.8 standard deviations of separation. Additionally, direct searches for Z decaying into different particles such as neutrinos or electrons/showers revealed no evidence for Z Z states produced alongside any of these particles.

Let $\tau (m)$ represent the $m$-th Ramanujan $\tau$-function, which is a coefficient in the Fourier expansion of the Siegel modular form $E_{3,2}$ as described by S. K. Agarwal. This paper investigates $p$-divisibility in $\tau (m)$, based on certain conditions, leading to new information about $p$-divisibility in the terms of the Siegel modular form $E_{3,2}$, including its relationship to powers of $p$, the smallest divisor of $m$, and constants associated with the Ramanujan $\tau$-function. These findings expand upon previous work, notably those found by S. K. Agarwal, N. D. Barada, N. Somashekhar, N. S. Nagaraja, N. Srinivas R. and R. Vashishtha.

In this exploration, we examine the connection between homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups for spaces that have strong topological properties. Specifically, we establish that when we map spaces that have these properties to other spaces, the resulting group characteristics retain much of their original topological traits. Additionally, this study confirms the Nubert-Sz\'ecsi conjecture that concerns spaces with the properties in question.

Researchers have developed a theoretical framework to explore the creation of crystal structures composed of two colliding beams of ultra-cold ¹⁷Os atoms, which display entangled fermionic pairs under specific conditions. Employing the boson-fermion-density dynamics model and solving the Fokker-Planck equation, our model accounts for both fermionic and bosonic system complexities. Multiple stable crystal forms emerge, including the renowned Pauli crystal, along with novel crystal arrangements, which remain resilient against disorder-induced instability. The study provides the first theoretical outline of Pauli crystal formation, which may significantly contribute to field research.

The zeroing neural network (ZNN) method, distinguished by its inherent predictive qualities, has demonstrated success in solving various ordinary differential equations and their corresponding initial value problems in both analytical and numerical contexts. Notably, the standard ZNN algorithm, although accurate, poses a drawback - it cannot guarantee forward predictability, a characteristic desirable in many applications. This limitation has led researchers to modify the ZNN algorithm, aiming to make it applicable to a broader scope of problems while minimizing the impact on its original solution-generating capabilities. In our study, a revised discretized ZNN (DZNN) approach has been presented, incorporating a step-size dependent discretization process to enhance forward predictability. Furthermore, the DZNN has been shown to maintain its equivalence to the original ZNN method, as well as the standard ZNN algorithm, in terms of solution quality and initial error propagation. Importantly, the DZNN has been found to minimize the initial error without additional smoothing or regularization. To validate the DZNN's effectiveness, we applied the method to a range of problems, including well-known nonlinear systems, successfully demonstrating its forward predictability and accuracy. Additionally, the DZNN has been shown to improve its performance on a high-dimensional chaotic Lorenz system, outperforming the standard ZNN algorithm in many aspects. This study's findings have shown that the DZNN approach can provide forward predictability, high accuracy, and minimal initial error propagation without additional processing, making

Researchers have made significant progress in understanding the complex primary visual cortex (V1) and its response mechanisms to light. Recent studies have revealed that on-center and off-center pathways in V1 work together to process visual information. We present a new model, the Inexorant-Model, which mimics the behavior of V1 simple cells in response to different light stimuli. The model leverages a novel network architecture and utilizes a challenging optimization problem to fine-tune its parameters, ensuring the model's robustness and ability to learn complex patterns. The model enables efficient generalization and fast adaptation to novel stimuli, while remaining invariant to unwanted variations, such as changes in local or global light, as well as noise. Comprehensive testing confirms the model's impressive performance in a wide range of scenarios, surpassing competing models. Moreover, simulations of V1 pathologies demonstrate the model's capacity for accurate and efficient processing in conditions such as amblyopia and strabismus.

Computer simulations of parabolic X-ray mirrors, crucial in next-generation telescopes, depend on accurately modeling mirror deviation. Wolter I optics, consisting of a paired mirror reflecting surface, requires modeling to characterize deviations in both mirrors. Our research focuses on understanding and modeling higher-order polynomial deviations in these optics using data collected through interferometry, describing each mirror's deviations in terms of A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and G terms. This study is initially applied to the Hard X-ray Astrophysical Spectrometer experiment onboard the XLAM satellite, involving analysis of four pairs of Wolter I optics. Our research is set to underlie future spatial analysis of deviations in these optics.

A unique phenomenon referred to as reentrant reordering of atomic layers occurs when high-density electron populations cause large-scale shifts in the moiré structure of transition metal dichalcogenide materials, such as those consisting of tungsten or molybdenum atoms. As the external gate applies a corresponding electric field, multiple phases of tightly bound electrons alter their behavior in a stepwise fashion, producing an unusual condition where multiple patterns emerge simultaneously at the microscopic level. In line with theoretical predictions, our model accounts for multiple phase transitions through the formation of various sublayers, demonstrating that these are in fact stable states that emerge due to electron-electron interactions. These stable states can be attributed to the formation of various sublayers, an unusual condition known as charge order, and the unique phenomenon of a system transitioning between multiple phases as the external influence is increased. These results offer a framework that can be used to make predictions about the electronic properties of these complex materials, allowing for a more detailed understanding of their behavior at the atomic scale.

In our revised steganographic system, we enhance the secrecy of encrypted messages by using a modified iterative algorithm that incorporates the Lindley distribution. This distribution's properties enable us to establish a reliable lower bound on the secrecy of transmitted messages. Our analysis reveals that this enhanced system significantly increases the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared to the original method proposed in 2019 for various channel conditions. Furthermore, we calculate the maximum data transmission rate, or capacity, for this system and compare it to other existing systems. Notably, our system achieves a substantial capacity enhancement, outperforming other methods including theamma, gamma, and log-normal distributions.

In the context of unit commitment issues, the screening of operational constraints can significantly impact efficiency. Conducting this screening using machine learning models can yield improved efficiency and performance. However, standard supervisory neural networks face limitations, primarily due to their inability to efficiently handle high-magnitude data, encompassing large power values, as well as multiple input vectors. Consequently, they are not well-suited for screening unit commitment constraints. In order to overcome these issues, an in-depth modification of supervisory neural networks is proposed, enabling them to effectively handle constraints arising from unit commitment. This modified network architecture, dubbed SplinereNN, can accurately predict operational non-conformance and outperform traditional supervisory neural networks. Notably, SplineNN exhibits comparable performance to specialized machine learning models like kernel methods on a standard benchmark dataset. Most notably, SplineNN demonstrates a 5.2 times improvement in efficiency when applied to real-world datasets. This modification also facilitates the integration of heterogeneous data types, allowing for novel applications of supervisory neural networks that were previously unfeasible.

Re-examining the pressure-induced transformation in $\beta$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, our high-pressure resistance measurements now confirm that a phase transition occurs at pressures greater than 1.2 GPa, with further findings indicating that the high-pressure phase persists at the lowest temperatures sampled. Our results for the electrical conductivity under high pressure reveal a metal-insulator transition that takes place at pressures exceeding 1.2 GPa, with the insulating phase then remaining stable even at the lowest temperatures tested. In contrast to the established metal-insulator transition in Li$_2$IrO$_3$, our current data for the electrical conductivity show that the transition occurs more rapidly at the same pressure and temperature point, with the insulating phase then remaining stable even after temperatures as low as 5 K are reached.

Previous research has demonstrated the estimation of synthetic control weights using functional principal component analysis, incorporating additional relevant variables to address omitted variable bias. This paper expands the method to accommodate cases where target treatment variables may not be available for some units, ensuring causal estimates can still be obtained. It develops new estimators by taking average differences, controlling for target variables, a technique easily extended to estimate weights. The paper theoretically demonstrates the consistency of the new estimators, even in the context of infinite-knot kernel regression, and prefers them to established alternatives. Furthermore, the method allows for the reuse of potentially valuable information from control units previously unpaired with outcomes. Several datasets illustrate the method's practical effectiveness.

Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, contact tracing processes have drawn attention due to their potential to curb the spread of the disease by systematically tracking an individual's contacts.  Utilizing local differential privacy, the contact tracing process now protects sensitive information about contacts while gathering necessary data, such as daily recordings of interactions, training models for graph learning tasks.  Recent advancements in machine learning have made it possible to recover sensitive information from learned graphs, prompting the need to introduce a privacy-safeguarded graph learning method.  Our new approach, SafeGraph Learning, employs local differential privacy and a novel regularization technique, ensuring the learned graphs remain private and distinct from the original graph while meeting specified reconstruction error bounds.  Our results demonstrate that SafeGraph Learning offers a secure and private solution for graph-learned contact data.

The impact of the electronic memory on the Electron Temporal Focus following the absorption of an intense laser pulse is evaluated using the Fluid-Dynamic Quasi-static Electric Field Model. This model accounts for the influence of the Heavy ions present in the plasma. It is observed that when the laser pulse is followed by a second pulse with a different Carrier Envelope Phase, the two pulses create distinct plasma bubbles that may inject electrons into each pulse independently, with one pulse dominating the injection into its own bubble and impinging on a target, while the other phase determines the injection into its bubble and the total electron flow. However, the overlap of the two pulses enables mutual interference through their spatial overlap, modulating electron injection. Moreover, the second pulse can suppress the electron injection initiated by the first pulse when the two phases create an opposing electric field at the interface of the bubbles or the overlap region, potentially blocking the electron current injected into the overlap region. This effect offers opportunities for applications such as laser acceleration of particles or electron sources with a controllable temporal and spatial focus.

This study provides additional calculations for the l-dependence of a nuclear detector's reactivity to certain beta decay types and complex nuclear transitions. We specifically computed the sensitivity of detecting specific nuclear modes - a $2p$ and resonant $0p$ - in Pd isotopes as a function of electron shell involvement. Our work utilizes a nuclear transition amplitude model that incorporates multiple electrons. We observed that for the $2p$ mode, detectors are highly responsive regardless of electron shell Involvement, but they are most responsive to calculations involving lp = 1. This is in contrast to the resonant 0p mode, where detectors are more sensitive to nuclear transitions involving multiple electron shells. We also performed some calculations for the ionization peak following the decay of 107Pd to A = 97. We found that the decay generates intense X-ray emissions, with intensities ranging from a few hundred to several hundred thousand eV. These X-rays could be detected using a silicon detector with high resolution, thus providing evidence for the complex nuclear decay of 107Pd to A = 97.

Our analysis connects the interconnection of QCD currents to the ratio of the avor hypercharge to electroweak charge, yielding a relationship between renormalization constants, $Z_{F\tilde{F}} = \eta$. This relationship, established to all orders in perturbation theory, is tied to the squaring of the QCD mass parameter $\mu$ and the couplings $\alpha_s$ and $\eta$. This knowledge enables us to derive an important constraint on the QCD gamma matrix terms in the non-Abelian renormalization group equation. Our findings lead to a key outcome: if $Z_{F\tilde{F}} = \eta$, it is predicted that the QCD beta and gamma functions for the coupling $\alpha_s$ are each zeroed out in the non-Abelian RG equation, resulting in $\alpha_s$ being a full renormalization group invariant. This invariance holds both in the weak-coupling regime and within any generic generic self-mass correction. Our prediction may be validated through the $e^+ e^-$ colliders approach.

Recently, colorization based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) has garnered significant attention due to its high visual plausibility and richness in texture and color. However, existing colorization methods are limited in their ability to work with little to no paired data and often fail to produce accurate results when the subject's pose is significantly altered. In contrast, we propose a more versatile and efficient approach that employs a Triangulated Area Mesh (TM) to rapidly generate a 3D geometry model, which is then utilized to drive a 3D colorization model and produce more accurate and textured results. By integrating two scalable unsupervised learning frameworks, our system is capable of achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple challenging colorization tasks, including those involving large pose changes, without requiring any additional training. In our ongoing research, the system's ability to promote geometric and semantic coherence in its generated models has been empirically verified.

A higher-dimensional generalization of the Ermakov system is investigated. This system can be viewed as a particle moving in a specific geometric configuration with dynamics influenced by a quadratic function that can be interpreted as a 2-sphere. Under a certain condition, involving the system's quadratic function and geometric structure, the system's integrability and classification are determined. This leads to a generalization of the known integrability conditions for the 2-dimensional system.

The efficiency of public transportation systems greatly depends on well-functioning schedules, which, in many cases, are unclear or hard to access for the general public. This lack of information affects passengers, causing frustration and timing issues. Advances in data analysis technologies like data mining and machine learning now enable us to process and provide more user-centered services than ever. Utilizing these tools enables real-time schedule tracking and filling gaps in existing schedules. In this study, we introduce an integrated approach to determining operational schedules based on open data analysis. Firstly, we gather and cleanse open data to identify patterns and establish a baseline for service standards. Next, we calculate the schedule gaps and set realistic service level standards. Finally, we adjust schedules to optimize service levels, informing passengers and transportation service providers alike about service levels and timetable adjustments.

The objective of few-shot learning is to achieve accurate performance from limited examples.  Opaque boundaries between known and unknown classes complicate classification when data is scarce.  A proposed framework addresses this challenge by developing an effective framework to distinguish outlier samples, utilizing self-supervised representation and class-enhanced knowledge to improve classification.  Notably, the model can identify outlier samples automatically without manual labeling during the training process.  Experimentation across various applications, including semantic segmentation, meta-learning-based and contrastive few-shot learning, demonstrates the model outperforms other approaches on cifar100, miniImageNet, and SunDataset low-data scenarios.

We investigate charge defects created by time-reversal operators local to bosonic topological phases. Notably, our research finds that the time-reversal operator alone suffices to generate non-trivial charge defects. The properties of these non-trivial charge defects are insensitive to the underlying topological phase, and are instead determined solely by the symmetry and fusion categories associated with the topological phase. This theoretical framework is empirically supported by examining the charge defects within the 3-3-1 model of chiral gauge theory.

To determine the semi-transitive orientability of a given split graph, we first identify its induced graph with no cycle, then check if the orientation of its tree structure meets certain criteria. This process recognizes semi-transitive orientability in all split graphs with at most three components or a single-cycle component and two independent vertices. For split graphs that have four elements connected to only one independent vertex, we developed an orientation algorithm that leverages an initially introduced concept called semi-transitive orientation templates. Additionally, we examined the limitations of orienting split graphs and established bounds for semi-transitive orientation-stability in specific network topologies.

To evaluate various methods of distinguishing genuine tau leptons from fake tau leptons, which are caused by jets misidentified as tau leptons, we compared different approaches to tau identification. These methods were applied to legacy data gathered by the ATLAS experiment in 2015-2016 corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36.1 inverse femtobarns. Tau fake jet discrimination was measured using tag-and-roam and ghost interaction methods. When genuine and fake tau leptons were compared, the ghost interaction method showed improved performance. Performance evaluations were carried out at different tau pseudolepton momenta ranging from 18 to 225 GeV, which corresponds to different decay channels of W bosons, W tau neutrino, and tau leptons, as well as tau leptons in top quark pair production events.

A Bayesian Neural Network's classification precision can be enhanced by utilizing its uncertainty estimates for both individual inputs and overall generalization. In this study, we explore the application of BNN uncertainty in astronomical data processing, particularly in the context of the Gaia mission. Initially, we simulate a BNN based on a DenseNet architecture and train it on 2D color-density plots to mimic the classification of stellar types based on their colors and densities. By analyzing the stellar class, BNN uncertainty provides insight into the reliability of classification and potential stellar type overestimation. Additionally, BNN uncertainty can identify instances of unusual stellar behavior, such as pulsators, based solely on their color-density representation. This novel classification method demonstrates that machine learning can be used not only for classification but also for detection, serving as a complementary tool for mission analysis.

Photonic structure, particularly a step-index fiber, is examined for its thermal mechanical influences on Brillouin interactions. A mode's (m, m') polarization can be influenced by both longitudinal and longitudinal mechanical motions with various symmetries. One of the simplest mechanical system has a symmetry that causes some modes to experience forced oscillations while others remain undisturbed. Experimental results show that this simple mechanism is responsible for observable slow light effects, spanning multiple modes, and that this impact strongly correlates with the interaction between structure and light used to induce Brillouin effects.

The general standardized generating set of the finite classical Coxeter group Bn is called a generalized standard OGS of Bn. It's established that the exchange relations for this standardized generating set are governed by properties of Bn's Coxeter length and descent set. Moreover, it's proved that the standardized generating set of Bn consists of elements whose Coxeter length is n, which are also known as simple reflections in the context of Bn. Additionally, it's established that the standardized generating set of Bn consists of elements whose Coxeter length is n, which are also known as primitive elements in the context of Bn.

In recent years, various algorithms have been proposed to tackle the Subtour LP Relaxation (SLP) and Branch and Cut Procedures (BMCP) efficiently, especially in Electronic Vehicle Routing Problems (EVRPs) applications. The main challenge with SLP and BMCP lies in generating feasible solutions, as they respectively require a local tour reconstruction algorithm and manual initialization with a feasible solution across different branches. To address these limitations, we propose an enhanced local search algorithm, E2LS, which builds upon two key innovations: integrating Euclidean nearest neighbor (ENN) solutions and employing a tour reconstruction technique. The experimental results demonstrate that E2LS successfully provides high-quality solutions for two real-world problems, outperforming established methods in vehicle routing problems, including CPLEX, CLUSTER, and ANT COLONY OPTIMIZATION. The contributions of E2LS, specifically its integration in SLP and BMCP procedures, were found to achieve a 23.13% and 32.32% reduction in computation time, respectively, resulting in near-optimal solutions within a reasonable timeframe comparable to heuristic methods.

In recent years, the task of preventing churn has become a critical priority for companies and researchers, leveraging machine learning techniques to analyze customer time-series data and make predictive models. However, these models face a significant challenge in handling the complexity of time-series data, particularly when limited by resources and information. A thorough examination of the effects of data limitations on preventing churn through time-series analysis has not been conducted, and this study seeks to address that gap by investigating how the history of data influences the performance of predictions. Our research found that while models can demonstrate reasonable accuracy when trained on short sequences of data, they exhibit significantly improved predictions when given a longer history of data to work with. Notably, this study suggests that using the last 12 observations as the basis for preventing churn yields the best results, and highlights potential strategies for enhancing the capabilities of time-series analysis models in the absence of data limitations.

We take a conformal field theory with Ising field theory as a starting point and add an irrelevant operator, $L_{-4}$ times the product of two fermi fields $\bar L_{-4}$, to the Lagrangian. This operator, despite breaking integrability, demonstrates that there's a specific value that pinches the spectral gap when treated as a perturbation within the space of irrelevant operators in the Ising field theory. When the Ising field theory is conformal, this pinched spectral gap develops multiple distinct components, characterizing a unique gapped spectrum that differs from the non-integrable gapped spectrum resulting from the perturbation by $L_{-2}$ times $\bar L_{-2}$. When the Ising field theory is non-conformal, this pinched spectral gap develops distinct components that differ in mass scale, affecting the effective field theory's gapped behavior and field differentiation. Additionally, this analysis sheds light on the non-integrable nature of relevant and marginal perturbations in the Ising field theory, field differentiating, and the robustness of the gap in the presence of contact and heat operator interactions.

On the lattice, the geometric separation of the gluon TMD, $\mathcal{F}_1$, is investigated in relation to the gluon PDF, where the association between a certain lattice gluon TMD and the gluon PDF is demonstrated through factorization, concurrently validating the gluon PDF's systematics and the TMD factorization formula across multiple lattice schemes, while also enhancing the accuracy of the gluon PDF's systematics by constraining its "renormalization group evolution" with data from the gluon PDF itself.

The underlying physics of electron and positron production in high-energy collisions between heavy ions is complex and influenced by various factors. To gain insights into this phenomenon, researchers conducted a simulation of 200 GeV Au+Au collisions using a computational model. The study revealed some intriguing aspects of these interactions. Notably, electron and positron distribution patterns exhibited noticeable asymmetries when examined over specified angular range, with positrons being produced more abundantly at certain angles towards the beam's direction. Another significant observation was that these lepton yields noticeably decreased when examined over a 160-degree angular range, but surprisingly, their average momentum values remained relatively close to those obtained from Au+muon+X reactions involving the RHIC experiment's muon-arm data. The study also found that these lepton yields noticeably decreased when examined over a 160-degree angular range, but surprisingly, their average momentum values remained relatively close to those obtained from Au+muon+X reactions involving the RHIC experiment's muon-arm data. The study specifically demonstrated that electromagnetic interactions continuously affected the production of these leptons throughout their various stages. The observed production of these leptons, particularly electrons, at large angles towards the beam's direction, could be attributed to high energy intermediate mass conversion at these specific stages. A detailed comparison between this study and experimental data collected within the RHIC experiment also revealed that the theoretical model showed similarities with the observed production of these leptons, particularly electrons.

Our research proposes an analytical framework that enables the identification of
urban cycling risks and patterns through the analysis of publicly available
bike rental data. By framing the analysis from the perspective of risk
juxtaposition, we conduct an in-depth investigation of unsafe behaviors exhibited
by cyclists in relation to their law-abiding counterparts. Utilizing data from
the Capital-Bike share in Washington D.C., we employed a two-step strategy of
initial data truncation followed by textual scrutiny of police reports to create
a dataset of high-risk cycling incidents. By characterizing the operational
settings of these events, we pinpointed specific locations and time segments
where cycling risks are highest. Ultimately, we demonstrate the potential of
monitoring cyclist behavior for the mitigation of urban cycling hazards and
the optimization of city design to minimize hazards and curb law-breaking
cycling behavior.

This study tackles the challenge of creating robust robotic paths, particularly in environments where sensors have uncertainties that affect robotic systems. We develop a optimization-based model that takes into account the potential disruptions caused by other agents and uncertainties in system models, such as sensor inaccuracies. By integrating these uncertainties into a constrained optimization problem, parameters like collision avoidance and goal completion are given weighted values. We propose two approaches for tackling the complexity of this problem: a computationally efficient method that simplifies the problem and a more comprehensive algorithm using mixed-integer nonlinear programming. Both methods leverage sparse modeling techniques to optimize robotic path planning effectively. We evaluate the efficiency and performance of these methods against varying levels of uncertainty and agent disruption. Simulation results demonstrating the performance of these methods are presented for different levels of uncertainty and agent disruption.

This study examines the covering number of a ring, with certain exceptions, in the absence of multiplicative identity. It's realized that the covering number of such a ring can't exceed the covering number of its corresponding unital ring, albeit positively covering a zero divisor whose square isn't identically zero. Furthermore, it's demonstrated that the covering number of the ring without unity shouldn't necessarily exceed the covering number of the ring with unity. Specifically, there are instances where the covering number of the ring without unity equals the covering number of the ring with unity but is greater than the covering number of a unital ring containing it as a subring. Moreover, it's shown that the defined relationship holds true for arbitrary subsets in the absence of the ring's unity. It's also proven that the defined relationship holds true for arbitrary subsets in the absence of the ring's unity. On the other hand, it's clear that the defined relationship doesn't hold true in all cases for zero divisors. Research into the relationship between the covering number of the ring without unity and the covering number of the ring with unity, particularly in the presence of zero divisors whose squares aren't identically zero, is a promising area for future study.

Neural networks using identity mappings have a significant advantage in minimizing the impact of adversarial examples, as their error remains within the same range as their intrinsic noise. Notably, this property also provides robustness to a new class of attacks, which target intrinsic noise rather than the neural network's output. By accommodating both intrinsic and adversarial noise within a confined $l_\infty$ error constraint, this property results in zero-error robustness against these novel attacks. Importantly, this robustness requirement is the smallest constraint necessary for this robustness, outperforming existing methods such as GroupNorm and SplitWorld. Furthermore, this benefit comes with no computational or memorability costs, as this robustness is achieved using no new components or optimizations.

In an investigation into anomalous diffusion, we examine a vast array of convolution kernels as nonlinear operators for discretizing conservation laws. We demonstrate convergence of nonlocal solutions to entropy-friendly solutions of the original conservation law as the dispersion coefficient approaches zero. The rate and specifics of this convergence are characterized by the properties of the convolution kernel, such as its smoothness, convexity, and the smoothness of its inverse. Notably, our study reveals that dispersive effects can survive up to a scale as small as we desire, provided that the size of the dispersion coefficient is sufficiently substantial in comparison. The evidence comprises a thorough analysis of the behavior of solutions to a one-dimensional stochastic individual epitome, an exploration of the role of kernel properties in exemplars, and the statistical properties of random walks.

We investigate hyperbolic closed geodesics within the unit tangent bundle of a teardrop-shaped 3-manifold. Similar to the findings of MacKay and Strange on elliptic billiards, under a specific non-linear resonance condition, the directions of these geodesics become densely packed within the unit circle. Conversely, when no such resonance condition is met, the directions of the geodesics become arbitrarily close to any point on the circle except for four exceptions.

Our research links Total Correlation to the underlying structural connections within brain functional networks, revealing its potential as a proxy for underlying brain relationships. This association enables the use of Total Correlation-based networks as indicators of brain abnormalities or illnesses. Total Correlation calculates the mutual information between time series, providing a measure of functional connectivity that captures slower synchronization patterns. In large-scale brain networks, we demonstrate that connectivity based on Total Correlation can serve as a useful biomarker by comparing it to other metrics. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between total correlation-derived connectivity and underlying structural connections, revealing a strong association even with partial data. This connection holds promise for inferring structural connections from functional data, potentially obviating the need for high-resolution imaging in tasks such as functional mapping. Finally, we conduct a case study involving Alzheimer's disease, utilizing total correlation calculations to distinguish healthy from diseased brain states.

This paper introduces a concept of $L^2$ functions using a Clifford algebra, where the algebra's behavior in one, two, and higher dimensions mirrors classical results for real-valued and complex-valued functions. In scenarios where the dimension is greater than four, this work presents a decomposition of Clifford algebra-valued functions into integrable parts and shows that this decomposition preserves the algebra's action on them. A key focus of this study involves defining and examining geometrically the singular part of these functions.

Fitting statistical models that involve Gaussian processes can be computationally heavy, primarily due to the cost of fitting the models themselves since sampling a Gaussian process posterior is relatively straightforward. We introduce a method that increases the efficiency of sampling a posterior by conditioning on paths in a tree structure, which can also be used to improve the fit of models by eliminating unnecessary posterior samples. This results in significant reductions in computational cost for fitting models that involve a mean, noise variance, and kernel function variance. On the standard Gaussian process regression benchmark, our method combined with just one hyperparameter adjustment yielded a 26-second fit that matched the exact fit for all training data points and had a 95% confidence interval for prediction error of $0.5\pm0.025$. This surpasses the state-of-the-art in prediction error while being significantly faster than the exact fit. Our code is currently available online at https://github.com/jos Atom/cond GP.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are being heavily evaluated as transient communication towers to support internet connectivity in remote areas. To facilitate research into these technologies, accurate mathematical models of channel propagation are needed. Existing models, such as the Two-Ray and Free Space models, are useful but have limitations in their applicability to specific scenarios. In this research, we introduce an extended version of the Free Space model to predict the amount of signal strength received by ground sensors from a UAV at varying distances. To validate the efficacy of this new approach, we compare it to the Two-Ray model and Free Space model under realistic conditions, simulating different altitudes and terrain types. The results show that our new model performs similarly to the Two-Ray model, but with the added benefit of simpler mathematical formulation and broader applicability to different situations. This new model will serve as a vital foundation for future channel modeling and analysis for aerial networks.

The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) is a comprehensive LBNV experiment located at the SURF laboratory deep within Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. DUNE LC will utilize the same detector design as the main far detector, featuring a same tank and same photomultiplier same technology, yet differing in volume, with LC scaled down to 70% of the main detector's size. This design choice, where LC's smaller volume is balanced by increased concentration of components, maintains the high-quality photomultiplier coverage of the detector. DUNE LC will focus on high-energy particle physics, particularly protons decaying into muons, as well as long-tailed neutrino and antineutrino oscillations. With LC's upgraded design, the experiment will achieve improved signal detection and reduced background contamination compared to the main detector. DUNE LC will offer more competitive results compared to the current world standards for protons decaying into muons and long-tailed neutrino and antineutrino oscillations. With LC's upgraded design, the experiment will attain more superior results compared to the current world standards for protons decaying into muons and long-tailed neutrino and antineutrino oscillations. DUNE LC's upgraded design will enhance its capability for various areas of study. The Shapley framework facilitates analysis of features within machine learning models by assigning values to individual features, highlighting their contributions. Notably, features in image datasets often comprise combined elements like edges, textures, etc., which hold no inherent significance on their own but gain importance when arranged differently as parts of an image. The challenge lies in interpreting features as regional indicators on the input image. Our study delves into the capabilities of Shapley values in distinguishing between different image classification techniques utilizing local explanations. We examine the capabilities and limitations of Shapley values in recreating regional explanation maps and their effectiveness in distinguishing between classifications generated by deep neural networks and other methods. Additionally, we discuss further research opportunities that could enhance the ability to extract meaningful features from explanations generated by DNNS.

This chapter focuses on Virtual Observatory (VO) development, specifically the creation and implementation of VO services, and presents a systematic approach to building such services based on the SOFA C++ library. The paper begins by providing a high-level overview of the VO concept and its components, before detailing the fundamental principles of abstraction and specialization in software development. The authors then describe how to address specific challenges in VO development, including the variation of abstract concepts among different instantiations and the necessity of adapting existing software to fulfill specific functionalities. Ultimately, the chapter demonstrates that a methodical and abstract approach to VO service development can contribute to the achievement of the goals set by the astro community.

Off-policy reinforcement learning, particularly when combined with variance reduction and learned experience replay, offers a promising approach to tackling the challenge of biased gradient estimation in policy gradients. The existing variants of off-policy policy iteration, despite providing a theoretical guarantee of convergence at an optimal rate, fail to provide an accurate estimate of the gradient with respect to the target policy. Our newly introduced variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework aims to enhance policy gradient estimation by enhancing the off-policy framework. VRER achieves this by integrating a modified version of off-policy policy iteration with variance reduction and learned experience replay, effectively reducing the variance in gradient estimates and providing an accurate representation of the true gradient. The effectiveness of VRER is further exemplified by demonstrating that it yields an optimal rate of off-policy policy gradient estimation. Furthermore, VRER is exemplified in the context of two widely employed reinforcement learning benchmarks, with VRER successfully showcasing its efficacy by greatly reducing the number of required samples in comparison to the standard policy gradient method and variance reduction based experience replay (VER) methods.

Utilizing superbosonization, an advanced variant of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation that treats quantum fluctuations in different particle states independently of each other, we prove the integrability of the one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model when spin projection is zero, and also derive general expression for its partition function.

A new module for Detail Context Block (DCB) has been developed, effectively integrating multi-scale and temporal information, thus enhancing the performance of spatiotemporal learning significantly. DCB's context module uses an attention mechanism to automatically identify detailed contexts from previous information and filter out irrelevant data, thereby temporal information can be transferred more accurately across different scales, leading to better prediction outcomes. Furthermore, the filter's learning ability is significantly improved since it can be trained with both the main stream's temporal information and the filtered detailed contexts. Experimental results have demonstrated the efficacy of our module in terms of prediction quality, particularly in tasks such as gesture recognition, human fall detection, and vehicle behavior prediction.

Imperative programs written in high-level languages benefit from type systems enforcing memory safety through checks on pointer types, preventing errors, and further ensuring efficiency through performance-curtailing errors. Current formal tools for verifying memory consistency in imperative programs are restricted to specific programming models or fragmentate the standard programming structure. A new tool called Vipverifies has been developed to verify memory consistency in the broad spectrum of C and aims to fill the current gap in research, as C remains widely used today in operating systems and systems software despite its complexities. A novel verification method for C has been designed using a module-based approach, incorporating fundamental memory properties within the framework. Each module includes a statement verification component ensuring the correct use of pointers and a new heap property module that sets the stage for a comprehensive verification system, as illustrated by three case studies demonstrating the functionality of Vipverifies in verifying real-world C codes, including a file system driver, a task scheduler, and a malloc alternative.

Heavy neutral leptons with slight masses can cause lepton number violation in weak interactions. This is rooted in the intrinsic nature of these particles, which has far-reaching implications for their production processes. Our focus will be on lepton number violating interactions of heavy neutral leptons within the context of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT}. This involves considering terms up to dimension 13 that encompass operator types $4N/2$, $2N$, and $N$, in addition to similar patterns with gauge bosons. This comprehensive framework expands on our earlier work in SMEFT involving lepton-Smarr neutrinos and a single heavy neutral lepton. To gauge the feasibility of detecting heavy neutral leptons, we will examine the parameters' optimal alignment for single production via $W$-boson interactions and subsequent decays of the top quark. This will be complemented by analyzing the sensitivity of the ATLAS and HL-LHC experiments in identifying signatures involving the $t\bar{t}+j\ell_N$ channel. Specifically, our study indicates that reaching the completeness sign plane for the $N$ lepton-Smarr neutrino scenario may be challenging, whereas there are reasons to be more optimistic about reaching the completeness sign plane for the single heavy neutral lepton scenario, albeit with narrower margins. This contrasts the $N$-lepton-Smarr neutrino with single heavy neutral lepton scenarios. Further research is needed to explore production channels involving $b$

This study introduces an innovative joint decoding approach for pre-transformed polar codes, comprising CRC and SPC combinations, that can be applied to various lengths. The proposed method simplifies the decoding process by merging two inner decoders into a single unit, enhancing its performance relative to existing separation-based decoding techniques. The results show the newly suggested decoder surpasses the previous separation-based approach, especially in scenarios with limited pre-transformations, and nearly matches the performance of separate decoding without restrictions. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the proposed joint decoder can reach the optimal error rate boundary for pre-transformed polar codes with limited length-specific constraints.

The lack of consistent telescope information leads to inconsistent point spread functions (PSFs) across individual images when using simple adding or mixing algorithms for combining data. As a result, stars appear more like a blend of several brighter and dimmer stars, making their PSFs difficult to determine. This problem can be resolved by utilizing advanced algorithms such as the median or a clipped mean, which eliminate the impact of unusual, distant, or poorly focused stars by setting a limit at the 3 sigma level. Although these methods prevent the distortion caused by unusual objects, they fail to produce consistent results due to the remaining objects within the images. To address this issue, a new approach centered on the Gaussian Mixed Model (GMM) has been developed to identify and exclude unusual objects while maintaining a consistent limit at the 3 sigma level. As demonstrated in the study, GMM-based clipped-mean offers the best results among all the methods, producing consistent results as the widely-used LAMPT approach but with several key differences, including the ability to easily identify and exclude objects with abnormally bright or dim values. Furthermore, our method offers enhanced flexibility in terms of the selection criteria for objects based on their brightness or dimness. As such, this tool has the potential to improve the precision of determining PSF dimming and identifying consistently focused objects in the near future.

A two-dimensional analysis of stress near a sharp notch in an otherwise unstressed material reveals that the notch tip develops singularities in both stress and strain. Notch notches of all shapes can be analyzed using an equivalent circle representation, allowing calculation of the stress and strain distribution along an equi-strain path centered on the notch tip. It is observed that any given notch will develop an instability at its tip, leading to finger-like fractures emanating from this point for certain types of notches. Notch-induced fractures are found to be influenced by several factors, including the material's fracture mobility, the work required for fracturing, and the stress accumulated at the fracture origin. Notch notches of all shapes can be analyzed using an equivalent circle representation, allowing calculation of the stress and strain distribution along an equi-strain path centered on the notch tip. It is observed that any notch will develop an instability at its tip, leading to finger-like fractures emanating from this point for certain types of notches. Notch-induced fractures are found to be influenced by several factors, including the material's fracture mobility, the work required for fracturing, and the stress accumulated at the fracture origin.

We will discuss the newly defined chordal Schramm--Loewner evolution, a type of stochastic process occurring in 3-dimensional space, and demonstrate its relationship to "imaginary surfaces" through the solution of a specific differential equation.
