The overture of modern technologies such as IoT, SW updates, and mobile apps has brought about expansive distributed control systems, necessitating a control framework that can accommodate vast networks. This distributed framework offers flexibility in its architecture; systems operators can choose between performance and efficiency to achieve an optimal balance. This flexibility is represented by a variable called the 'cost-of-performance tradeoff' parameter; adjusting it facilitates an optimal distribution of control duties among interconnected nodes. This parameter allows system operators to regulate resource allocation efficiently. Despite being fundamental to distributed control systems, there is a lack of comprehensive studies on this 'cost-of-performance tradeoff' parameter. To bridge this gap, this paper delve into its principles, offering open-ended research opportunities. This tutorial explores the tradeoffs and characteristics of control distributed across networks, focusing on system performance, communication costs, and energy efficiency in various network architectures. It includes real-world applications, such as wireless sensor networks and IoT, highlighting the importance of energy efficiency in control systems. Additionally, the tutorial examines the impact of data bit allocation on system performance in networks with imperfect channels and highlights literature studies on the 'cost-of-performance tradeoff' parameter. Ultimately, the tutorial serves as a valuable resource for control engineers seeking insights into the tradeoffs inherent in distributed control systems.

Image identification is an essential application with numerous practical uses.
This study focuses on developing an image identification technique that is both
high-performance and resilient to manipulations. Active indexing, a technique
that utilizes active search, enhances the robustness of image identification.
Comparative analysis of various active indexing strategies on a well-known image
database revealed that the most effective strategy focuses on the most significant
visual elements and uses distance to transform information while active indexing
can be applied to pre-indexed databases with minimal additional processing time.
Moreover, active indexing improves the robustness of image identification by 40.6% 
compared to traditional indexing and achieves a false positive rate below 10^-6 
with 95.2% accuracy on a practical image identification application, showcasing
its superiority.

In a case where a transmission is not confirmed to have originated from the intended sender, the receiver suffers an impairment known as the impersonation threat. Impersonas can implement specific forms of attack, namely, the impersonation attack using a white noise message or the impersonation attack using any possible message. Existing solutions, such as those developed in prior research [R1] and [R2], aim to mitigate these threats, but this work takes a different approach. We explore the possibility of modifying an existing channel code to prevent impersonation attacks while authenticating the origin of transmissions. If the coding rate approaches zero as the number of code words increases, the code can be modified in order to prevent impersonation attacks. If the coding rate is nonzero, the code cannot be modified in this manner. In the scenarios examined here, all channel codes with a positive coding rate can be modified, but only through methods [R1] and [R2]. If authenticating the origin of transmissions using these methods is not possible, the only remaining option is to use a code with an asymptotically negligible coding rate. In the contexts of binary and max-min channels, specifically, min-max Gaussian channels and min-max erasure channels, these equivalently correspond to the $p$-intrinsic information and $p$-min-information scenarios, respectively, with a value of $p$ equal to zero-point-five.

The asymptotic behavior of a system of overlapping Brownian particles in a periodically modulated, gravitationally driven potential is examined. The system's diffusion dynamics converge to 1.5-dimensional super-diffusion, characterized by a non-uniform scaling of temporal and spatial fluctuations. Within the super-diffusive regime, particle distributions are collected into distinct classes determined by phase shifts with respect to the driving potential's periodicity, and these classes undergo uniform scaling. Notably, the system's super-diffusion exponent remains invariant to the driving strength and particle counting, ultimately tracing its origin to the inter-particle interactions. Utilizing functional Taylor expansions, high-order gradients of the collective phase-shifts are analyzed, and fluctuations within these phases are studied in the system's weakly-coupled limit.

This research is part of a larger effort to develop a multi-sector macroeconomic model that incorporates the complexities of the real and financial spheres. We focus on a fundamental question: How do disturbances in the financial sector, such as the collapse of credit or the disruption of funding channels, affect the macroeconomy? We answer this by building on a basic framework that describes the interactions between households, banks, and firms, and incorporating the idea that financial shocks have distinct effects based on their size and orientation. Direct access to financial markets enables firms to mitigate credit risks, while relying on banks, even with imperfect credit channels, allows households to do the same. This framework leads to critical insights that transcend traditional boundaries between monetary and financial economics. We verify the accuracy of our model by analyzing phenomena including the funding liquidity crisis of 2007 and the disruptions caused by the shutdown of interbank lending in 2008.

The growth of momentum due to the interaction with the vacuum's own photons in a narrow, spinning band of energy follows a logarithmic pattern when the electron's motion within those energy levels is circular and symmetrical. This phenomenon occurs at a specific point in energy where the electron's motion within those energy levels transitions from being circular and symmetrical to elliptical and asymmetrical. Using complex mathematical functions to describe motion within those energy levels, researchers have discovered that this point in energy corresponds with a specific energy level that is closest to being circular and symmetrical, and has found expressions for describing the growth of momentum due to the interaction with the vacuum's own photons in those energy levels. This point in energy plays a significant role in other phenomena, such as the breaking of laws preventing recoil and the generation of angular momentum, and has implications for the behavior of particles in narrow, spinning bands of energy under external influences.

In the realm of NLP, specifically neural network-based entity linking, the type of encoding used for each mention can significantly impact performance. Nevertheless, current models treat mentions in an isolated environment, applying the same encoding activation across them, despite the fact that different mentions require varying levels of semantic information. The challenges of learning entity features and representation regularization hinder this process. To address these limitations, we present FGNET-RH, a framework that refines the representation of each mention through an enhanced attention mechanism, generates composite mention representations by fusing low and high-level semantic information, and implements a semantic representation regularization using a graphical neural network. As a result, FGNET-RH achieves top-tier performance in the entity linking task on two benchmark datasets, surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art models.

This paper investigates a distinct class of functions known as $\beta$-univalent functions within the unit disk and derives several functional equations stemming from these functions. Furthermore, certain subsets of $\beta$-univalent functions are identified and characterized by numerical criteria. Moreover, a subset of weakly star slant harmonic functions in the unit disk is defined by $\beta$-univalent functions, and their functional equation is also determined in this context.

Cloud providers can significantly reduce energy costs and resource overallocation by scheduling Virtual Machines (VMs) efficiently. Scheduling before resources are fully utilized allows them to operate at near full capacity, which is why methods like Prepartition have been developed. This approach, a variation of First-Fit, focuses on efficient resource allocation. However, the issue with traditional first-fit scheduling arises when resources are allocated to VMs one after another, leading to over-allocation and under-allocation in subsequent VMs. To overcome this, Prepartition introduces a balancing mechanism to minimize the disparity between the total allocated resources and the total required resources. Balancing ensures the sum of allocated resources remains as close as possible to the sum of required resources throughout the scheduling process. A simulation-based evaluation demonstrates that Prepartition surpasses first-fit in balancing, resulting in a 10% reduction in average power costs. Moreover, the average time spent scheduling (SST) is substantially reduced, declining by 42% in low load scenarios and 30% in high load scenarios compared to first-fit.

The majority of deep neural networks are geared towards predicting solitary optimal states; however, there's a pressing need to develop archetypes for network function that can predict multiple possible optimal states, particularly equilibria in games. In the realm of artificial intelligence, finding equilibria in multi-agent systems is a challenging task, yet identifying the underlying network architecture capable of generating meaningful functions to achieve this goal has been a mystery until now. In our research, we introduce a type of neural network, referred to as a Nash Fixed Point Network (N-FPN), specifically designed to identify equilibria in games. We demonstrate that this network architecture is versatile enough to generate a wide range of functions that can be applied to various games. We further illustrate the importance of neural architecture design by showing that conventional architectures, such as ResNets and Transformer, struggle to capture the essence of Nash equilibria in games. In contrast, our proposed N-FPN is capable of identifying equilibria in games, predicting policies at equilibrium, and generalizing to new tasks. Moreover, we highlight the essential role of non-conjugate structure in N-FPNs and propose a novel regularization technique. The effectiveness of our proposed network architecture is substantiated through experiments on both synthetic games and real-world environments.

This study draws attention to an unexplored connection between dimensionality reduction techniques and causal inference.  We demonstrate that popular dimension reduction methods can significantly alter the equilibrium position in causal analysis, shifting the balance between bias and estimation power.  The extent of this impact depends on various factors, including the original level of correlation in the data, the number of involved variables, and the scope of the focus set.  Furthermore, we present an exemplar instance that highlights the significant influence of dimension reduction methods on equilibrium positions in causal analysis.

This study presents a cutting-edge method that allows for the real-time monitoring of cyber systems to detect stealthy attacks, particularly in Industrial Control Systems. By incorporating a unique fault tolerance feature into a dynamic model, our approach effectively identifies the likelihood of stealthy attacks and provides accurate attack detection without requiring comprehensive system data. Utilizing the Kalman filter, this method can seamlessly integrate into existing control systems to provide robust real-time monitoring within cyber physical systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting stealthy cyber attacks through simulations of a power grid system.

Automatic document summarization is crucial for extracting key points from extensive materials and has been researched extensively. Despite the advancements made through employing Graph Attention layers in graph-based summ models, these graph-based methods face challenges in generating comprehensive and coherent summaries due to their graph construction limitations. In contrast, summ models relying on pre-trained language models like BERT tend to suffer from high computation costs. To address these issues, we present GAE-ISumm, a hybrid approach that builds upon GAT layers and pre-trained language models like BERT to create informative and coherent summaries efficiently. We also present a novel unsupervised summarization task known as Single-Document Summ, aimed at extracting key points from documents containing one main idea and numerous sub-topics. We develop a new evaluation metric to assess the performance of Summ models and test their capabilities in achieving better summ performance compared to existing single-pass and iterative summ models, utilizing the created SDA-Dataset and Single-Document Summ task. The GAE-ISumm model achieves superior performance to models like the Top-K, Top-F, TEDER, and EBSumm in the SDA-Dataset and Single-Document Summ tasks.

Let R be a ring that is Noetherian and locally factorial, and let A be a quasideterminant ring over R. We consider the category of left R-modules that have a certain property (0), resulting in a quotient category Mod(A)/0. We prove that if the dimension of injective modules in Mod(A)/0 is bounded, then the associated ring 0 is an independent S-ring of Krull type A. Conversely, we demonstrate that if 0 is an independent S-ring of Krull type A, then the dimension of injective modules in Mod(A)/0 is bounded. Additionally, we provide examples of quasideterminant rings where the injective dimension of Mod(A)/0 is finite but the injective dimension of Mod(A) is infinite.

The First Light Deformable Mirror Adaptive Optics Theory Team is working towards making image quality-enhancing adaptive optics available for future large telescopes. As part of this effort, the team is exploring how a specific mirror, designed for the MICADO first light offload, performed under realistic operating conditions during experiments at the E-ELT Model M4.

Optimizing the balance between accurate reconstruction and information compression is crucial when training a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). Although an optimal compression matrix C is theoretically attainable through maximum likelihood estimation, adopting a simplified approach with a specific structural form can still yield superior results. In this paper, we focus on utilizing an orthogonal compression matrix C and aim to find the optimal orthogonal carree ture approximation (COJT) matrix with a specific structural sparsity form. Our study suggests that structural sparsity learning is an efficient method for optimizing COJT, while utilizing variational sparsity learning yields superior COJT capable of extending theoretical bounds. Our proposed approach demonstrates its superiority by achieving results on CIFAR10 and MNIST datasets that closely approach the theoretical upper limit established by Ref. \cite{tresser2019optimal}, outperforming non-structural sparsity learning methods.

A proposed system aims to enhance smart home security by developing an intelligent localization system. To achieve this, radio signal strength (RSSI) based trilateration is first improved by correcting its limitations using machine learning. By incorporating a multi-objective optimization algorithm, the system identifies the most suitable antenna module for localization. Additionally, the system incorporates anomaly detection powered by data-driven localization to minimize errors. Through testing on various antenna modules, the system showcases superior accuracy compared to traditional methods, achieving a high localization rate and minimizing energy consumption while detecting anomalies in the process.

A new approach to quantization is introduced, primarily aimed at modern neural network models which produce high-dimensional outputs. This approach involves a three-step process: first, determining optimal quantizer locations using an information maximization objective, second, using these locations to define a piecewise constant quantizer, and third, incorporating this quantizer into a DNN by retraining it to maximize the objective. Importantly, only the network needs to be retrained, not the quantizer. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms previously established quantization schemes, including those based on mutual information and equidistant quantization. Additionally, when applied to the ResNet-50 model on ImageNet, our approach achieved performance comparable to a floating point model at a bit cost of just 3, outperforming state-of-the-art models like LFIQ and MIQ.

In general, treewidth serves as an crucial characterization in multiple areas, effectively capturing up-to-date model instances while facilitating efficient algorithm parameterizations.  Broadly applying this, we can say that treewidth-based parameterized algorithms are well-established for unweighted graphs; however, the situation becomes more complex and diverse when considering weighted graphs.  Specifically in directed graphs, efficient algorithms do exist that take treewidth and weight diameter as parameters, but there remains a significant gap in understanding the parameterized complexity of weighted graphs with a fixed treewidth.  To address this, we now investigate the parameterized complexity of the weighted graph path problem, where the weight of a path from vertex $u$ to vertex $v$ in a directed graph $G$ is defined as the minimum number of edges required to connect $u$ to $v$, and this value is denoted as $G[u,v]$.  Our results show that this problem admits efficient algorithm parameterizations when either the treewidth or weight diameter is taken as a parameter, contributing theoretical insights into the distinct nature of weighted graphs in this context.  Moving beyond this, we also now investigate the (parameterized) coloring problem in weighted graphs with a fixed treewidth.  Our findings demonstrate that by treating the treewidth as a parameter, we can achieve efficient algorithm parameterizations that match the state-of-the-art in unweighted graphs, allowing us to efficiently contract colored graphs while preserving any valid coloring.

Deep learning algorithms are highly efficient but often assume that training and testing data are accurately labeled, assuming the absence of uncertainty. However, labeling processes are often subjective and subject to variability. To address this issue, ensemble modeling is employed to develop a neural network that generates a distribution of potential labels, rather than assigning a single label, allowing for the inclusion of uncertainty and potential misclassification. By analyzing the output distribution, a decision threshold can be set to provide classifications and calculate the associated likelihood of error. Experimental results using medical image data of musculoskeletal tumors demonstrate that an ensemble method outperforms single-model classification and achieves a more realistic balance between the number of false positives and false negatives by adjusting the decision threshold. By analyzing the output distribution, we find that the model is not overly specialized and retains adequate generalization capabilities.

This paper investigates the behavior of transfer operators in semidynamical systems, specifically in uniformly and non-uniformly expanding semiflows. We examine the correlation decay of these operators under a uniform schedule and, in cases of uniform expansiveness, determine precise rates of decay. Initially, our findings are for semiflows on compact manifolds; however, they are subsequently extended to the case of locally-compact spaces. Notably, the latter's proof presents an innovative criterion for evaluating the asymptotic stability of families of operators, which may have independent utility.

A uniform covering array, denoted as UCA, is a generalized version of covering arrays, with the added constraint that each string of length t can appear at most k times in the array. In contrast, a standard covering array has k set to 1. In this study, we aimed to find the minimum size of uniform covering arrays, denoted as nu(t, k), for a given string set Sigma and length t. We also sought to determine the maximum allowed repetition, or the smallest possible size of nu(t, k) for a given repetition k. This investigation built upon previous research by Berman et al., who focused on strings of length t = 2. Our results revealed the lower bound of nu(t, k) as e((k*t)/k) * (t^k) * (1/(e^k)), with an accuracy of +1, and the upper bound of nu(t, k) as 2^(k*t) * (1 - (t/k) * (1/(e^k))), with an accuracy of 1, using Sage for the lower bound calculation. Additionally, the investigation provided the binary uniform covering array construction, thus offering an alternative upper bound of 2^(k*t) * (1 - (t/k) * (e^(-k)))

We examine a scenario where two players compete to acquire fewer than k copies of a bipartite state |Ψ\rangle, and we find that the players' chance of winning this game is rooted in a single-qubit reduced state ρ_1. The possibility for players to share many copies of the bipartite state affects the strategy and the optimal strategy is found using the quantum benefits and limitations of state merging. This game represents a type of economic model that explains how multiple copies of a quantum state are distributed among players. The special case where the bipartite state has maximally entangled qubits reveals a connection to the quantum Fisher information, while the collective quantum Fisher information cannot be used to upper bound the winning probability in this case.

Artificial intelligence-powered tools are used to automatically identify and model software crashes. There's concern that these models may not provide a thorough explanation for why a crash is occurring, which raises questions about their reliability. We tested EvoCrash, a widely-used model, and discovered instances where it cannot reproduce the crash it's trying to predict. Our results imply that EvoCrash may be missing essential information when learning crash predictions. Additionally, we found that EvoCrash often develops dependencies on third-party libraries during compilation, which can be inconsistent, and suggested using static compilation instead.

In this research, we introduce an adaptation of the Peierls structural transition as a model for the melting of the vortex lattice in underdoped $c$-tilted YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7 - \delta$, and explain the results of the melting transition through an interplay between disorder and hollowing of the Fermi surface. Utilizing a variant of the functional renormalization group, we have previously demonstrated that the melting of vortices in clean superconductors exhibits self-similar patterns matching the transitions in the vortex lattice and exhibiting two distinct singularities, coinciding with the predicted vortex lattice transitions and displaying resilience against disorder. Notably, this effect is analogous to that seen at the van Hove singularities in the Fermi surface of metals. Here, we apply this framework to analyze charge 3 and charge 5 instabilities in disordered superconductors, and find that melting of vortices is facilitated by transition across a structural phase transition of the Peierls type. Moreover, this model for melting of vortices in disordered YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7 - \delta$ is supported by our research, involving angular resolved ARPES measurements, taken near the melting transition temperature. The evidence for this transition matches predictions of a first-order structural phase transition of the Peierls type, further suggesting that melting of vortices in disordered superconductors exhibits properties of a first-order phase

Using the String-Midrapught model, we have generated simulated data of proton, proton-antiproton, helium-3, and helium-3-antihelium pairs from 2p and p-bar annihilations in 200 GeV proton-proton collisions. We have calculated the Bell coefficients to investigate initial state effects, particularly focusing on the second and third flow coefficients as indicators of quark-gluon plasma and novel spin-3 multipoles in particle distributions. We have discovered that these coefficients can reveal details about the spin-3 multipoles in particle production, offering insights not available through conventional spin-1 methods. We have further found that the third coefficient is sensitive to the anisotropic flow and can serve as an indicator of quark-gluon plasma formation, in addition to supporting its association with spin-3 multipoles. We have compared our results with available experimental data, noting that additional research is required to refine the models for a more accurate comparison.

In this work, we study the electronic properties of two highly frustrated lattice configurations, the triangular and kagome structures, using an SU(N) model. By combining self-consistent t-matrix approximation with a non-zero temperature approach, we investigate how collective effects affect the dynamics of SU(N) photons across a wide frequency range. The observed collective behavior is linked to specific spin configurations, with spin energy and spin structure factors serving as measurable indicators for these states. The SU(N) model's SU(N)-invariant electronic and spin properties ensure the SU(N) photon's dispersion is determined solely by the bare SU(N) photon's speed of light and the Heisenberg exchange coupling constant, thus enabling a direct comparison with theoretical spin waves and experimentally obtained spin waves. The SU(N) model's SU(N)-invariant electronic and spin properties ensure the SU(N) photon's dispersion is determined solely by the bare SU(N) photon's speed of light and the Heisenberg exchange coupling constant, thus enabling a direct comparison with theoretical spin waves and experimentally obtained spin waves. The findings serve as a foundation for understanding SU(N) photon behavior in other spin models and model-independent light-matter interactions, with potential implications for understanding the light-matter interaction process in spintronic systems and quantum spin dynamics.

This research focuses on employing two statistical methods, BSSF and infeasible SBF, to boost the capacity of discovering an overall treatment effect in genome-, epigenome-, and expression-QTL mapping studies, while maintaining a controlled false discovery rate at a pre-set level. Building upon the framework established by Hsu et al., 2012, these methods are designed to be robust against varying effect sizes and multiple testing correlations. Notably, in contrast to BSSF which adjusts for multiple comparisons using an approximate p-value approach, infeasible SBF employs a more accurate iterative method to re-estimate the false discovery rate. Utilizing simulated data from multiple testing scenarios mimicking real-world QTL studies, the findings indicate that both methods successfully control the FDR across the majority of simulated datasets at the specified FDR levels for both direct and indirect effect testing scenarios. Moreover, when the FDR is set to 0.1, both methods demonstrate enhanced power relative to the naive Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg procedures for identifying overall treatment effects. Ultimately, the methods proposed in this research may be instrumental in facilitating QTL studies particularly in understanding gene regulation via expression-QTL mapping studies.

The temperature fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background are driven by inflationary perturbations.  The relationship between these fluctuations and the primordial power spectrum is well established, making a precise measurement of the power spectrum a primary goal of current CMB experiments.  The inflationary perturbations that generate the temperature fluctuations are also the source of gravitational waves with a Compton wavelength much larger than the horizon scale.  The amplitude of these gravitational waves is defined by the tensor power spectrum, a key property that is challenging to measure directly.  However, the Gravitational Wave Spacecraft will be capable of detecting a Grushin tensor power spectrum of much smaller scales, allowing for a new constraint to be imposed on the Grushin tensor power spectrum.  The ratio of the Grushin tensor power spectrum to the Zeldovich curvature power spectrum can be bounded using the Grushin tensor power spectrum detected by Grushin, and the Zeldovich curvature power spectrum estimated from CMB experiments.

Alghani & Nasser recently explored the two Higgs doublet model in relation to resolving anomalies in the muon's magnetic moment and W boson mass, specifically when using the two Higgs doublet model's type-X variant. In our study, we've extended their work by applying the electroweak precision observable constraints, which were initially imposed by the Large Hadron Collider's findings. Our results reveal that even under these stricter constraints, the model still exhibits compatibility with deviations observed in the muon's magnetic moment and W boson mass, although it rules out any significant contribution type-X two Higgs doublet model might have to the observed anomalies in the electron's magnetic moment. In a related development, we've found that the model's lightest physical scalar, when being predominantly electron or muon flavour, can interpret the observed deviation in the muon's magnetic moment solely, while its counterpart can interpret the observed deviation in the W boson mass alone. Furthermore, we've found that the model's lightest physical scalar, when being being predominantly electron or muon flavour, can interpret the observed deviation in the muon's magnetic moment solely, while its counterpart can interpret the observed deviation in the W boson mass alone.

Crowdsourcing can tap into external expertise to perform tasks that are time-consuming or inefficient when done internally. In the context of requirement-driven concept location, crowdsourcing allows developers to leverage external expertise to identify relevant concepts quickly. Although concept location concepts are non-technical and easily understandable, solving them necessitates technical expertise, making them suitable for crowdsourcing. We've conducted a Crowdsourcing-driven Concept Location (CCL) experiment where tasks were performed by individuals without programming experience. Surprisingly, concept location task solvers without experience showed consistent results compared to professional developers, suggesting that crowdsourcing can improve concept location by tapping into external expertise. Furthermore, data analysis indicates that solvers' performance is linked to their search strategies, implying that concept location could be enhanced through training and expert systems. By integrating crowdsourcing, developers may now locate concepts more efficiently and even gain competitive advantage.

Our investigation into neural conversationalist models, which engage in spontaneous conversations with a pre-defined structure, reveals the existence of a distance metric that distinguishes live conversations from AI-generated ones. By analyzing the patterns of temporal relationships in dialog sequences, we found that the Neural Entrainment Distance (NED) effectively indicates the presence of human interaction as measured against a Corpus of Natural Speech (CONS) - a database containing unscripted conversations. The NED's ability to identify artificial conversations reliably outperformed other criteria for both the GPT2 and T5 models. Additionally, the effect of incorporating a sequential structure in model training became apparent when utilizing the NED metric, underscoring its value in assessing conversational coherence.

We've developed a machine learning strategy that identifies and classifies galaxies based on their optical spectra. Our approach begins with pre-processing to select key features in a specific wavelength range ($3750-5250$\AA) and employs BPT diagrams in a supervised training process. This process uses a neural network to create an alternative, more robust classification system, freeing it from the limitations of the traditional diagrams. Our results show that this method leads to enhanced performance and robustness when detecting and identifying star-forming galaxies and active galactic nuclei.

Action recognition research has given little attention to accurately dividing whole videos into individual actions versus detecting action sequences. This discrepancy leads to disjointed data partitioning, hindering performance. Presently, existing methods of segmenting videos into actions rely on limited neighboring action observations, restricting their effectiveness. To address this, we propose Co-occurrence Action Parsing (CAP), CAP aims to optimize action co-occurrence statistics to accurately segment entire videos into individual actions. This innovative approach integrates diverse action probabilities to pinpoint accurate boundaries. CAP achieves notable ATE improvements of 2.5% and 5% on JHMDB and UCF101-Action, respectively, outperforming previous methods significantly. Notably, CAP, a sparse action model, achieves performance comparable to higher-complexity action models without expensive optimization. CAP's success shows that leveraging action co-occurrence statistics can greatly improve action segmentation accuracy, facilitating more accurate and meaningful performance comparison with future models.

Building on the research by the LHCb collaboration, specifically on b-hadron decays at the LHC, researchers calculated the relative production ratios of various particle combinations created alongside a J/psi particle in the decay of a Lambda b hadron. They used a modified version of the inclusive decay formula to derive these ratios from standard model processes. These observations were made in the context of a collision between protons at energies of 7 and 8 TeV and in samples totaling 3 and 2 inverse femtobarns, respectively. Researchers found that the production rates of certain particle combinations created alongside a J/psi particle, such as muons, electrons, strange mesons, and strange b-hadrons, showed standard model-like behaviours, while processes involving the creation of a c c bar pair showed significant statistical power to detect unusual trends. Furthermore, in an analysis that included all observed modes, researchers found the marginality to be -2.9 annealed sigma, consistent with the predictions of a variety of theoretical models.

When teaching introductory programming, professors face a crucial decision on the type and amount of feedback to offer students. In this study, we examine two scenarios of CS1 instruction - providing timely regular feedback versus limited periodic feedback - with a focus on the effect of such feedback on students' performance. By employing examination grades, students' code coverage, and questionnaire responses as metrics, we assess the effect of varying levels of instructor feedback. A total of 899 students across two CS1 courses at a Turkish university participated in this study, with the aim of determining the effect of timely regular feedback on students' performance and their study experience. Our analysis indicates that students receiving regular feedback wrote more code and attained higher examination grades compared to those receiving periodic feedback. Furthermore, students receiving regular feedback performed better on programming assignments and examined more code compared to those receiving periodic feedback. Interestingly, students receiving regular feedback wrote slightly fewer test cases but covered more code compared to their counterparts. A set of six factors, derived from relevant theory, was originally proposed to explain the effect of instructor feedback on students' performance. By analyzing the relationships between these factors and performance metrics, we found notable correlations. A partial zero-order correlation analysis revealed that the effect of instructor feedback on students' performance aligns with the theory. Notably, the study findings show that instructor feedback has no significant effect on the quality of test cases written by students. Based on the results, we recommend that instructors consider providing regular feedback to improve student performance. Additionally, we discuss

Unquarantine, a novel challenge, requires unsupervised domain adaptation without access to the source domain's ground-truth labels. Traditional methods are rendered ineffective in this scenario as they rely on source data to calculate domain-invariant features. To address this issue, we propose Union of Distribution Challenges, a framework that generates a combination of multiple training distributions to enhance generalizability on target datasets. We evaluate the effectiveness of Union of Distribution Challenges in various unsupervised domain adaptation tasks and find that it succeeds in the absence of source data, in addition to traditional cases. Our approach is demonstrated to be competitive on multiple public datasets, considering both low- and high-dimensional settings.

The primary goal of a core reactor is to convert radioactive waste into electricity through high-pressure gas, but achieving this requires significant technological advancements, including improved resistance to pressure and high-temperature resistance for extended operation. Since the pressure inside a reactor is directly related to its efficiency, our study focuses on the relationship between pressure and output power to inform design parameters. Using a Monte Carlo simulation to analyze various pressure values between 5 and 50 MPa, we identified an optimal pressure of approximately 28 MPa for maximum power output. These results will aid in designing a stable and efficient gas core reactor.

We suggest a novel neural network design tailored for task-specific applications in experimental particle physics. Our approach builds upon established neural network architectures, incorporating a trainable component that adjusts in conjunction with the rest of the network and a static component infused with prior expertise from detector development. To effectively leverage existing detector information, we present an intuitive interpretation of a particle reconstruction problem as a semi-supervised process, devising a pseudo-labeling technique to maximize information from expert-designed observables, and demonstrate the significance of incorporating expert knowledge. Furthermore, we experimentally verify the robustness of our approach against variations in its training settings, highlighting its potential as a generalised method for a wide range of task-specific applications in particle physics.

The equilibrium gas giant models, often utilized in eclipse spectroscopy, exhibit minimal changes when employing various temperature-dependent absorption profiles from the extensive TiO line-lists. However, these line-lists are crucial in atmospheric model simulations for exoplanets and early M-dwarf stars. The underlining molecular dynamics of TiO are governed by the collisions with Ar, resulting in variable outcomes under the intense conditions found in these hot atmospheres. The underlaying static equilibrium models are consistent in ignoring these dynamic factors, leading to uniform TiO abundance usage across different scenarios. The study simulates the thermal equilibrium of TiO and O2 using a 1700 K surface Ar partial pressure in its static equilibrium state, revealing that TiO's temperature-dependent absorption profiles are minimal changes away from equilibrium models using various Ar-based collision rates. The underlaying static equilibrium models are consistent in acknowledging that TiO's abundance is largely dictated by its static equilibrium state. The study simulates 1600 K surface Ar partial pressure in its static equilibrium state.

The AGGR predicate in Answer Set Programming, which evaluates aggregate functions, has been restricted to non-nested applications. However, in the realm of logic programming, the subsumption resolution method can freely utilize recursive aggregate queries. A new Approach, AGGR-Delta, is introduced to Answer Set Programming, enabling the processing of non-standard aggregate rules. This involves resolving subsumption rules in a manner similar to the subsumption resolution method, while incorporating computed assignment tables to facilitate the propagation of aggregate values. This allows AGGR-Delta to handle recursive aggregate queries, while striking a balance between rules interpretation and computational cost. A revised evaluation method for simple aggregate rules has also been proposed, yielding a computational model that mirrors the well-established evaluated clause evaluation used in prolog.

A general method is developed to establish a unified framework for the thermodynamics of multiple resource theories. We define essential work quantified by a tensor that represents the coupling between the system and thermal baths as well as other external influences. The change in work and entropic excess are formally defined as specific contractions of this tensor. It's shown that the first law of thermodynamics for these theories reduces to conservation of total entropic excess. Additionally, we prove the second law of thermodynamics by establishing that the total entropic excess of a system plus its surroundings must decrease. Our approach is applied to thermodynamic states of multiple quantum systems, including finite temperature systems, and we verify the first and second laws of thermodynamics for them.

Building upon previous research establishting the MOME (Moments of random variables and their mutual information) framework, novel estimators for diverse information measures, such as mutual information, Chernoff bound, and capacity, are developed. The MOME framework leverages moments of random variables to estimate essential quantities like marginal and conditional entropies. This work presents a unified theoretical foundation for the MOME framework, including a complete set of estimators derived from moments. The MOME framework offers flexible estimation approaches for different problems involving entropies, while its suitability and preferred methods for quantities like mutual information and Chernoff bound are rigorously assessed. Experimental investigations confirm the effectiveness of the MOME approach in estimating mutual information compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper presents an improved method for estimating the number of common stochastic trends in multivariate time series data using a step-by-step approach. Building on a previous study by Chevallier-Loizos et al. (2021), who used local Gaussian approximation, we employ a hierarchical testing technique to estimate the degree of persistence in these data sets. Our method overcomes assumptions related to normality and the distribution of errors in our previous work and maintains robustness under heavy-tailed conditions. Moreover, we show that the estimators for the number of common stochastic trends converge to the true value as the sample size increases, achieving the desired asymptotic properties in a more comprehensive framework. Our method is adaptable to a wide range of time series modeling including vector autoregression, factor models, econometric models with heteroscedasticity, and long-range dependence. Our method's performance in practice is supported by an extensive simulation study. Additionally, we apply the method to data from two well-known economic sectors in the United States.

We develop a family of quantum codes, specifically using quantum Cayley complex methods, incorporating hypergraphs and rooted trees. Our codes leverage the unique left-right asymmetry of the associated hypergraphs and employ a root-based projection strategy. This results in a family of quantum codes capable of tolerating combinations of particle fusions and projective measurements. Utilizing graph-based approximations, we analyze the quantum code parameters, showcasing versatility through combinations of hypergraphs and trees. Notably, our approach simplifies the subcode of the quantum Cayley complex associated with the symmetric group $\mathbb S_n$ using the branching of the Robinson-Schensted-Tao algorithm for permutations.

This work provides a solution for the distance-$r$ dominating set problem in distributed models using a single communication round for a specified $r$ in bipartite graphs. Specifically, for any $r \geq 2$, we have a combinatorial solution and a deterministic, distributed algorithm that efficiently solves the distance-$r$ dominating set problem exactly in $O(\log n)$ bits of communication. These results extend existing solutions for smaller values of $r$.

We examine a one-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian with disorder that forms higher-order topological insulators with notched edges. In the bulk, the band gap is constrained by the band edge effective mass. Contrary to the minimal model, the edge notch width is not influenced by the notch depth in the bulk gap. Instead, it is determined by logarithmic corrections. For large bulk gaps and edge notch widths, we find the notch width to be dominated by the bulk gap being much larger than the notch size multiplied by the fine structure constant, and for large notch depths it is dominated by the notch being much smaller than the bulk gap multiplied by the fine structure constant. This implies that for large bulk gaps, the edge notch will be much smaller than the bulk gap, and for large notch depths, the notch will be much smaller than the bulk gap, both multiplied by the fine structure constant. Ultimately, we resolve the discrepancy between the minimal model and notched band edges by showing that the edge notch width is much smaller than the bulk gap multiplied by the fine structure constant, and for large notch depths it is much smaller than the notch depth multiplied by the fine structure constant.

This study explores the possibility of detecting compressed, long-lived charginos in "mono-X" final states using the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at 13 TeV. The search focuses on chargino decays weighing 100-120 GeV, with the CMS detector's ability to track particles with the ionization energy loss of the LHC's proton beams. Three distinct signatures involving different final states are examined: hadronic, electron-based, and photon-based signatures. These searches cover the production of charginos decaying into the w boson and the lightest supersymmetric neutralino in scenarios where the higgsino or wino make up either the bino or neutralino component. The results are based on data spanning up to 35.9 fb^-1 in proton-proton collisions, collected in 2016 and 2017. No significant anomalies have been found; upper limits have been placed at a 95% confidence level on the chargino lifetime, with the results suggesting that for specific mass values above 110 GeV, the decay width tends towards compressive values. These new findings have expanded the search parameters for charginos decaying within the LHC's run 1 and run 2 datasets.

This paper introduces a novel view interpolation method for light field rendering. Our approach utilizes geometric constraints to enhance the learning of scene geometry when given only a few views, without relying on prior geometric information or memory. We find that multi-view constraints naturally improve the learning of sparse views and render high-quality images. Our method further leverages intra-view relationships to refine pixel-wise color matching. We evaluate our approach using the REVEAL dataset and demonstrate superior results among state-of-the-art methods in terms of geometric reconstruction and rendering performance. Our code and dataset are publicly available at github.com/azatilab/LF-ICI.

In a recent study, the speckle interferometry observations of 232 close star pairs or subsystems, conducted at the AO facility of the Gran Teide Observatory in 2020 using the mentioned equipment, provided us with a comprehensive summary of the results. Utilizing a combination of the square and round apertures at the telescope, our observations resulted in the detection of 20 new pairs or subsystems, bringing the total number of such subsystems known to rise to 858. Furthermore, our findings include the determination of binary parameters, including wide separations and proper motions, as well as the calculation of angular and speckle interferometric probabilities for subsystems. Alongside this, by employing the speckle interferometry probability criteria, the demarcation line, and the spectroscopic subsystem classification, we outline substantial evolution stages in the star-forming processes of subsystems, including subsystems star-subsystems and subsystems-triple systems that are in various stages of evolution.

In self-dual quantum field theories in 4D space-time, specifically those possessing $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetry, we explore the chiral structure of the operator-product expansion (OPE) relevant to scalar-superScalar-super scalar interactions. Our focus lies in understanding how this OPE structure connects to solutions of the operator product equation, their infrared behavior, and associativity principles. Moreover, it is established that tree-level associativity is tied to the global properties of the OPE. Furthermore, we calculate the next-to-leading order corrections to the central charge and the anomalous 'c' term, derived from the solutions of the operator product equation, leveraging tree-level and next-to-tree level associativity data. Our solutions are anchored in light-cone gauge vector field equations, specifically the critical component $A^+$ of the vector potential, and resulting four-point functions. Additionally, in the context of superScalar-super scalar-matter interactions, defined within the light-cone gauge framework, the chiral structure of the OPE is derived, revealing the role of chirality within the theory.

A type of solar radio burst called a type II burst typically exhibits two distinct features: a slow-moving shock and a fast-moving (fast) solar jet. Although the shock and the jet are sometimes thought to share a common source, such as a coronal mass ejection, it isn't clear if the jet is the source of the type II burst. We've studied a recently recorded type II burst that occurred during a jet's movement and found the shock moves at about 167 km per second, while the jet moves much faster at about 160 km per second. The type II burst's speed increased as it moved farther from the jet, suggesting the jet might be driving the shock and the type II burst could be an early sign of a mass ejection, like a coronal mass ejection.

We have developed a software platform for investigating various physical scenarios and their effects on future collider observations. Our initial examination focused on the general two Higgs doublet model, which yielded several notable predictions: future colliders may detect enhancements in specific B meson decay processes and certain lepton violation events, such as $\ell^+\ell^-$ production, especially when produced in association with $b$-quarks or alone. These predictions include enhanced production rates and branching fractions for these processes, which could materialize as enhanced Z gamma events, among others. This model's forecast of future detections at the HL-LHC, FCC-hh, and ILC also highlights potential implications for various astrophysical phenomena, including the muon (g-2) anomaly, the electron (g-2) anomaly, the b anomaly, and the excess in the (g-2) mass of the W boson, as well as the origin of dark matter and certain observed phenomena in the bosonic sector, such as the theta_23 and CP phases within neutrino oscillations and matter-antimatter asymmetry.

The efficient numerical solution of three-dimensional fluid flow equations is crucial in various engineering applications, one method being body-fitted finite volume schemes, especially with the semi-implicit algorithm used in naval engineering. However, the algorithm's efficiency comes with the drawback of complex body surfaces, affecting the simplicity and accuracy of the flow calculations. A new approach aims to overcome this issue by introducing a novel dynamical system for removing vortices, applicable to Cartesian grids. This innovative method promotes numerical stability, allows semi-implicit algorithms to maintain high accuracy, and simplifies the flow calculations by removing vortices, thus increasing solver efficiency. A thorough theoretical foundation and numerical experiments are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness and performance of this new approach.

In a study on the sum of absolute differences between consecutive n in a sequence of random numbers, we investigated the entanglement of a two-part system with varying n and Q values, demonstrating a relationship that mirrors the thermodynamic behavior of the system-as-it-heats-up. Two critical findings emerged. Firstly, the entanglement decreases as the value of Q approaches the number of photons, and Secondly, the entanglement decreases asymptotically with increasing n, consistent with the idea of a temperature-dependent behavior (at high temperatures), and the limit approaches a non-zero, constant value.

The emerging field of machine learning for personal health analytics holds vast potential for gaining insights into human physiology, however current systems face significant challenges in adapting to diverse data formats and sizes. In our study, we addressed the issue of finding predictive variables from large-scale time-series gene expression data using relevance learning and localization. We then further refined this approach to accommodate the unique characteristics of RNA-time series data, enabling efficient identification of genes whose temporal expression patterns correlate with clinical outcomes. By leveraging RNA-expression data and medical information, we demonstrated our methodology can also predict patient responses to treatment with anticancer drugs. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our methodology in analyzing both simulated and actual RNA-time series data datasets, such as whole-genome models of cancer and expression sequences from breast cancer microarray experiments. The application of our methodology to whole-genome models of cancer successfully pinpointed several genes whose expression patterns are linked to patient survival in less than one minute, in addition to predicting patient responses to treatment with anticancer drugs in under two minutes. Similarly, in breast cancer microarray experiments our methodology was capable of pinpointing twelve important genes in under five minutes, which correlates with known cancer-causing genes. The computational performance of our methodology impressed, processing on average within two hours for each dataset, regardless of dataset scale. The method employs parallel processing to efficiently utilize multiple CPU's and/or GPU's, in our study we utilized eight processors. In the field of optimal control within partially observable environments, the model reduction approach, also known as approximate Bayesian optimization for a sequence of independent tasks (ABOAT), employs recurrent neural networks to map histories to hidden states that serve as beliefs regarding the current state and relevant properties. We address the issue of end-to-end learning in such settings, where one can treat the hidden states as an abstract representation of beliefs. End-to-end learning, in this context, means directly optimizing the hidden states, eliminating the middle layer of demonstrated control. We explore this approach, in which the hidden states are treated as a single, unified variable to be optimized. We provide a theoretical foundation, showing that, under specific conditions, end-to-end learning is equivalent to the model reduction approach. We also present empirical evidence supporting the learned connections between histories and hidden states and their performance in a series of independent tasks. We further demonstrate that the hidden states obtained can serve as a form of abstract imitation fuel that enhances the performance of subsequent tasks.

The study of actions in videos has seen significant advancements in recent years, largely due to improvements in video representation models. These models have allowed for more accurate predictions of actions in videos. This research explores the use of self-attention and Graph Convolutional Networks in action detection, using a multi-scale approach that takes into account contextual information. This novel approach integrates features from different temporal scales and leverages relational data to improve performance. What sets this work apart is its parallel processing of videos, unlike existing methods that rely on serial prediction techniques. This structure enables end-to-end training and efficient video analysis. Evaluations have demonstrated the efficacy of our approach on action detection benchmarks, outperforming state-of-the-art models and effectively handling complex, relation-dependent actions.

This research introduces a novel approach to image identification, leveraging deep learning. The method utilizes a combination of saliency analysis and spatial pyramidal abstraction, paired with a hard attention mechanism, to analyze and compare images. An adaptive metric to compare feature maps allows the method to handle differences in image resolution. The technique also incorporates progressive similarity analysis, assessing feature similarity at multiple stages and incorporating these results, similar to soft attention. The method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions, demonstrating improved performance in various benchmark tests. Specifically, it exhibits accuracy rates of 100% for CUAA and SUNDB, as well as high F1 scores on other benchmark sets. Notably, it outperforms top-tier approaches while requiring reduced computation time, including notable increases in efficiency compared to the previously best performing method, SCDNN.

The article investigates the existence, uniqueness, and continuity of solutions to a certain type of parabolic equation-based initial-boundary value problem involving the vector-valued Leijzerovitz operator on a 2D plane. Similar analysis has been conducted in other studies for problems with Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, but the present case offers distinct observations and results due to its inherent differences. Using techniques from functional analysis, the study demonstrates the main outcomes, which are then consolidated into a comprehensive theorem outlining the necessary requirements for a solution to exist. It is then feasible to leverage these findings to examine a specific case involving a geometric diffusion equation with Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. Results indicate that existence, uniqueness, and continuity are guaranteed for diffusion equations with Dirichlet conditions, whereas this guarantee does not apply with Neumann conditions.

Our research focuses on studying nuclear matter at zero temperature, both with and without magnetic fields, utilizing the Density Functional Theory for QCD. We employ the Thermodynamic Function formalism to derive the free Energy Density and respond to its thermodynamic principles. The study shows that in the absence of a magnetic field, both energy and spin polarization maintain symmetry at zero temperature. The results indicate a need to improve the initial DFT potential since it fails to meet thermodynamic principles and results in a negative Pressure in the presence of a magnetic field, demonstrating a challenge in reproducing the Equation of State (EOS) of the finite nuclear matter correctly. With a magnetic field, the DFT approach is able to reproduce the correct EOS of nuclear matter but fails to accurately describe its correct Equation of state of bulk neutron matter by imposing the correct Energy per particle relation at the correct density. These issues are resolved through reflections and suggestions for future DFT studies. Additionally, we have established a novel DFT approach in the Landau gauge for describing magnetic matter in the presence of a magnetic field. In a related investigation, we explored a DFT approach in the Landau gauge for describing magnetic matter in the presence of a magnetic field. The results show promise for describing a range of phenomena involving magnetic fields in dense matter, such as neutron stars and various phases of dense cold matter.

Federated learning's renowned compression method has a previously overlooked connection to Differential Privacy (DP). We have demonstrated DP's utility in describing how compression spreads encrypted data's statistical properties under varying levels of distribution. This understanding justifies employing widely recognized statistical DP bounds in the context of compressed FL algorithms. Conversely, we have also challenged the conventional thinking that more aggressive compression leads to tighter privacy guarantees, revealing scenarios where less aggressive compression results in tighter privacy guarantees. This counterintuitive behavior is rooted in the interaction between compression and data distribution. These findings are set to expand the existing DP framework's applicability to the field of distributed machine learning.

Our research reveals the complex relationships between radio, UV, and far-UV light across 100 parsecs in the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus region, observing how this area emits and interacts with various forms of radiation, including molecular hydrogen. To achieve this, we analyzed data from the Far UV Survey of the Milky Way and the Hydrogen Epoch of Formation project, while also conducting radio continuum observations. Our findings show that in most complexes, radio emission accounts for the majority of far-UV intensity, but in the Taurus-Auriga complex, hydrogen fluorescence contributes substantially to the overall far-UV intensity. Notably, the UV and far-UV light emitted by the Taurus complex appears to originate from its central regions. Furthermore, by comparing our radio continuum findings with statistical analysis of the Far Far Far Ultraviolet Catalog, we identified 34 complexes and complex fragments, ultimately discovering that the average radio sensitivity is approximately 10 millijansky. This sensitivity corresponds to a total radio power of 300,000 solar units. We also found that in over half of the complexes, hydrogen brightness exceeds the quiescent level by more than an order of magnitude, indicating the presence of radio-emitting outflows or other mechanisms generating radio power. Extracting table structure from documents is an intricate task due to the diverse designs and layouts of tables. The recent advancements in deep learning techniques have led to increased interest in addressing this challenge. Traditional object detection methods focused on tables tend to overlook relationships between table elements, relying solely on location and spatial data. As a result, table structure extraction capabilities remain limited. In response, researchers have suggested the use of Graph Neural Networks to capture interconnections between table elements. Recent developments in Graph Neural Networks have involved treating node and edge embeddings as intermediate steps in the learning process. Consequently, novel graph-based methods have been proposed that incorporate GNNs in the table extraction pipeline. However, current solutions have inherent drawbacks due to their reliance on pre-existing table bounding boxes, thus limiting their application in tasks such as table detection and extraction within unstructured documents. In order to address these shortcomings, we present TTENet, an end-to-end system utilizing GNNs to simultaneously detect and extract tables from document images. The integrated graph-based system combines table character detection with GNNs to capture the interconnections between table elements. In order to validate the superior performance of the proposed framework, we conducted comprehensive experiments on publicly available benchmark datasets, including Indextank and CEB, against state-of-the-art table detection and extraction methods.

In the Basek Group's 'Face' game, where players with varying levels of experience encounter unfamiliar objects (faces), it has been observed that more experienced players tend to make different decisions compared to less experienced players, leading to better outcomes for higher-level players, while lower-level players make decisions that lead to better prices, resulting in less profit for higher-level players.  By incorporating agent experience into the game model and treating the object (face) as an unfamiliar item, researchers were able to better explain the outcomes of the test results.  Notably, experiments conducted using the OpenAI Gym framework supported the model's predictions, demonstrating that the proposed method successfully captured the different decision-making strategies employed by players of various levels of experience, leading to an increase of up to 300% in profit for higher-level players.  By incorporating different decision-making inputs and experience levels, researchers were able to simulate diverse decision-making behaviors in complex systems, revealing how these interactions affect the overall outcome of the game, and leading to potential applications in more accurately modeling the behavior of systems composed of players with different levels of experience and exposure.

Predicting the spread of diseases is a crucial capability for many applications, yet it often relies on disease-specific data, making it inaccessible to the general public.  Many infectious disease outbreaks are initially monitored by early warning systems that rely on publicly available data, such as geographic location, population size, and time stamps.  A system capable of predicting disease spread based on this information would significantly reduce the time it takes to identify and respond to outbreaks.  Previous research, including our own, demonstrated that estimating the area affected by an outbreak improves predictions, but a comprehensive comparison with other existing methods was not made.  In this study, we further refined our previous approach by incorporating additional methods for modeling disease spread and comparing the results with other available techniques.  A specific focus was placed on predicting the spread of diseases in regions with limited data available.  Our improved predictive model incorporated additional factors, including movement rates and the rate at which new cases are reported, and demonstrated better performance than existing models, including an enhanced spatial model.  Furthermore, we compared the performance of machine learning algorithms, such as decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks, to see which could predict the spread of diseases reliably with limited data.  Ultimately, combining the enhanced spatial model with a neural network capable of handling missing information resulted in significantly better predictions than existing models, particularly when data is limited.

A proposed method involves developing static filters by marking key points on a graph to prevent unnecessary computations. The idea is that by simplifying matching processes, one can improve efficiency, effectiveness, and other aspects of template-based matching systems. The main goal is to minimize reductions in performance, which is an open problem in the field. The new approach aims to address this challenge by integrating techniques for identifying filtrable structures and static filter design. The results of the experiments show that static filters can significantly reduce false positives, maintain high levels of performance, and even improve scalability compared to previous methods.

We've proposed an in-depth mean-field simulation method based on an anisotropic, effectively non-rigid pendulum model to study one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensates in highly anisotropic traps. This model helps clarify the classically harmonic motion and motion patterns that result from the conversion of atoms to molecules and the emergence of instabilities in a quantum system. Additionally, we've used this model to enhance the accuracy of anisotropic Bose-Jensen models in studying dipolar condensates, such as bosons with dipolar interactions, and spinor condensates.

The versatility of Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) makes it a versatile method for solving complex fluid dynamics and multiphase flows. However, traditional SPH methods often struggle with high-density ratios, resulting in inaccuracies in phases, voids, and other issues. To address these problems, a multi-phase SPH model has been revised to incorporate a more advanced formulation that improves thermodynamic balance and density preservation. By integrating multiple equations of state, this revised model provides precise thermodynamic relationships. Furthermore, a new formulation incorporating multiple parameters and mixing energies accurately represents phase densities and energies. This revised model accurately simulates voids, phase separation, and other phenomena. To maintain stability, a new formulation incorporating multiple parameters and mixing energies has been developed, demonstrating promising results for modeling higher-density ratios. This revised model shows great promise for modeling a broad range of multiphase flows with various density ratios.

A well-known approach to clustering with the O(1) quantum query complexity is presented, specifically in the context of K-means clustering where the data points lie within a d-dimensional vector space. The quantum query complexity of this method is analyzed and it's discovered that the query complexity is sublinear but greater than O(1), with an upper bound of O(√(d/k)) and a lower bound of Ω(1/√(k*d)), indicating that the quantum algorithm's efficiency improves as the dataset size grows relative to the number of clusters. Additionally, performance comparison based on data from real-life applications shows that the quantum algorithm surpasses its classical counterparts for small to moderate datasets containing points; however, the benefits of using the quantum algorithm become questionable for very large datasets.

Utilizing neural speech synthesis models to generate speech with specific pitch trajectories is increasingly significant. Current methods for pitch-conditioned speech synthesis rely on a predetermined 2D latent space, but the inclusion of the pitch attribute in the latent code leads to significant optimization difficulty and restricted 2D space coverage. In an effort to circumvent these difficulties, our proposed framework shifts the optimization burden from the latent code to the speech input frame representations and introduces the 1D augmented pitch vector that corresponds to a variable number of pitch parameters. Beyond incorporating the pitch augmentation, our proposed approach leverages extensive pitch-augmented training datasets to refine the pitch controllability of the neural speech synthesis models. We develop and utilize a novel 2D U-Net architecture, named the Vector-Vector Interspeech (VVI) approach, for pitch-synthesis that utilizes the modified latent space and augmented pitch frame vectors. The superiority of our proposed model is demonstrated through subjective and objective assessments on the TTS system. Moreover, our TTS framework is utilized in a real-world application to develop the VeraTTS system, an open-access, high-quality, multi-format, and customizable Czech TTS. The model is accessible at https://github.com/tensorflow-community/tf-VeraTTS.

To tackle this, we aim to develop object-centric reasoning that focuses on the characteristics of each object rather than just the scene as a whole, and to achieve this, we develop a new method that teaches a model to compare and contrast objects across multiple videos and scenes. A well-established tool for simulating charged-current Drell-Yan observables, based on a simplified Standard Model framework, has been examined to see if it matches the actual data from the DeepInelastic Scattering experiments. The tool, called CC-FeynDy1, has its underlying particle distribution tweaked in various ways to mimic different scenarios. The comparison between the simulated results and the actual data found a significant mismatch in one particular measurement - how different-particle-pairs-are-moved based on their speed. The tool's settings were such that about 30% of its predictions conflicted with the actual data when considering speed as the variable, which is known as a 2σ discrepancy. However, it's worth noting that this tool is still being fine-tuned.

This study examines the user experience of operating Telepresence Robots and presents the findings from a study conducted with navigation and visual interaction. The data collected through interviews with 11 users revealed that users distinguish between the visual and navigation aspects of their experience, and that these aspects are perceived as contributing to overall satisfaction differently. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of usability in visual interaction and suggests that navigation design is more forgiving. The study's findings have significant practical implications for the design of Telepresence Robots, and serve as a foundation for further research and development in this emerging field.

Hierarchical models are typically used to analyze patterns in data, establishing links between variables at different levels of organization. We have developed new hierarchical models to investigate the responses of two model algae, Nannochloropsis salina and Nannochlorophysis polyspora, to nitrogen and phosphorus in their growth environments. Our models successfully captured the nutritional limitations on these algae's growth rates. The precise nitrogen levels even affected the size of individual cells, while phosphorus levels primarily impacted the algae's reproductive potential. Our findings demonstrate that hierarchical models can serve as a valuable tool for understanding and predicting the complex behaviors of microalgal populations.

Mafia is a multi-round online text-based game involving detection versus deception, attracting significant global attention with millions of players. Through extensive analysis based on extensive simulations, our findings reveal the significance of player screening capabilities, deception possible, and screening effectiveness in shaping game dynamics and outcomes. Further investigation focuses on verification quality and the minimum requirement needed to guarantee victory or defeat for either group. Moreover, our research shows that the implications of these findings can be applied to support game participants through real-time data visualization and decision-making recommendations provided to players.

The discovery of numerous transiting hot jupiters and their host stars through the TESS and Kepler missions has laid out key mass data that can be utilized to examine the dynamics of gas giant planetary formation. A recent study presents a new theoretical model to explain the accumulation of massive gas giants during planetary accretion within a protoplanetary disk. This model attributes planetary mass growth to the rapid convergence of accretion streams originating from the protoplanet's solid core and disk material, either due to the perturbation caused by the growing protoplanet and/or secondary mass accumulation mechanisms. We simulate this process through a set of mathematical equations that model the dynamics of a protoplanet accreting gas and dust, making key assumptions about the core mass and disk conditions. We investigate the impact of varying disk radius, core mass, and disk gas surface density on the final mass of planets accreting in this manner, finding notable similarities with the observed mass distribution of hot jupiters. Our model also considers the potential influence of disk perturbations, showing that planetary migration can lead to the delivery of planets to the "hot zone" around their host star, aligning with observed trends in data. Finally, our model serves as a foundation for future investigations into the relationship between the formation of massive planets, their migration, and their ultimate placement in the host star's "hot zone".

mechanism was primarily responsible for the observed electronic transport, particularly
when the carbon nanotube film was explored in both the parallel and perpendicular
