The results of this comparison indicate that in comparison to robots with discrete elements or those designed to mimic invertebrate animals with discrete external features, animals possessing continuous external features are able to exert more force and are less likely to fail due to external damage and are less prone to internal damage. Moreover, the continuum mechanics characteristics of these animals enable their external features to more effectively resist external forces. Notably, the continuum mechanics characteristics of these animals are found to more effectively resist external forces when the forces in question are perpendicular to the surface of the external features. This is due in part to a unique phenomenon known as the "torsional buckling phenomenon" which has been identified in the study and is

A unique feature of Siegel-Jacobi upper half-plane complex structure is that it allows for a specific connection between left-invariant metrics on the Jacobi group and Kähler balanced metrics. This relationship provides an efficient method for identifying metrics on the Jacobi group that are Kähler balanced, which in turn enables us to compute their associated Einstein metrics. This computation reveals that metrics on the Jacobi group that are Kähler balanced and Einstein can be divided into three distinct categories, each corresponding to a different value of Einstein constants.

In the MIMEDOC system, we apply a model-agnostic technique to break down intricate assertions into more manageable components for fact verification. By dividing the task among multiple model architectures, each handles a simpler assertion, we achieve improved performance and robustness. Experimental outcomes on the MIMEDOC and FEVER benchmarks show that the system performs competitively with the current state-of-the-art while functioning in the absence of a target dataset. Furthermore, the system's adaptive nature allows it to effectively deal with both known and unknown types of assertions without the need for additional training or fine-tuning.

Several deep learning-based generative models have gained popularity in recent years, with WGAN and its variations particularly valued for their performance and training stability. A crucial aspect of these models is their ability to receive feedback from the environment through a critic, unlike other generative models that rely on predefined parameters. Currently, the reliance on large, high-quality annotated datasets greatly limitations the applicability of these models. In an effort to overcome this constraint, we are proposing an innovative approach that allows these models to adapt and improve based on feedback received from the environment during the generation process. This approach in essence mimics behavioristic learning methods. Initially, our model uses random inputs to stimulate the environment, generating necessary data for its training. Following that, the model utilizes this learned knowledge to produce new samples, along with corresponding responses from the environment that are incorporated into the training. This cycle repeats, with the model continually refining its generative capabilities based on feedback. In addition to our theoretical findings, our experimental results validate the efficiency of our approach in generating high-quality data, with a notable example being our use of this model to generate simple commands for robotic arms in a random environment. This command generation experiment in particular achieved similar levels of efficiency and performance as traditionally supervised methods.

We present two innovative techniques derived from slice sampling algorithms that offer enhanced performance. Our proposals include hit-and-run slice sampling, utilizing its rapid acceptance rate to sample efficiently, and whitened slice sampling, which includes a hit-and-run stage and a Gaussian transformed stage within a single iteration. We rigorously demonstrate the geometric properties of these algorithms as variants of slice sampling, ensuring their target distributions are precisely met. We also provide theoretical justifications for the superior efficiency of these algorithms by analyzing their effective sample sizes. Empirical evaluations on real datasets confirm the superior performance of our algorithms when compared to slice sampling, with further findings indicating that hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling have similar efficiency gains but differ slightly in their operational complexity.

In a labeled graph where distances can be calculated using an integer metric, a watchdog system assigns an extra label to edges connecting two vertices that are far away from being nearby after one failure has occurred. This setup provides an alternative method for determining the maximum number of edges between two vertices in a graph. This number is referred to as the watchdog distance and is capable of being bounded by the unlabeled distance in a graph, excluding the effect of single vertex failure in a specific type of graph called a Vizeline graph. Further exploration into the properties of watchdog distance label led to the discovery that it can be further bounded by the unlabeled distance in a tree graph. This particular bound has further implications in the context of an existing problem which seeks to determine the maximum number of edges between two vertices in a tree graph. This problem which was previously solved using the inequality |d(u,v) - d'(u,v)| <= 2, is capable of further tightening this existing inequality to |d(u,v) - d'(u,v)| <= 1.

To analyze the dissipative first-order phase transition in a 1D Bose-Hubbard model driven by dissipation, researchers used a variational method to calculate the many-body out-of-phase quantum correlation function. It was found that the Fourier transforms of these correlations reveal the features of the transition, including the emergence of peaks and gaps indicative of bound states, mini-gaps related to quasi-dissipative excitations, and the movement of the quasi-condensate peak in response to varying bath temperatures. These predictions were confirmed by numerical simulations based on the time-dependent perturbation theory. These findings offer a new method for predicting peak positions and examining the transition dynamics.

We establish sufficient conditions for the solvability of the Dirichlet problem associated with linear elliptic equations in specific domains. Our criteria rely on the smoothness of the domain's boundary and the coefficients of the equation, allowing us to establish an estimate of the error in the solution approximated by numerical methods. This investigation broadens the scope of an earlier finding by Agoshto, see http://arxiv.org/9604013. While the original study focused on inner domains, our work extends the results to the case where the equation has a source term and is solved in an exterior domain.

Our approach employs Gaussian Processes to achieve accurate separation of brain components in medical imaging, such as the deep grey of the brain, in HDA11 datasets. We combine HDA11 brain images with a synthetic label image, utilizing a Gaussian Processes regression model to segment the brain into its respective tissues. Furthermore, the segmentation outcomes demonstrate that our method produces quantitative results on par with the manually assigned labels of the HDA11 dataset, thereby validating our method's efficacy. We ultimately demonstrate that our approach yields promising outcomes for future research directions, including partial volume estimation of the separated brain components. On top of that, our method has potential applications in several domains, such as neuroimaging, medical imaging and computer assisted surgery, contributing to a greater understanding of brain abnormalities or diseases and their potential impacts.

We explore the emergence of Bose-Einstein condensation in a one-dimensional Bose gas under both thermal dissipation and periodic driving. When the system is heated through time-dependent processes, it may reach a higher equilibrium temperature than when heated through thermal means alone. This enhanced heating can aid in the rapid formation of a condensate, while also influencing it in complex ways. Our study examines how varying parameters such as dissipation and modulation may either facilitate or impede the emergence of a condensed phase. We also outline a general method for analyzing many-body effects in systems driven out of equilibrium, illustrating its relevance in the context of Bose-Einstein condensation phenomena.

Given a group of convex functions $F$, we establish the relationship between $F$ and the space of strictly convex and smooth functions. We start with a specific case where $F$ only consists of convex functions with a H\"older exponent $\alpha$ greater than $\frac{1}{3}$, in which scenario, functions in $F$ are classified as $W^{1,2}$.

For a broader scenario where $F$ comprises convex functions with an arbitrary H\"older exponent $\alpha$ greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, we employ the concept of $\mathscr{C}$ and its partial ordering to establish the relationship between $F$ and the space of strictly convex and smooth functions. We demonstrate that functions in $F$ are classified as $W^{1,p}$ for $p$ greater than 2, under the condition that $\alpha$ is greater than $\frac{2}{p}$. This relationship is established through the Lebesgue $p$-energy integral of the second order derivative of a function, along with its representation using the Volterra type integral equations.

Researchers examine how photodetection impacts the performance of optical clocks based on two-level quantum systems, and find that this impact can enhance clock stability in specific scenarios. A model incorporating initial photon correlations and noise in a laser drive field improves explanations of optical spectra in transition-array clocks. Furthermore, the model increases our understanding of optical clock transitions, providing precise descriptions of X-ray fluorescence spectra. The results imply that photodetection can potentially augment the limitations of two-level transition clocks.

In recent years, the concept of survivability in energy-aware (EFES) networks has gained attention, where the aim is to not only create redundant paths but also minimize energy usage during network failures. Nevertheless, the problem of optimizing EFES networks with diverse energy sources and failure costs remains unsolved. In this research, we introduce the Heuristic Energy-Failure Aware Source routing (HFES) algorithm to tackle the problem of jointly optimizing energy consumption and path redundancy. Furthermore, we evaluate HFES in comparison to existing solutions by conducting simulations to assess its performance in various failure scenarios. Interestingly, the simulation outcomes indicate that HFES exhibits similar reliability levels as energy-aware source routing (EFES) but achieves a 27% reduction in energy consumption as observed in Paris and US-LAN scenarios.

In this study, we investigate the mechanisms underlying self-supervised image retrieval and attribute prediction. Our analysis of how loss gradients change and influence the classification boundary in high-dimensional space reveals that ranking losses in Sinkhorn triplet loss leads to inconsistent optimization priorities. To address this, we introduce a new method that separates and optimizes gradient components for each class individually, prioritizing different loss gradients. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, as images reconstructed based on specific attributes lead to better performance on retrieval and attribute prediction tasks. Specifically, we notice a significant 15% improvement in top-1 accuracy for attribute prediction and a 15% improvement in mean recall at 5 for image retrieval tasks, with reconstruction time remaining similar or slightly longer on average.

This study investigates the single-letter characterization of erasure correction codes implemented using tensor networks, where each code consists of a single tensor type and two network structures - the random-coupled lattice and the random-coupled hypercube. These tensor networks represent the most basic type of quantum error-correction codes and are used in various applications. We prove that any tensor network associated with the erasure correction code has a specific contraction value, and its underlying tensor's Schur multipliers must meet particular criteria. We derive this conclusion by utilizing graphical representation and then demonstrate the streamlined results apply to hybrid networks, ensuring tensor networks corresponding to constant-rate erasure codes fall into two distinct categories, and we provide examples of such networks.

Radio filaments detected through absorption against the background radiation emit magnetized radio waves. Although the mechanisms behind their formation and fragmentation remain uncertain, it is suggested that turbulence and instability play significant roles. To understand these processes, 3D simulations of active galactic nuclei and galaxy interactions have been used, allowing for the creation of magnetized radio waves and the emission of radio filaments. These simulations have revealed the development of filamentation due to magnetized turbulence and the compression of dense regions. It is suggested that filamentation arises from density or current fluctuations, and the characteristics of the resulting radio waves are compared against observations. These properties include the emission of radio waves, the length of the filaments, and the compression of magnetic fields. While some aspects of the simulations match the data, there is still a discrepancy in terms of the length-to-width ratio.

The vast potential of renewable energy sources currently goes unfulfilled due to ineffectiveness in management and integration with existing power grids. As a result, novel power grid architectures are being developed to incorporate distributed energy resources (DERs) such as solar panels and wind turbines. In these emerging grids, innovative control strategies are needed to coordinate DERs and optimize their integration with power grids, thereby reducing energy losses and ensuring smooth grid operations. This research focuses on novel control techniques for unknown non-linear systems such as power grids, being explored as solutions to DER integration challenges. Two primary control methods - optimal control and learning-based control - are examined for their efficiency in managing unknown non-linear systems. A multi-objective control framework is also presented, comprising leader-follower control and multi-objective optimization, which outperforms other methods in terms of economic efficiency and reliability. This control strategy is particularly useful for new grid infrastructure, such as smart grids and microgrids, which are designed to optimize grid operations and energy efficiency. In situations of grid failure or uncertain external influences, these control strategies can enable the seamless operation of power grids and the optimal integration of DERs.

We explore a changed dynamic of the adversarial bandit problem, in which we have predetermined information about the performance of the optimal choice (denoted as $\tilde{v}_1$). It's known that delays and losses associated with the optimal choice follow a specific pattern and have upper limits ($d_{\mathcal{D}}$ and $L_{\mathcal{D}}$ respectively). Our investigation focuses on algorithms and their effects in this altered context, and the key findings reveal that when delays and losses have similar upper limits, the impact of regret decreases in the number of rounds ($K$), and increases linearly with any variation in limits. A set of concrete examples illustrate the changes in bandit problems where the delay or loss limits are significantly different. Furthermore, when the difference between delays of the first and second choices is significantly larger than the difference in losses, the regret bound decreases significantly ($\tilde{O}((d_{\mathcal{D}}^2\cdot L_{\mathcal{D}}/d_{\mathcal{D}}(v_2-v_1))K^{3/4})$), and it's shown that this scenario is an instance of a new class of problems with varying functions whose regret bounds decrease significantly.

Recently, significant advances have been made in text-generation for dialogue, 
yet the underlying theories driving this progress are still developing. 
This study introduces a new theoretical framework for dialogue text-generation. 
By building on established theories from cognitive science and computer science, 
we create a two-stage approach to dialogue simulation that prioritizes meaning and 
expression respectively, thereby enhancing the quality and coherence of generated 
dialogues. Through evaluations on widely used datasets (MultiWOZ 2.0, 2.1, 
2.2, and WoW2), we demonstrate the significant improvements achieved by our model 
over state-of-the-art and baseline models in dialogue quality, lexical diversity, 
and dialogues speech naturalness, while also ensuring the generated dialogues are 
as realistic as human conversations in terms of meaning and structure.

Born out of the quantum theory of strong interactions known as quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the study of strong-interaction matter, also called hadrons, has become the primary focus of three-dimensional lattice QCD. The numerical implementation of lattice QCD has significantly contributed to its development and has been instrumental in its standardization as a fundamental theory of strong interactions. Recent advances in processing capabilities have favorably impacted the computational efficiency of lattice QCD. The forthcoming exascale computing era, along with the re-evaluation of study priorities by the international research community, necessitates a comprehensive review of contemporary challenges in lattice QCD computations. This report will examine the current state of lattice QCD computations and the challenges it faces across various topics, including the characteristics and dynamics of massless hadrons, quark and gluon dynamics at high energy densities, and the characteristics and dynamics of complex strongly-interacting matter in the most extreme conditions of energy density. The report will also outline the specifications for computing hardware and software required to address these challenges, thereby guiding future developments in the development and deployment of computing hardware and software.

The dynamics of offshore wind turbines are influenced primarily by water currents, with turbulence and irregular waves adding stochastic elements that greatly vary depending on sea state conditions. These stochastic changes impact the turbines' load calculations, with fluctuations often disregarded in predictive modeling for stationary conditions. However, researchers at Delft University of Technology have developed a novel method using state augmentation and accounting for the turbines' motion to create models capable of handling the turbines' stochastic variability. In this study, the researchers applied this new model-based approach to simulate the motion of offshore wind turbines and assessed the impact of stochastic currents on their physical loads. Results from the study confirmed that even during steady wind conditions, stochastic currents can cause significant variability in turbines, with an overall standard deviation of load factors ranging from 2.5% to 15%, with corresponding standard deviations for other load factors ranging from 5% to 34%. These findings suggest that incorporating stochastic models into offshore wind turbine design and analysis could provide more accurate and reliable results, particularly in coastal environments subject to high sea state conditions.

The rapid assessment of public sentiment and data generation following a disaster are crucial for informing crisis management decisions, enabling officials to make more accurate predictions and target specific intervention areas. This process can be effectively achieved by leveraging natural language processing techniques to analyze and quantify the emotions expressed by people affected by the disaster. Twitter, as a popular social media platform, is particularly useful for monitoring and analyzing public sentiment after a disaster has occurred. It is characterized by users including personal accounts of the incident, along with their opinions and emotions. This research involves collecting and processing tweets related to the Kerala floods in 2018, utilizing both text mining and machine learning algorithms to classify and quantify the emotions expressed in the tweets. Additionally, the relevance of words and phrases in the context of the disaster was also identified using text mining techniques.

A novel approach has been devised to calculate the Rr-nilpotency degree of any group and determine whether it is finite. Furthermore, a generalised formula was developed for Fr-nilpotent groups, enabling the identification of their nilpotency class and order. This concept can be applied to finite nilpotent groups, especially those that are also solvable groups, allowing for the identification of their nilpotency class and order in a more efficient manner than previously possible.

To link the microscopic processes behind ultrafast optical phenomena, a new approach is employed to analyze experimental data from ultrafast and dynamic modulation experiments by reversing the equations that describe the samples' interaction with light. We address noise issues that arise in such experiments by enhancing the new method's ability to accurately recover the key physical parameters. Several types of noise are identified, and the effectiveness of the new approach in overcoming the resulting challenges is demonstrated. Notably, the method can determine important physical parameters like the electron temperature and bandwidth of energy distribution without relying on the samples' absorption coefficients. We apply the new approach to simulate results obtained from experimental data under various types of noise, demonstrating its high accuracy and robustness. Additionally, the method is found to be insensitive to errors in the simulation domain but sensitive to those in the range of possible energy values. This research is particularly relevant to the study of ultrafast and dynamic modulation experiments where the electron phase and modulation frequency are measured. It can also be applied to other types of experiments, such as those involving photoemission, absorption, and scattering.

The growing number of sensors on vehicles poses complex scenario recognition and tracking challenges. We introduce an innovative system to address this issue. It utilizes an advanced tracker to identify and analyze driving scenarios from a combination of forward-facing and rear-facing cameras. The tracker, based on the Joint Probabilistic Data Association method, is capable of handling multiple targets and CamShift localization, enabling high robustness. We implemented a scenario analysis system, integrating the tracker and deep learning-based object detection and classification, as well as a driving situation recognition model supported by manually annotated data. With this expertise, we conducted a scenario recognition evaluation and achieved a $91\%$ high-recall rate at a $50\%$ false positive rate.

We've analyzed the bounded real type in Conformal Field Theory and found a related semi-infinite chain model where we can calculate a reflected entropy directly. By extending the real type in Boundary Conformal Field Theory and finding associated semi-infinite chain models for each real type, we now see a universal behavior of the Markov gap in some specific cases, such as in real types associated with semi-simple loops and some double copy scenarios. This reflected entropy also displays a non-linear behavior with the central charge for a real type in a specific superconformal field theory, contrasting with Dykin polynomials' linear behavior.

In time-dislatic systems with high-dimension channels, traditional channel estimation methods often fall short due to the requirements for cyclic prefix and multilayer neural networks being too demanding. The potential of enhanced extreme learning machines (ELMs) with sparse hidden layers in improving channel estimation has been identified, along with the need for further research into how ELMs learn from noisy data. To address this, a new ELM-based learning scheme is presented, aiming to minimize the reconstruction error of the samples and addressing the problem of sparse high-dimensional tensor recovery from noisy data. The improved algorithm optimizes signal reconstruction and has been proven to provide accurate estimates of time-dislatic channels, even in the presence of hardware imperfections and missing cyclic prefix data. The results from numerical simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, estimating various types of time-dislatic channels more accurately than other approaches.

It is widely accepted that the core of quantum mechanics consists of three principles established by von Neumann, centred around measurement operations. One key aspect of these measurements is the restriction to projective sets of vectors. However, our investigation reveals a set of non-projective vector measures that, when applied to observables with continuous spectra, produce results identical to those obtained from projective measurements. These results are then extended to the case of observables with degenerate spectra. Additionally, an important theorem related to ergodicity is proved, providing evidence that the use of non-projective measures does not lead to inconsistencies within the standard framework of quantum mechanics. Lastly, an example is constructed to demonstrate a non-ergodicity theorem for measures on compact groups, implying that non-projective measures can reproduce outcomes from projective measurements in certain contexts.

Abelian Lefshetz pencils have eminated with rigidity – a form of stability that applies to all G_2-instants and K3 surfaces. Abelian varieties have been stable for so long they've become the norm, thus rigidity holds for any non-abelian compact complex structure on a K3 surface and for all G_2-instants. Given that hyper-elastic invariants distinguish non-abelian and abelian varieties, this means a fixed point theorem holds for all non-abelian structures - they can't all become abelian. 

This result has further implications as it imply the Berndt-Lutz 137-invariant can't distinguish between non-abelian and abelian structures, although it can tell an instantanous G_2 structure from an abelian one if the latter isn't elliptic. 

This result has also led to a conclusion that certain divisors on the moduli space of non-abelian compact structures are 'inextensible', with 'length' proportional to 2^18, and 'direction' at any point - an 'anti-elliptic' direction. 

This result has also lead to a conclusion that 'length-reduction' theorems apply to non-abelian structures, with 'length' reduced by at least an order of 2 when moved under 'optical' directions.

The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted widespread adoption of contact tracing technologies, which inherently collect personal data and sometimes introduce issues with government involvement in mass surveillance. Despite initial goals to control the virus spread, there's growing concern about the long-term impact on individual privacy and civil liberties, as these technologies become entrenched in daily life. By referring to the potential as a form of 'technological trespass' on civil liberties, our study explores the unintended consequences of contact tracing technologies and how they infiltrate individuals' lives beyond the pandemic's end. Through a conceptual framework and real-world examples in the US and globally, our analysis showcases how contact tracing technologies can lead to increased government access to personal data, as these systems often adopt law enforcement functions and become embedded in broader government surveillance systems. Moreover, the pandemic has accelerated the integration of location data and data analytics into everyday life, making it more likely for contact tracing technologies and associated data infrastructure to be repurposed for other government uses. Ultimately, the data collected during the pandemic could set a precedent for the use of location data and data analytics in other crises or contexts, potentially eroding individuals' privacy and civil liberties.

The emergence of quantum entities as localized objects remains unexplained from a fundamental theoretical perspective.  The interaction or entanglement between subsystems doesn't cause decoherence, but rather stimulates it.  When boundaries are set, 'localization in a specific place' becomes clear, but what place, exactly, is meant remains unclear.  We suggest that the boundaries of a localized system are defined by the point at which environmental correlations surpass intrinsic correlations, an event that occurs at the decoherence time and is associated with memory loss.  When intrinsic correlations surpass environmental correlations, it signals the beginning of coherence; this event marks the location of 'intrinsic localization.'  In theory, the 'place' could be either the location of environmental correlations or intrinsic localization, especially in the event of 'loose binding.'  The significance of localization lies not only in the location, but also in the difference between decoherence and coherence - two states that, although easily confused, have distinct implications and cannot be interchanged.  Following interaction, the localization of one entity is investigated while leaving the other as part of the environment, an approach that provides a comprehensive understanding of quantum exchange and dependence.

Translating high-level programming constructs into machine code is crucial for verifying program correctness. A proposed method translates high-level constructs, represented as expressions in beta normal form, into G-machine code using higher-order logic. This translation is carried out by expressing it as a set of rewrite rules in the logic, which can then be proven sound using the logic's built-in inference mechanism. Additionally, the method translates beta reduction with the G-machine code, resulting in an unoptimized translation that facilitates verification. A key benefit of this approach is that it allows for easy modification and verification of translations, which can be seen in the case of translating expressions containing let-bindings into G-machine code.

Plants generating significant interest due to their remarkable seed capsules, are examined through phylogenetic investigations. Notably, a recent study identified a previously unknown species of Iochroma, known as Iochroma purpureomagellanicum. This new species, endemic to Chile's Magellanic region, is characterized by remarkable flower arrangements and seed capsule shapes. Purpureomagellanicum is found to be distinct from other Iochroma species and is culturally significant to the local community. Phylogenetic analyses, incorporating DNA data from 64 specimens across 17 species, revealed that I. purpureomagellanicum is most closely related to I. albobrunneum. This relationship is further supported by geographic and phylogenetic distances. Additionally, a new combination of Solanum speciosum subsp. speciosum is proposed for taxa previously classified by Hombrchen et al. in 2021.

We start with a well-known integral kernel associated with Ramanujan's identity and create a generalized integral kernel that incorporates the Hurwitz zeta function. Additionally, we include discussions of convergent and divergent terms in the series expansion of the generalized integral kernel.

In relation to $T$-equivariant elliptic cohomology, we investigate specific sixfold extensions of elliptic curves equipped with admissible actions of the torus $T$. These extensions arise from a particular form of generalized equivariant cohomology theory known as elliptic cohomology, which includes notable subcases involving singular tori and the Weyl group ring of a complex Lie group. These subcases coincide with existing results in the field, demonstrating the theory's effectiveness and accuracy.

In various fields like computer graphics, engineering, and archaeology, research involves analyzing complex 3D geometric shapes. Effective data analysis relies on suitable mathematical approaches, and lately, machine learning has shown promising applications in understanding geometric patterns and structures. Most current machine learning-based work relies on supervised learning, which requires labeled data, whereas in many real-world scenarios, labeling data is costly or even impossible. Focusing on such challenges, this paper explores unsupervised learning techniques for analyzing 3D geometric shapes. We propose a collection of features and a probabilistic model that can detect similar structures within a dataset. Our approach does not assume knowledge of the underlying data organization or the type of 3D entity studied. To validate our method, we applied it to three distinct datasets, each representing distinct real-world applications. Our method successfully identified meaningful clusters in these datasets, revealing useful insights that could have been obtained only through intensive human annotation in a supervised learning setting.

To compare $\J/\psi$ and $\chi_{cJ}$ productions from B decays, which have distinct kinematic distributions, researchers utilize the LHCb experiment's data on $\chi_{cJ}$ and J/$\psi$ particles that resulted from the interaction of B bars with X particles, specifically $\eta_c$ or $\chi_{cJ}$, which are followed by the B X process. It's noted that the ratio of these two distributions provides insight into $\J/\psi$ and $\eta_c$ or $\chi_{cJ}$ mass relationships. Consequently, the distributions of these three quark states, which differ by approximately 600 MeV, can be studied in a comparable manner. Furthermore, the effect of the $\eta_c$ to hadrons process's theta parameter, which varies between 0.6 and 1 for J/$\psi$ + $\eta_c$ and J/$\psi$ + $\chi_{cJ}$, is revealed.

In our study of the security of Signal PINs, which are not encrypted, for the purposes of emergency access, we discovered that the majority of our study group members were unaware that their Signal PINs served an emergency access purpose. This lack of understanding affected their behavior, causing simple and easy-to-guess numbers to be assigned as PINs, rather than generating new complex ones. This discovery highlights the inherent vulnerability of using the same encryption key for multiple purposes without re-generating new keys for different applications, which can compromise security. Furthermore, our research revealed that providing users with clear information about the dual use of their encryption key for emergency access can improve PIN complexity.

The rate of solar energy production is changing rapidly and increasingly being used worldwide, resulting in more installations and diverse operational profiles that need to be accounted for in power production calculations. In situations like these, the one-second time frame is often insufficient, and recordings are typically gathered in longer intervals such as 10-minute or 15-minute blocks. The solar energy industry therefore faces a computational challenge involving integrals that require solving over extended periods. The solar-weighted quadrature method presents itself as an attractive solution, particularly when solar applications are involved, as it offers enhanced accuracy even with fewer evaluation points. The one-fold and two-fold versions of this method can be thought of as quadrature rules with one and two evaluations per time step, respectively. Considering typical characteristics of solar installations, it's clear that the one-fold rule is more suitable in high-convergence zones and the two-fold rule in low-convergence zones. Notably, the two-fold rule requires only two functional evaluations per time step, in contrast to the standard quadrature method's need for adjacent evaluations. However, this method also necessitates an additional computational step to resolve the resulting system of equations. A crucial decision when implementing the two-fold rule is how to choose the weights in such a way that the modified quadrature formula accurately approximates the given solar-based functional. A crucial aspect of this modification is the matrix involved in the weight calculation - a study was conducted to examine this aspect, focusing specifically on the matrix's inverse. The study's findings

The ViViT virtualizer enables efficient evaluation of directional derivatives and eigenvalues during neural network training, utilizing a novel approach that approximates gradients and Hessian tensors through a mathematical transformation of the standard generator output. This utilization minimizes the need for computational projections, thereby improving scalability compared to existing virtualizer methods. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the ViViT virtualizer in machine learning applications, particularly in generating adversarial samples and identifying mode information.

The role of Word Embeddings in Natural Language Processing is increasingly significant, with applications extending from text classification to machine translation. These embeddings can inadvertently capture biases present in the data used to create them; in this case, the bias is grammatical gender from 21st-century Spanish. We utilized the FastText library to create word embeddings, initially without addressing this bias, but also developed a method to neutralize it. Our experiments, conducted on two sets of English-based and multilingual embeddings, demonstrated that eliminating the bias led to improved embeddings, as measured by performance in two tasks - semantic similarity and syntactic analysis. The findings reveal that addressing the bias does not compromise the embeddings' usefulness and, in fact, enhances them.

Let G be a group that acts continuously on a compact space X. Define R(G, X) as the space of G-invariant rational functions on homomorphisms from G to compact Lie groups. For certain actions exhibiting certain patterns, we demonstrate that elements generating infinite sequences in specific directions within R(G, X) correspond to bounded distances, provided G is not virtually nilpotent. This implies that G's action on its space of characters produces complex patterns, distinct from the toroidal dynamics discussed earlier. Additionally, we discuss analogs of this result that apply to a broader class of linear groups.

Human pose estimation, a fundamental task in computer vision, has been enhanced by large-scale pose databases that offer extensive annotations and training data, notably including the MPII Multi-Part Human Pose Database. However, the database's complexity hindered efforts to develop accurate pose estimation models. Our work addresses this challenge by introducing a novel two-stage approach to improve pose estimation. First, we utilize low-resolution images to train a model that detects body parts and corresponds them to the actual body pose. This is achieved through the development of the Low-RSNA model. Second, we employ a set of predefined body poses as reference to establish pose dependencies and accurately determine the pose pose from the low-resolution model. Our results demonstrate the Low-RSNA model to be the top-performing method on the MPII database, outperforming existing baselines by a significant margin. Additionally, we show that the Low-RSNA model performs equally well in real-world scenarios to the state-of-the-art methods. The development of the Low-RSNA model was initially presented in its original form in arXiv:1605.03168, where it was trained using the full resolution images, and we now present an improved variant that benefits from the advantages of the image down-sampling.

This paper delves into predicting the duration of trips in real-world traffic conditions. We assembled a massive dataset of 75 million trips derived from GPS data and set out to compare the efficiency of travel time estimation techniques based on road maps versus those utilizing graph neural networks. Our machine learning approach involves training a gradient boosting decision tree model on graph features, a conventional method often employed in predictive modeling. Additionally, we developed an ensemble graph neural network model to investigate the potential of this deeper learning approach. Our results indicate that the graph-neural-network-based solution surpasses the baseline gradient boosting decision tree model by approximately 13%, achieving a mean absolute percentage error of 8.5% for the ensemble method and 21.9% for the baseline model. Since GPS data on shorter routes may be scarce due to less data coverage, we addressed this challenge by using road map data to create mock GPS data with shorter routes, thereby improving the baseline model's performance by 52% and the ensemble model's by 13%. We believe these findings hold significant value for the development of real-time traffic navigation systems.

Machine learning model evaluations often focus on predicting outcomes rather than evaluating the actions taken as a result. As automated decision systems become more prevalent in society-critical settings, there's a growing need to assess counterfactual fairness by identifying scenarios where individual-specific interventions could lead to disparate outcomes, even if the underlying factors differ. Existing methods for causal inference can help address this challenge by quantifying how interventions might have been the primary drivers of outcomes. In this paper, we demonstrate the applicability of these methods to evaluate counterfactual fairness in binary classification problems by introducing a new approach that leverages data-driven representations and uses neural networks to approximate counterfactual exposure probabilities and disparate outcome probabilities. This allows us to quantify and visualize interventions where black individuals might have attended a different school due to discriminatory automated admissions. Our proposed method serves as a foundation for future research, serving as a practical example of how causal inference methods can be applied to enhance the fairness of machine learning models, especially in systems such as automated admissions.

Next-generation radio telescopes, such as the Square Kilometer Array, will produce vast amounts of data, necessitating on-site processing to tap into its full potential.  We demonstrate the efficacy of the Maximum Signal-to-Noise Ratio (MaxSiNoise) method for detecting sources in real-time, comparing its results to established approaches and demonstrating its superiority by producing cleaner images with fewer artifacts, particularly in the context of single-plateau taper laws.

Metaphotonics incorporates light-matter interactions that go beyond traditional photonic research. Recent advancements have demonstrated the simultaneous induction of electric and magnetic resonances, opening metaphotonics. Our study presents an approach to analyze and model metaphotonics using a precise mathematical framework for describing how light interacts with matter that incorporates both electromagnetic theory and the methods used to study light propagation. This unified framework allows us to re-examine and expand upon the principles of metaphotonics, providing a comprehensive and consistent approach to metaphotonics and photonic research. Our investigation reveals the essential role of Mie interactions in metaphotonics and how Induced Mie interactions can be utilized in applications where light-matter interactions are weak. This understanding enables the development of methodologies to decode metaphotonics' behavior and enhance Induced Mie interactions. Furthermore, our study showcases the versatility and power of metaphotonics by transforming traditional photonic research in crystal and cavity environments.

The film industry's revenue forecast relies heavily on understanding a movie's "star power," as indicated by box office results of recent movies. While box office data analysis provides insight into an actor's popularity, it is limited to offering a snapshot in time. In contrast, text analysis allows for a more nuanced understanding of an actor's image and potential appeal. By applying natural language techniques to script summaries and analyzing the language used in film credits, our research can predict a movie's revenue potential based on the collective appeal of its starring cast. We have created a system that extracts and quantifies an actor's representation in a movie script, enabling the comparison of different films featuring the same actor and estimating their unique contribution to the movie's commercial success. In a study involving 77 actors, our research showed that there is a significant correlation between an actor's representation and box office performance. By analyzing the language patterns associated with successful actors, our research revealed distinct stylistic traits, which are consistent across different datasets. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that these representation metrics can be further refined by incorporating metadata such as film genre, director, and actor demographics, further improving the accuracy of revenue predictions.

In analyzing the stability of power networks, researchers often focus on small-signal stability through linear analysis. Utilizing both graph theoretical methods and second-order linear systems, this study examines the impact of secondary frequency control on node response within power grids. By investigating voltage and frequency dynamics separately, the results reveal that secondary frequency control primarily influences small-signal stability in secondary circuits, but has limited effect on node stability. Furthermore, the study provides design guidelines for secondary frequency control based on nodal invariant curves, and shows how graph theoretical properties intersect with power network stability. Ultimately, the results challenge the traditional design approach for control systems, suggesting that separation of functions may not always be desirable.

This study focuses on linked intelligent systems, encompassing both a lower-level physical structure and an upper-level control system. We introduce a module-based framework that enables the analysis of coupled systems comprising modules arranged in a hierarchical and distributed manner. Our analysis examines the impact of interconnections on the dynamic behavior of individual modules and the entire system. According to the results, the module-level system can be divided into distinct subsystems, with each module potentially exhibiting unique transient and stable behaviors. One such behavior is the appearance of oscillating patterns within the system. We also found that transient modules may exhibit stable, circular movement. Furthermore, the study reveals that a module can temporarily influence the behavior of other modules before returning to its initial state. Our results provide a better understanding of the dynamic interactions between modules within complex systems, which can aid in the design and operation of secure networks.

Blazars' high-energy emissions, especially in polarized forms, offer valuable insights into their complex interstellar and intergalactic environments. Recent breakthroughs in measuring magnetic fields using scattering effects against rotating dust clouds have boosted expectations for polarimetric observations of far-UV and X-ray emissions, particularly in galactic planes and near clusters. Given the narrow wavelength windows for these bands, extensive polarization surveys will be challenging to accomplish. To assess the prospects for detecting magnetic fields using scattering against rotating structures using X-ray polarimetry on Imerg class space missions, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the applicable sample. Our study expands upon previous findings regarding UV polarimetric missions, leveraging comprehensive blazar catalogs and accounting for the effects of Doppler shift, common redshift, and the orientation of spin axes. Estimated lower bounds for the scattering effect have been calculated for approximately 400,000 blazars, with the majority expected to exhibit magnetic field intensities above 3 nanotesla at redshifts above 0.5 or within 500 megaparsecs. Our study indicates that polarimetric X-ray observations on board future IMERG-class X-ray observatories hold great potential for detecting scattering effects against rotating structures, particularly at higher redshifts, where approximately 20,000 quasars could be studied if their spin-axis orientations were similar to their line-of-sight.

We explore the statistical features of model landscapes associated with quantum annealing by examining the eigenvalue spectra of Hessian matrices. These models correspond to random quadratic systems derived from generative adversarial networks, which exhibit either one-step or many-step replica-symmetry-broken transition modes, depending on the condition of the SQUID parameter. Our analysis of Hessian matrix eigenvalues shows distinct patterns that differentiate between these modes and enable classification. Notably, we find that landscapes associated with one-step transition modes display more diverse eigenvalue spectra. Additionally, we discover a correlation between SQUID and eigenvalue distribution, particularly, large (small) eigenvalues predominate in early (late) stages of the quench process for one-step transition modes. These findings provide insights into SQUID parameter optimization for quantum annealing. Moreover, our study suggests that Hessian matrix analysis may be a practical and efficient method for SQUID parameter optimization. Moreover, along with numerical results, our analysis based on the quantum tunneling rate indicates that, in the wake of a quench, quantum tunneling contributes to success rates, particularly when quantum annealing crossing energy levels. These findings suggest a route to improve the performance of quantum annealing by tuning the SQUID parameter via Hessian matrix analysis.

Investigating quantum classification involves identifying specific characteristics of quantum systems. We focus on a family of online schemes for both pure and mixed states, designing algorithms adaptable to varying input sizes. These schemes encompass two types: one-based and track-and-regret methods, which can be applied to various objectives. Our study extends existing methods in several ways: first, by achieving a perfect identification rate for pure states, we outperform previous results. Secondly, we evaluate how well these methods perform in identifying multiple states with constant overlap and constant Hamiltonian values. Notably, online schemes perform better than expected in this case, even for 10 distinct states, especially for small input sizes. Additionally, we human-tested the effectiveness of these methods in identifying multiple states with constant Hamiltonian values.

Using the mass relationships of light mesons to model the masses of light baryons in QCD, we explore the connections between their mass spectra. By applying a non-relativistic color-dielectric model, we derive the regulatory terms needed for modeling baryon masses, based on the characteristics of the QCD kernel. With this understanding, we create a simple, three-parameter model that accurately predicts the masses of light baryons, excluding the dynamically changing long-range forces present in QCD. This model's effectiveness is confirmed by comparing its predictions to the experimentally measured masses of light baryons.

The speed of acoustic waves traveling through the sun can reveal crucial information about the underlying flows that drive the sun's movement. By using waves generated by a sophisticated sun model, we've found a way to quantify the speed of the sun's horizontal flows. To make this information accurate, we've developed a new optimization technique that takes into account the speed of the sun's waves as they travel through different layers. By comparing the speeds of the sun's waves and surface fluctuations, we've found evidence supporting the existence of a complex, multi-scale system controlling the sun's movement. Based on this, we believe we can set a specific range for the speeds of the sun's waves and surface fluctuations.

Within approximately one second after the Big Bang, a primordial magnetic field started generating differential motion in its cells, which in turn affected the initial gravitational waves by altering their horizontal velocity gradients. This alteration occurred when the magnetic field lines rotated, thus pushing the boundaries of their cells and introducing new gradients into the initial gradients associated with the gravitational waves. Changes in the velocity gradients directly impacted the rate of expansion and contraction of the cells, which in turn indicated the magnitude of the dynamical effects resulting from the primordial magnetic field. This effect was analyzed through the dynamics of gravitational waves in both an isolated universe and in the context of inflation, with the latter involving three dimensions. Computational calculations revealed that, in an isolated universe with an energy density roughly equal to one percent of the energy density associated with the gravitational waves, the expansion and contraction of the cells could be described by a dimensionless growth factor approximately equal to ten times the inverse of the square root of the inverse of the wave number, with the wave number expressed in units of one over the expansion scale. This effect was found to be particularly significant in the context of inflation, with the latter yielding larger growth factors and smoother cell boundaries, which in turn resulted in a reduced dynamical impact on the initial gravitational waves. This led to the latter maintaining its original characteristics, with the potential consequence being an increased likelihood of detecting the initial gravitational waves. This was particularly significant, with the potential consequence being an enhanced likelihood of detecting the initial gravitational waves at higher frequencies,

Light field imaging technology, which captures the light rays subsampling in pupil planes, is used to create 4D scenes by interpolating these rays, allowing various novel computing and caching techniques to be applied. Nevertheless, the substantial size and complexity of 4D data significantly hinder its efficiency in processing and storage. To resolve this, a proposal for utilizing the disparity-aided model in compressing 4D light fields has been developed. By dividing the scene into non-overlapping blocks and calculating the corresponding disparities, the proposed method efficiently encodes these blocks. The results demonstrate significant improvements in compression efficiency, achieving 12.4 dB higher in terms of PSNR and 65.8% in terms of bit rate compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the proposed technique extends the applicability of existing light field compression models, such as HEVC-4D and TMLF, in compressing 4D light fields.

This study addresses the issue of transferring knowledge from large-scale monolingual sources to enhance cross-lingual information retrieval, demonstrating the potential for semi-interactive mechanisms to yield better results. A novel approach called LISA is introduced, incorporating a semi-interactive process to leverage context via retrieval augmented attention and allow for user feedback, thereby improving search output. Experiments on English and Chinese datasets yield a significant 43.8% and 42.3% increase in MRR in CLIR and 27.2% and 29.5% in MRR with 3 iterations in CIR, respectively. LISA's code and models will be openly available.

Spatial models with precise details are needed to capture variations in data related to population demographics, genetics, and disease patterns at a fine scale. Traditionally, Bayesian and Frequentist approaches have been used for inference in such models, with the latter gaining significance over the past two decades, particularly in the field of genetics where large datasets require faster computation. However, recent spatial approaches often involve complex computations and optimizations that make it difficult to determine the underlying spatial structure of models. Therefore, we present a novel object-oriented approach to spatial modeling, accompanied by the "spatOO" package in R, which facilitates the transition between Bayesian and Fre Frequentist models with respect to spatial dependencies. Additionally, the package enables the simulation of spatial processes and object creation corresponding to geometric areas. We perform spatial regression and survival analysis case studies to illustrate its use. Furthermore, we also discuss methods to identify the underlying structural components of these models using clustering techniques, with a focus on normal regression models. Finally, we conduct an empirical assessment of the "spatOO" package by comparing its performance with the existing "splancar" and "spatstat" packages in various computational benchmarks.

By casting the quantum memory betting model in the guise of a high-stakes gambler known as "Quantum Morten," we investigate the model's outcomes using a fundamental theorem in gambling theory. This "Fortune's Formula" calculates expected returns as a product of the player's wealth and a function that arises from modeling the game as a Markov process. With this formulation, we identify the optimal betting strategy for achieving maximum returns, which proves to be a straightforward raise-the-bet approach. Simulations corroborate our analytical findings and demonstrate the substantial gains from adhering to this optimal strategy.

We calculate electronic quasiparticle spectra of bulk silicon, germanium, and sn by merging ab initio many-body perturbation theory with density functional theory. By combining these approaches, we significantly reduce computational complexity, from originally expensive O(N^3) operations to O(N). This mixed approach merges Green's function and action functionals to obtain the one-particle Green's function, allowing for accurate simulation of semiconductors' corrugated electronic bands and correct prediction of band gaps and quasiparticle energy relative to experimental values. Furthermore, our predictions for silicon and germanium align with empirical findings, and our results for tin align with previous research. This approach also enables the computation of electronic properties at zero temperature, demonstrating agreement with experiment and other theoretical results for silicon and leading to predicted properties for tin that differ from existing measurements and calculations.

Researchers performed an experiment at the Brookhaven National Laboratory's CESR using 2.22 x 10^31 e^- pair interactions to search for a specific Sigma+ particle decay into a K+ and Kaon, followed by additional Xs radiation. The investigation aimed to detect this decay process for the first time. A second part of the study focused on examining two modes of Sigma+ decay into a K+, Kaon, and pi+ phi particle. The results of the search did not yield any detectable occurrences, thus allowing for limits on the decay widths of the processes. The limits placed on the widths are less than 0.04 x 10^-7 GeV for the initial process and less than 0.83 x 10^-7 GeV for the second process. The first measurement corresponds to a 90% confidence level and the second to a 95% confidence level of detection.

A novel approach using deep learning has been successfully tested in identifying intricate patterns within a protoplanetary disk. By applying autoencoders to observations from the ALMA telescope, researchers analyzed how turbulence affects the movement of material around a protoplanetary disk. This analysis revealed the presence of underlying patterns that describe how material is structured and moving in the disk. Key regions, including the zone near the middle and upper layers, were found to exhibit contrasting levels of turbulence. Notably, the trend of varying turbulence levels was consistent across different observing frequencies. This approach marks one of the initial applications of deep learning in analyzing the structure and movement of material in a protoplanetary disk, and it further lays groundwork for using deep learning to map complex celestial objects and phenomena.

A key component in ground-based astronomical observations, atmospheric dispersion compensation (ADC) systems, which overcome spectral aberrations, have been in use for over a century. Despite its importance, there have been limited studies on modern variations of the system. All previous research, which drove the development of various atmospheric dispersion models, relied on theoretical calculations or empirical approaches. However, there has been no evaluation of the performance of these models, which is necessary to inform the development of new ADC systems. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive analysis and assessment of five different atmospheric dispersion models: the Wedge, Parabolic, Sine, Cosine, and Sinusoidal models, which have been proposed over the years. To evaluate their performance, we directly compared their predictions to measurements obtained using spectroscopic methods. According to our findings, the Sinusoidal model outperforms the others, especially in the blue spectrum, whereas the Wedge model fares the worst. Notably, we find that the performance of the Sinusoidal model is not uniform and relies on the specific wavelength range. Based on this, we recommend the Wedge model as a last resort and the Sine model as a backup option, with the understanding that a new, more accurate model may be necessary for the development of high-precision ADC systems, especially for applications requiring hyper-spectral imaging.

Our variant Bayesian neural network uses a Bayesian neural network with a Horseshoe prior and adds an extra step that employs a Bayesian neural Spline using the FUSZ basis function. This addition allows the Horseshoe prior to be applied to input variables on a per-dimensional basis. As a result, our approach can effectively identify which input variables need more precise modeling and which can be modeled simpler, thereby reducing overfitting and improving the overall modeling. In our numerical tests and real-world experiments, the improved modeling yields better performance, specifically resulting in better prediction outcomes for higher dimensions and a significant 2dB increase in performance for certain low-dimensional cases in particular, an approximately 85% reduction in the amount of data required for training and prediction. Notably, in our real-world experiments, the more efficient data usage resulted in a substantial reduction in processing time.

Our analysis ties the local theory of continuous logic's type spaces to a specific aspect of algebra, establishing a clear analogy. We demonstrate that a particular aspect of groups corresponds to a duality, with implications for the foundation of our logic. By utilizing this finding, we can generate all local logics associated with specific types of groups. Notably, this ties the local theory of specific logics, such as the inclusion logic of interval graphs, to a significant area of algebra known as Grothendieck duality. We provide a comprehensive view of the underlying theory of groups and illustrate how it relates to a well-known duality in algebra.

The data-driven era has significantly contributed to growth, with machine learning algorithms playing a crucial role in the data science landscape. However, concerns about the fairness, transparency, and trustworthiness of the outcomes have emerged, particularly in how they are derived. To address these ethical concerns, novel machine learning techniques and standards are being developed to mitigate risks and increase users' confidence in the outcomes.  Although technical solutions like differential privacy and algorithms can mitigate risks, techniques such as federated learning and explanations offer more practical solutions to address concerns at a larger scale.  In order to build robust solutions to these issues, a multi-faceted approach that integrates technical and non-technical methods, standardizations, and guidelines is required to address concerns in complex real-world environments.  By understanding the inherent privacy and fairness limitations of machine learning, organizations and data practitioners can leverage proven methods and APIs to develop and deploy algorithms that meet rigorous standards, ultimately leading to the development of trustworthy data technologies and practices.

In dark matter models incorporating the Dark Matter Mirror Invariant (DMI), the DMI's influence results in a metastable $Z^\prime$ resonance characterized by a mix of gauge and Yukawa-like couplings to standard model fields and dark matter. This results in a significant impact on dark matter abundance and searches for the $Z^\prime$ at particle colliders, particularly in searches involving dark matter annihilations, direct production, and vector boson fusion processes. Consequently, regions rejecting such regions in collider searches appear overly restrictive when considered in dark matter searches, thereby failing to adequately align with dark matter abundance constraints in the most sensitive collider-induced dark matter annihilations processes. This imperfection in constraining the $Z^\prime$ resonance occurs when the $Z^\prime$ couple predominantly to the dark matter, particularly in the mixed-gauge-Yukawa coupling scenario. This issue arises because searches for the $Z^\prime$ at colliders inadequately consider the conversion of dark matter into missing energy, particularly in the dark matter-dominated regime of the $Z^\prime$ resonance. This limitation in interpreting $Z^\prime$ searches occurs when the dark matter mass approaches the $Z^\prime$ mass and the $Z^\prime$ couples predominantly to the dark matter. In order to address this issue, we recommend a revised $Z^\prime$ discovery strategy for future colliders that involves analyzing the $Z^\prime$-associated production with invisible Higgs bosons. The rapidly evolving nature of 6G wireless communication poses difficulties for conventional optimization techniques in achieving optimal performance. To address this challenge, a novel approach based on deep unsupervised learning and a genetic algorithm is presented in this study. The DL-GA method first leverages deep unsupervised learning to identify key parameters and create a security-aware backbone structure, which is then refined through genetic algorithm optimizations to achieve enhanced performance. Notably, our results indicate that DL-GA achieves better quality, faster processing times, and lower computational costs compared to conventional genetic algorithms, demonstrating substantial improvements of over 1800x, 1200x, and 23,000x, respectively, in processing time and computational cost while boosting security by up to 4.88 times.

A novel approach has been developed to describe the relationship between a parent nucleus' beta strength and its resulting daughter nucleus. 
This model, based on lattice simulations, determines strength distributions that are influenced by variations in nuclear shell configurations between parent and daughter nuclei. 
Comparisons with experimental data from numerous isotopes show that this model's predictions are accurate for a broad range of nuclear shells.

In scenarios involving multi-TeV dark matter, substantial intergenerational mixing occurs between dark matter and neutrinos due to the presence of singlet scalars. These singlet scalars not only create mixing but also offer a connection between dark matter and neutrinos, thereby affecting the dark matter concentration. As an extension of the standard model involving three right-handed neutrinos and a singlet scalar, this research explores the effect of $A$-term on the dark matter and neutrino fields, resulting in the generation of a dark matter relic density through resonant or inelastic annihilation. This setup further enables the regulation of baryon asymmetry, resulting in a satisfying alignment between the relic density of dark matter and $N_{\rm eff}$. In addition, this research introduces the notion of 'dark $\tau$', suggesting that dark matter might specifically interact with the heaviest right-handed neutrino, creating a significant disconnection between the dark matter and visible sectors. This research highlights a promising possibility where this underexplored dark $\tau$ might be directly detected through its relic density at future facilities.

Despite considerable progress in using machine learning for control systems, most existing techniques still face significant challenges when dealing with incomplete knowledge of the system dynamics. Our research focuses on addressing this problem by proposing a novel approach that combines learning from demonstrated behavior with reinforcement learning. This method utilizes an anatomy-like system model constructed through geometric identification, using features extracted from high-dimensional data. Both the system model and the controller benefit from this extracted representation. Under moderate data constraints, both learning and performance outcomes surpass those achievable through traditional reinforcement learning methods. Interestingly, even in scenarios where data constraints are severely diminished, the learned system model exhibits remarkably reduced inaccuracies compared to conventional representation learning methods.

A three-dimensional representation of elevent rank symmetries exists within Toda conformal field theories. This is known through spin-three Ward identities which reflect higher-spin symmetry. An explicit model has been constructed for a particular type of four-point conformal amplitude in generic Toda models, involving a cascade of unitary conformal field theories with highest weight conjugate to the weight that characterizes the model. This explicit model has also been shown to match a previous calculation within the $\mathcal{N}=2$ Liouville theory.

Recent advancements in GAN architecture have led to even more realistic image generation. This study proposes a novel Generator architecture, termed Relation-GAN, designed to mirror the human perception of object relationships. By incorporating a network that evaluates pairwise relationships between feature maps, our approach enhances the GAN loss function, forcing the generator to keep image relationships consistent. Experimentation reveals that the Relation-GAN surpasses existing methods on four datasets, producing more diverse images and fewer unsynthesizable outcomes. Moreover, our findings indicate that the relationship evaluator can be adapted for other tasks, such as detecting image pairs with consistent relationships.

A new approach for twin-field quantum key distribution using vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers has been developed, incorporating a global phase reference. In this approach, two entangled photons' polarizations are connected through the application of a reference frame, ensuring the correct alignment of measurement angles. This approach eliminates the need for adjusting relative phases between the two main fields and facilitates a global phase reference establishment. This method simplifies the implementation of twin-field quantum key distribution and improves its scalability.

This paper focuses on connections between Toeplitz operators and spaces of symbols within p-Bergman and p-Fock spaces. It reveals that certain classes of Toeplitz operators can be constructed using symbols within Lp space, and also introduces a kernel theorem for the p-Fock space. Furthermore, the paper discusses the relationship between the Wigner transform and Volterra-type operators within p-Fock spaces.

Object detectors have specific requirements for annotated boxes. Yet, given the laborious process of drawing boxes around objects, pseudo box annotations emerge as a viable option. Researchers initially used pseudo box annotations to simplify annotation, often combining them with category labels. However, their methods were limited by their reliance on training data and evolution into hybrid annotation schemes. In contrast, we focus solely on pseudo box annotations and adapt them for both training and self-supervised knowledge transfer. By treating pseudo box annotations as a corroboration signal, we develop a method to improve pseudo box quality for training. Furthermore, we show that pseudo box annotations can be used to teach weakly-supervised object detectors the spatial relationships between objects and between objects and scene boundaries. The method even enables cross-dataset knowledge transfer without categories. The technique's flexibility is demonstrated by its application to various datasets, resulting in significant performance improvements, such as a +13.7% AP on Pascal VOC and -12.1% AP on MS-COCO when using pseudo box annotations for training, and +5.6% and -3.9% when using them for transfer knowledge without categories.

Our research focuses on how young stars influence their surroundings through outflows and winds, and how this affects the local gas within protostellar disks and outflow cavities. By incorporating key physical processes, such as absorption that impacts spectral readings, we analyzed various stages of star formation using comprehensive, three-dimensional simulations. These calculations took into account the movement of all involved particles and used advanced methods to model radiation exchange. As a result, our simulations accurately replicated the behavior of HII regions surrounding young stars and revealed how these systems change over time. Interestingly, our calculations showed that both ionized and neutral gas produce similar spectral patterns due to mixing at boundaries. Moreover, our predictions closely match the recent Hubble Space Telescope observations of the Perseus molecular cloud. Finally, our simulations allowed us to track the movement of grains in these systems, which could provide a new line of inquiry for investigating the birth of stars and planets.

Transformers have taken over data-driven industries but still struggle with common sense. We argue that this challenge stems from the fact that Transformers lack certain signal processing features found in conventional networks and other attention-based models. In contrast to convolutional networks, which include a built-in notion of localized invariance, Laborde et al. (2022) have introduced a family of scalable, generic invariance modules for use in models like Transformers. These modules can be incorporated into existing architectures, such as the Transformer, which we have done within the context of a simple image classification task, revealing notable benefits in terms of performance and efficiency. Additionally, we have observed notable improvements in the state-of-the-art performance of the Transformer-XL model, which exhibits more localized characteristics in its output.

The effectiveness of forecasting models for future mortality rates can be enhanced through considering time-varying factor loadings in an ARFIMA-LM model framework. The model integrates a traditional auto-regressive and fractional integration model with a linear factor model, allowing for flexible and meaningful projections of future mortality trends. The factor loadings in this context represent key indicators of underlying mortality drivers, such as disease patterns, that evolve over time. By including these time-varying factor loadings, the ARFIMA-LM model demonstrates superior performance to the classical Lee-Carter model, especially when forecasting periods far into the future stretch significantly beyond recent history. Moreover, the model's projections of factor loadings offer valuable insights into the underlying mortality drivers, facilitating policy-making and operations. Inferences regarding factor loadings are meaningful and actionable, providing key indicators for policymakers to monitor in relation to future mortality trends. The model's architecture enables a straight-forward and efficient estimation process, encompassing parameters for both ARFIMA and linear factor models, thus streamlining the pursuit of inferences and predictions. The model's performance benefits in forecasting mortality into a future that significantly surpasses recent history in time duration, yet narrowly approaches age. The model's performance benefits notably when forecasting ages that significantly surpass recent history in time duration, yet narrowly approaches age.
