In various social settings, humans are expected to collaborate with robots that are capable of adapting to their preferences by adjusting parameters such as speed, force, and accuracy. However, robots often struggle to comprehensively understand an individual's expectations before making adjustments. To address this challenge, we conducted research to explore how humans would prefer robots to make adjustments in collaborative tasks and what information robots should disclose to facilitate efficient adaptations. In this study, we devised a simulation game in which humans specified preferences for adjustments in tasks, such as dragging objects, and then interacted with robots that were programmed with various policies to adapt to their preferences. Unfortunately, we discovered that robots that were aware of the specific task preferences humans desired were inefficient due to changes in their strategy made by other humans, which led to a misalignment of preferences. Moreover, our study found that revealing the robot's chosen action was less time-consuming but less precise than when humans directly adjusted the parameters, but this inefficiency disappeared when parameters and robot actions were shared with the human. To mitigate these inefficiencies, we developed an evolutionary algorithm that allows robots to adapt to statistical trends in human preferences, even when multiple individuals provide different preferences, which was found to lead to better efficiency and precision. In a subsequent multi-step experiment, we discovered that robots that were able to adapt to statistical trends were able to leverage this information to make adjustments in a variety of collaborative tasks and were even able to explore unfamiliar parameters with high payoffs, which was found to take advantage of

Global metric maps are commonly used for navigation in tasks such as reinforcement learning and robotics localization, but they come with disadvantages including large storage needs and processing difficulties due to the calculation of distances and motions in high-dimensional manifolds. The HiTMap data structure offers a new alternative by locally simplifying global metrics through the utilization of spatial hashing techniques. However, this comes with the challenge of handling loops in the environment, leading to contradictions when trying to identify the start point of a route using current methods. In order to address this issue, a new HiTMap feature is introduced that incorporates access information and gradient data of routes, taking into account the starting point and direction in addition to the environmental map when calculating and handling loops. The updated HiTMap data structure is referred to as HiTMap+. Our research found that HiTMap+ effectively resolves navigation contradictions, also demonstrating its ability to handle tasks such as finding the shortest route, transferring maps, and predicting environmental gradients with notable ease and precision compared to the standard HiTMap.

A novel method is presented for creating a two-dimensional Z-complementary array code set (ZCACS) based on modified Boolean functions with modified input/output characteristics in terms of Boolean operations. Unlike traditional general Boolean functions, the ZCACS construction process involves a two-dimensional code matrix where all PMs are zero, differing significantly from the conventional approach. Notably, the proposed ZCACSs exhibiting uniform property are derived using a specific type of generalized Boolean functions with 2^n input outputs, where n is the prime number. Utilizing a four-dimensional hyper-chessboard, a systematic approach is developed to identify the functions with a specific property, thereby enabling ZCACSs with various error-correcting capabilities to be constructed in different PMs. Consequently, a set of four-dimensional ZCACSs with diverse error-correction capabilities in different PMs are constructed, including PMs based on the Hadamard matrix, the $N \times N$ matrix $P_N$ matrix $L_N \times N$ matrix $Q_N \times N$ matrix $R_N \times N$ matrix $M_N \times N$ matrix $X_N \times N$ matrix $Z_N \times N$ matrix $Y_N \times N$ matrix $T_N \times N$ matrix $L_N \times N$ matrix $Q_N \times N$ matrix $R_N \times N$ matrix $Z_N \times N$ matrix $Y_N \times N

A novel two-stage approach is presented for computed tomography (CT) image reconstruction, addressing inconsistencies in data due to diverse noise patterns. This method combines statistical features common to CT scans with prior knowledge of noise types and distributions in limited-arc scans, effectively removing erratic pattern distortions while preserving essential image features. Experimental results showcasing the substantial improvements facilitated by this technique are demonstrated through both numerical simulations and real-world scans from a CT research system.

The local gap model's inaccuracy for predicting how light travels through amphibian skin's complex structure led to the development of a new approach. By breaking down the skin into various gaps and using the multiple scattering theory, we've increased the precision of our light travel predictions. In comparison to the local model, this approach provides results closer to the actual values when examining key factors such as transmission rates, spectral changes, and the distances light travels before being absorbed or scattered. Since the determined gaps are not physical and can vary depending on the model's parameters, we've introduced a method to identify the physical properties of the skin's gaps, enabling us to simulate the skin's semi-transparent appearance more effectively.

Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER) aims to contextually match user queries with entities from unstructured text. The initial step involves selecting relevant entities from the text, and later, disambiguation is performed to identify the most suitable entity based on the provided context. The CNER process typically relies on models trained without access to user feedback, which is often provided after the fact and can be used to retrain the model or refine the retrieval process. Traditional methods rely on post-retrieval methods such as ranking or re-ranking to incorporate user feedback, restricting the process to already retrieved entities. In this study, we take a different approach by incorporating user feedback into the selection of candidate entities directly from the text. The proposed feedback-driven contextual named entity retrieval method integrates the collection function and ranking function into a single pipeline, and to achieve this, we adapt the annealed jumpfield model to incorporate user feedback and retrieve relevant candidates. Our results show that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art CNER methods, including those using log-linear models and annealed jumpfield with limited candidates. Additionally, our method has the advantage of allowing users to provide feedback at any stage of the retrieval process and efficiently utilize sparse user feedback across existing models.

This paper explores the potential uses and modifications of temporal plots, particularly in creating adaptive visualizations that respond to user input or changes in context. We suggest extending temporal plots with three main components: (i) an underlying graph to show cause-and-effect relationships, (ii) a set of related instances depicted on a spatial map, and (iii) an animated sequence of concepts related to the main subject. This multi-faceted approach aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of temporal data by incorporating complementary views.

The effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in analyzing Electronic Health Records (EHRs) is significant when modeling patient relationships and disease correlations.  GNNs, specifically heterogeneous graph neural networks, face the challenge of producing highly variable outcomes due to their inherent bias toward certain node features over others.  As a result, they may lead to overfitting and overemphasize certain characteristics when making predictions, which is an issue that deep models often face.  To counteract this effect in HGNs, the implementation of hard and mix-up data augmentations can help a model to learn more even-minded features.  By applying these techniques to GNNs, the model can predict more accurately and be less susceptible to overfitting and adversarial attacks.  Tests on the large clinical datasets, MIMIC-III and ICU-2018, have shown that using mix-up data augmentation helps the model to achieve better generalization and mixture transparency in predicting patient outcomes.

We analyzed electrolyte properties near a charged soft surface using computer simulations, exploring how properties are affected by varying key factors. Specifically, we examined the effects of varying surface charge, ionic size, and temperature on the distribution of ions and the surface's effective zeta potential. Our results validate previous theoretical models for small, hard ions and provide new insights for large, hard ions. Additionally, we derived a general model that can be applied for a broad range of ion sizes, which accurately predicted our simulation outcomes. This underlying theory emphasizes the importance of the surface's charge density and the ion's size and mobility in determining the surface's charge distribution, which evolves to stabilize the surface by reducing the energy due to the ion's finite size and the long-range repulsive forces between ions.

To determine if BERT, a pre-trained language model, is effective in analyzing software text, we conducted an experiment. We compared BERT's performance to that of fastText and ELMo on identifying software requirements within the Android app dataset. The results indicated that BERT outperformed fastText but fell short behind ELMo, prompting us to investigate the potential for fine-tuning BERT to improve its performance.

This study explores energy-saving strategies for cooperative networks consisting of multiple users and relays. To minimize power consumption, both relay scheduling and power allocation are optimized in order to obtain the best performance in a network that follows the CR-MMSE model. To resolve this complex optimization issue, an algorithmic solution is introduced, comprising a successive convex approximation algorithm for power allocation optimization and a binary linear programming method for relay scheduling optimization. Furthermore, a sub-optimal algorithm is proposed, using a semi-definite programming relaxation and cone decomposition theory, resulting in a more efficient solution with less computational overhead. Both algorithms exhibit asymptotic optimality and convergent properties, and their effectiveness is validated through comparative simulation analysis with the actual optimal values obtained using a genetic algorithm.

In a two-dimensional electron gas, where spin-orbit coupling is present, our research focuses on the impact of electron scattering from magnetic impurities on their spin-resolved density of states. We reveal that, under specific conditions, the scattering of electrons by magnetic impurities or dimers causes shifts in the electron density's peak positions compared to a non-scattering situation. We find that non-magnetic impurities result in the YSR state peak splitting into two in a spin-resolved density of states, with each peak having a linear relationship between the scattering potential and energy position. Conversely, the scattering of electrons by magnetic dimers causes the YSR state peak to split into four, with each having a quadratic relationship between the scattering potential and energy position. Moreover, the scattering of electrons by magnetic dimers causes the YSR state peak to shift towards the Fermi level.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has released the latest results for the decay chain K+ → e+ νν̄ and K+ → μ+ νν̄ with an unprecedented level of precision. Using data collected from 2016 with a total dataset of 4.3 × 10^11 potassium decays, the experiment set an upper limit on the branching ratio for K+ → π+ νν̄ at 0.010% and derived a value of 0.232 × 10^-10 for the decay K+ → e+ νν̄, which is consistent with the Standard Model predictions. Similarly, the upper limit on the branching ratio for K+ → μ+ νν̄ was not constrained further due to being already below the detection capability.

Down-sampling point clouds can enhance the accuracy of LIDAR registration, especially in areas with moving objects. An innovative approach, described in this paper, utilizes geometric attributes and point density to develop a sampling strategy. By identifying key points with distinct properties, it outperforms previous methods focused solely on spatial attributes. The efficacy of this technique is tested across various datasets and it proves particularly effective in challenging scenarios with high mobility, outperforming previous methods significantly.

Recent advancements in deep learning for satellite image processing have led to promising performance outcomes but also introduced several areas of application limitation, primarily due to their exceptionally high computational and memory requirements. These constraints effectively preclude the use of more trained models. A notable exception is the use of GPU accelerators, yet even this solution fails to address more complex processing tasks or enable analysis of images exceeding the capacity of typical GPUs. A different strategy involves employing specialized hardware, such as the NPU, which offers high levels of both customization and energy efficiency. Although this special hardware is still relatively new, there has been a notable surge in recent advancements focusing on the development of NPNs, suggesting that this emerging technology may soon play a crucial role in the AID sector. The FET Project EPIC has recently combined the potential of the NPU with the benefits of fluctuating energy supply, offering a more sustainable energy model, capable of being adjusted to meet EPIC's processing demands throughout the day. The fluctuating energy source has short-term fluctuations that are correlated with the availability of surplus energy, while its long-term behavior is influenced by factors such as weather forecasts, energy storage, and mobility. Interestingly, utilizing non-constant energy sources results in significant reductions in the average power consumption of the EPIC network by approximately two-fold. Moreover, integrating the non-constant energy source with smart charging strategies enables the EPIC system to be fully adaptive to the fluctuating energy supply, effectively allowing it to reach top-notch performance even

We have generated deep sub-wavelength structures in thin metallic nickel targets using high-intensity laser pulses to observe nonlinear changes associated with plasma-grating formation. Experimental results reveal a significant enhancement in third-harmonic generation when pulse fluence exceeds a particular high threshold, contradicting predictions based on nonlinear models which anticipate a decrease at high fluences due to a lack of mobile charges. Utilizing numerical simulations, we attribute this increased harmonic generation to significant electron transfer within the material, allowing for a more efficient change in frequency. This finding has implications for various applications including plasmonic design, lasing protection, and ultrafast data storage.

Protecting Deep Neural Network-based systems from malicious attacks is a crucial task. In the realm of computer security, mitigation techniques often involve devising countermeasures to outmaneuver adversaries by utilizing similar technologies, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs). This paper introduces an innovative defense framework utilizing both GANs and variational autoencoders (VAEs) to safeguard image classification DNNs. This unified architecture combines the capabilities of GANs and VAEs to effectively detect and neutralize adversarial attacks through the generation of fault-free samples that classify similarly to malicious inputs. The proposed framework demonstrates robustness on several types of adversarial attacks in both compressed and uncompressed image datasets, while also showcasing superior compression efficiency. The synergy between GANs and VAEs creates a powerful system that outperforms existing approaches in adversarial attack resistance and compression efficiency.

A significant obstacle when studying Multiple Sclerosis is the lack of standardized data, particularly imaging and clinical data, which hampers the development of highly effective automatic lesion detection and segmentation tools. To overcome this challenge, a novel learning approach is proposed, leveraging a model that can segment MS lesions across diverse datasets with distinct characteristics. This method draws upon experience replay, where a database is created by reprocessing a substantial quantity of clinical datasets from multiple institutions, facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the varied data. During autonomous, institution-independent evaluations, segments of MS lesions that were obtained through Experience Replay are applied to newly acquired, unseen data, thereby improving segmentation accuracy and expressing a more reliable probabilistic outlook. Moreover, Experience Replay enables fine-tuning a model using knowledge gained from multiple institutions, thereby mitigating bias towards a specific dataset. Our study showcases the robustness of Experience Replay in tackling data heterogeneity, a persistent issue in MS research. To address this challenge, our approach incorporates Experience Replay in conjunction with Experience Guided Training, a novel technique that combines semi-supervised learning and experience replay. This model is initially fine-tuned using Experience Replay, allowing it to recognize MS lesions in newly acquired data, then adjusted using Experience Guided Training to correct lesions that were previously unidentified in newly acquired data, thereby improving overall segmentation accuracy. Our study confirms that combining Experience Replay and Experience Guided Training results in highly effective automatic lesion detection and segmentation, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques in the field.

We introduce a novel methodology for comparing metrics in a concise fashion by
building upon the principles of optimal transport. This alternative approach to
Gromov-Hausdorff metric comparison is marked by its relative simplicity and
efficiency, as it remains sensitive to metric structure, particularly where
distances are equal to zero. Furthermore, this new comparison method is tied to
the continuity of optimal transport, resulting in a potentially more accurate
representation of metric relationships. In turn, this enables us to extend the
Gromov-Hausdorff distance in a manner that preserves its continuous dependence
on the metrics in question. Additionally, this new comparison method also finds
applications in the classification of metric spaces, much like its more famous
Gromov-Hausdorff space counterpart.

The integration of prior domain knowledge into machine learning models is particularly significant when dealing with limited data. Despite improvements in learning hybrid models, the evaluation of learning performance using imperfect domain knowledge remains an unresolved issue. In contrast to purely data-driven models, hybrid models' efficiency are measured by how well they utilize this domain knowledge. We establish a framework for evaluating learning performance when domain knowledge is subject to errors. Furthermore, we conduct experiments to assess how five classification kernel methods perform when supplied with imperfect as well as flawed gold standards. The findings indicate that hybrid models' efficiency depend on multiple factors, including the source of domain knowledge, dataset characteristics, and specific learning algorithms used.

The birth of high-mass star clusters remains poorly understood, particularly in how core formation and star birth are interconnected. To gain insight into the origin of high-mass star clusters, researchers examined the development of massive molecular cores within the central region of the Rosette Nebula, a site that has previously been known to host young high-mass stars. Using the Garching HHATR instrument, researchers obtained high-resolution Doppler shift maps of a particular region, identifying several high-mass cores and assessing their velocity and internal motion patterns. When analyzed alongside existing data on thermal motion and radiation properties within the cores, researchers were able to infer the mass growth patterns of the cores, revealing a link between core development and the eventual birth of high-mass stars. Furthermore, researchers discovered a pattern where younger stars within the area exhibited varying velocities, while older stars showed generally similar patterns, suggesting a sequence of events where younger populations were embedded in the same high-mass cores. When considered alongside existing data on stellar distribution and temperature, researchers were able to piece together a detailed 3D map of the area, showing a shape that reflects the overall structure of the massive star cluster, a phenomenon that has begun to form and evolve over the past few million years.

A potential discrepancy exists between cosmic microwave background measurements of primordial black hole density and observed rates of gravitational wave events attributed to black hole mergers.  If primordial black holes aren't simply masses above a hypothetical threshold, but rather objects with distinct observational characteristics, it's possible to detect them through microlensing events.  By simulating the LIGO and Virgo gravitational wave dataset with the Dorado galaxy model, our study reveals a range of predicted microlensing events associated with primordial black holes, assuming various masses and mean PBH values.  Comparing these estimates with estimated events produced by stellar mass black holes that have evolved and merged within the Dorado galaxy, our analysis suggests that microlensing events attributed to primordial black holes could surpass those of stellar mass black holes, assuming a mean PBH mass of approximately 30 solar masses.  However, this ratio decreases significantly with increasing assumed mean PBH mass within the previously proposed "knee" range.  Our study also finds that, depending on the assumed mean PBH mass, the difference in detection probabilities between cosmic microwave background and gravitational wave/ microlensing events can provide insight into the yet unresolved nature of the "knee" feature.

Numerous studies regarding polar systems have concentrated on systems featuring interactions that are range-1, whereas more recent research exploring interaction effects that vary spatially (i.e., range-2) is relatively limited. In this research, experiments involving charged particles confined to a flat surface are employed to explore range-2 interactions' impact on forming polar crystal structures. Range-2 interactions lead to the formation of unprecedented polar crystal structures exhibiting frustration, namely a 2C and 8C type. These phases exhibit internal degrees of freedom that show no long-range order. A study using Monte Carlo simulations confirmed the phase transitions and analyzed the correlation patterns within these structures.

Pretrained language models have become the standard for natural language processing tasks. Although often viewed as a standard step, using special tokens in these models have a significant impact on performance. This study delves into the role of special tokens in these models, including segmentation, padding, and other distinctive tokens, and explores their effects on performance in tasks where these tokens are present. This investigation draws on the performance of various language models across multiple tasks to understand how these tokens affect model performance in different contexts. Further, this research suggests a simple data augmentation technique to mitigate the negative performance effects caused by these tokens. The results indicate that while segmentation tokens can improve performance in specific tasks, padding tokens and other special tokens generally degrade model performance. This motivates the development of a large language model that is explicitly designed to ignore these tokens, known as the BLORST-LM. BLORST-LM is a simple modification of the standard large language model architecture that is capable of ignoring special tokens at training time, and demonstrates improved performance over standard language models across a range of tasks.

The static network semantics evaluation of expressions has been fine-tuned for use with sets and lists, and a new, improved dynamic evaluation method has been implemented for use with these data types as well as numbers and booleans. The old function for evaluating sets and lists is now obsolete and has been replaced by the new, more efficient function. In a context where elements are added to a set or list, the new evaluation method can handle these operations more effectively by comparing the added element or value to each element in the collection, resulting in better performance, especially for additions to lists. The new function also takes advantage of shortcuts in list and set operations, reducing the number of comparisons needed and thus running faster. In operations involving lists and sets, the system can also take shortcuts by skipping unnecessary operations, further improving performance. When using the 'for each' operation to iterate over a list or set, the new function will now start the operation from the beginning of the collection, rather than from where the pointer currently sits, resulting in better predictability and performance. In response to a user request for a function to join strings, a new function called 'join' has been added to the system. The new function preserves the current behavior of the system by concatenating strings in the existing manner, and also supports the addition of strings separated by a specified delimiter. There is consensus that non-equilibrium systems, such as those made of glass, operate according to a universal set of rules, analogous to equilibrium statistical mechanics. The rules of "thermodynamic scaling" were first proposed for 2D fluids and have since been applied to numerous simulations and experiments. However, the scope and validity of this concept have been and continue to be debated. The primary goal of this work is to examine thermodynamic scaling's observed applicability to non-polymers in 2D, 3D, and 3D-like systems, such as granular materials, while also addressing its relationship to time-dependent observations and probing its connection to age. The findings presented are intended to offer insight into the underlying mechanisms of thermodynamic scaling, as well as contribute to discussions surrounding its theoretical foundations.

Our study examines the impact of distinct negation types on the natural language inference task in a semantic parsing framework. Notably, we find that NLI models like BERT fail to adequately distinguish between certain types of negation, leading to inconsistent predictions. By investigating the effects of three primary categories of negation - moral, semantic, and syntactic - in both NLI and semantic parsing tasks, we identify improvements that can be achieved through the incorporation of a novel classifier for negation sense. Such a classifier not only enhances the accuracy of semantic parsing by 1.7% but also increases the accuracy of NLI by 2.8% when negation plays a crucial role. Additionally, our research highlights the value of negation information in NLI, showcasing improvements of up to 1.4% in accuracy for NLI when utilizing negation information.

We propose a look-ahead attention mechanism to model connections between phrases further down the sentence, enabling direct relationships between words and long-range dependencies in sentences. This attention type can be incorporated into existing translation systems and we incorporate it into the Transformer model for our experiments. To determine the direct impact on translation, we compare baseline and modified outputs in a scenario with no post-processing, finding that LookAhead + MST achieves a significant improvement in BLEU score, specifically 3.85 and 2.70 in cases with and without beam search respectively. Additionally, the LookAhead model allows for an efficient method to generate sentences with a specified length of target words.

This note offers a straightforward symplectic framework for a broad class of geometric flows on cotangent bundles, drawing inspiration from a modified version of the Chern Simons equation, a concept previously explored in [21]. Notably, our approach diverges from Weyl's classic gauge theory framework, opting for a system with cotangent bundles. Within this framework, we can express curvature weights more simply and connections in a standard form more directly. By contrast, Weyl's approach yields a more intricate connection representation and a more laborious expression of curvature weights. We also observe that a certain flow on cotangent bundles is associated with a specific physical phenomenon, as described in [31]. Additionally, we have identified this flow as the Ottonello-Tanaka variant of the bimetric theory of the Chern Simons equation, as proved in a recent study [32].

A crucial link has been discovered between the IR and MI boundaries of (3+1)d conformal field theories, involving a thermal phase transition. This finding suggests that these theories undergo deconfinement, marking a turning point at the QCD critical point. Our analysis shows thermal entropy increasing with coupling in (3+1)d CFTs, contrary to the scenario in (2+1)vacuum CFTs. In the vicinity of the QCD critical point, the Gelder-Peltzer-Rey parameter replicates Wilson's polynomial for 4-dimensional CFTs. Utilizing the MIPerimeter entropy, our polynomial construction manifests a thermal phase transition, exhibiting a power-like polynomial variation during deconfinement. The MI entropy loss is proportional to the Gelder-Peltzer-Rey parameter in tandem with the polynomial exponent n, causing entropy to decrease as coupling increases below the critical point. Conversely, the EXPerimeter entropy exhibits a rise with coupling in both the MI and EX phases, adhering to the boundary Markov functional consistency conditions. Our polynomial construction is unique, featuring an exponential variety in time based on the polynomial exponent n. Our polynomial is uniquely defined by the EX data point, and subsequent time progression is deterministic, exploiting causality. Our analysis implies a percolation scenario for QCD deconfinement and suggests a new paradigm for 4-dimensional lattice gauge theory simulations, mimicking CFT deconfinement through causality-driven time progression of

This research presents an innovative method for computing the risk-neutral distribution of the sum of geometric processes by applying double Laplace transforms. The economic significance of this approach lies in its ability to relate to pricing rules of Asian options, which can further be enhanced by incorporating the single Laplace transforms' property of generalizing cash flow discounting. Moreover, by leveraging the Euclidean addition property on the circle group, we develop an algorithm to extend this technique for pricing general multiple-geometric Asian options. Numerical results demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of this method, which is exemplified by its successful application to real-world data with the European multiple-geometric Asian options market model from MSCI, involving data from 2020 with approximately  830 stocks from  50 countries, with a total EUWTS value of about 11.3 trillion, with the findings showing that multiple-geometric multiple-accuracy reductions yield minimized computational costs.

We created a comprehensive map of the diffuse gamma-ray background (GRB) using 13 years of Fermi-LAT data across the entire sky, with an improved resolution of approximately 1 degree. Our unique approach combines high-latitude sources from the Third Source Catalog with a detailed analysis of the thermal gas component from diffuse gamma-ray emissions, utilizing updated constraints on the spatial distribution of primary cosmic rays and inverse Compton radiation. These advancements allowed us to refine the estimated diffuse gamma-ray flux, with a total observed value of 5.26 ± 0.52 and 4.43 ± 0.63 units of 10^-5 cm^-2 s^-1 (1-100 GeV) for the Hadronic and Lepton models, respectively. We identified significant discrepancies between observed and predicted grb values in certain regions, with multiple templates failing to match the hadronic model's prediction in the Bootes void at a confidence level of 3σ. Furthermore, we calculated the grb contribution of galaxy clusters, quasars, and blazars, revealing that known extended sources account for a mere 12% of grb flux, with clusters potentially explaining a substantial portion of grb, up to 40%. We also determined the grb fraction attributed to known extended sources and pulsars to be approximately 52% and 5%, respectively. Our analysis revealed significant correlations between grb and cosmic microwave background radiation temperature, X-ray flux, and cosmic baryon mass

Inflation models with sharp features in the scalar potential or sound horizons are expected to produce distinctive signatures in the curvature perturbation and its nonlinear effects. However, when evaluating the impact of these features on primordial non-Gaussianities, a critical assumption often made is that the curvature perturbation is in the horizon scale. If this assumption is valid, the nonlinear source term, which depends on second-order fluctuations of the curvature perturbation, will be undetermined and presumed to be negligible. Consequently, a model-independent measure of non-Gaussianity, frequently employed in observations, would be forced to assume its value as zero. In contrast to previous conclusions drawn from models with sharp features, our research reveals that this negative result does not necessarily preclude the possibility of the feature having physically significant effects. Additionally, our findings suggest the possibility of detecting these features through the kinetic perturbation, which is highly correlated with the logarithm of the inflationary background.

We have developed the Latent Visual Semantic Explainer (LaViSE), a unique method that uses the capabilities of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to generate human-readable descriptions of their internal representations. LaViSE employs the concept of latent learning, utilizing additional, untrained neural components to provide insight into how CNNs operate. By combining the strengths of two decoding techniques - attention and autoregressive methods - LaViSE produces detailed, semantic explanations of CNNs, enabling better understanding of their complex learning processes. Our approach is versatile and can be applied not only to LaViSE but also to other techniques, offering a new standard for evaluating convolutional neural networks.

Inspired by the analogy between 1D and 2D cuprates, which facilitates the translation of knowledge from one system to another, we explore the possibility of leveraging research on Na$_2$IrO$_3$ to uncover the underlying mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates. Na$_2$IrO$_3$ and (120)-type NaIrO$_2$, which shares key characteristics with 1D Na$_2$IrO$_3$, have been found to possess correlated metals and Weyl-Kondo insulators with structural similarities to 1D and 2D cuprates. Furthermore, variations in their band gaps allow us to bracket a range of $t$-overlap and $t'$-overlap values in the 2D cuprate Hilbert space, while NaIrO$_2$ serves as a reference point for comparing with Na$_2$IrO$_3$. Additionally, studies on (120)-type NaIrO$_3$ have revealed the importance of the process of non-magnetic Ir$^{5+}$ gap formation in 2D systems, which goes beyond the dynamics of spin fluctuations that govern 1D cuprate physics. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that understanding the critical closing of the non-magnetic Ir$^{5+}$ gap, which results in a smaller magnetic gap than the smaller electronic gap in 2D NaIrO$_3$, is crucial for describing high-temperature superconductivity in

Investigating the link between the physical layout of HIV clinics and treatment uptake across South Africa and Uganda, our study revealed significant variations in the distance people travel to receive care. The majority of studies have focused on the overall distance to healthcare facilities, but we delve deeper by examining different components of the distribution and how they affect treatment access. Using travel time data, we analyzed how variations in travel schedule and duration influence individuals' decisions to receive treatment and identified patterns not present earlier. Specifically, our findings indicate that people familiar with the average time it takes to reach an HIV clinic are more likely to receive treatment. Furthermore, our study shows that both extremes of the distribution of travel times can hinder treatment access. Understanding these insights could lead to targeted interventions focused on specific aspects of the distribution of travel times to improve treatment outcomes, potentially improving access for individuals far from healthcare facilities or with unfamiliarity of travel times.

X-ray scattering research on a compound near the multiferroic transition - Cu$_{2}$(Cd$_{1-x}$Ni$_{x}$$_2$)O$_{7}$, exhibits complex magnetic phase transitions. The primary aim of this study was to utilize synchrotron radiation to analyze the magnetic phase transitions in this compound. The investigations revealed that when exposed to a certain temperature and pressure, Cu$_{2}$CdO$_7$ displays a stable skyrmion lattice which is characterized by left-handed and right-handed helical structures. The same investigations showed that the metastable skyrmion lattice transitions into a more stable magnetic phase under the influence of negative magnetic fields. Additionally, the research revealed the emergence of a conical phase which arises due to a specific magnetic field strength. The study also discovered that the transition temperatures for the helical and conical phases have an asymmetrical response to varying levels of pressure. The research results are consistent with theoretical predictions of the material's magnetic properties, thus confirming its complex magnetization patterns.

High-dimensional dynamic factor models have widespread applications across both theoretical and practical avenues. We contribute to this theory by developing singular ARMA models, incorporating singular coefficients that yield unique statistical properties. By combining these models with high-dimensional factor data, we derive efficient estimation methods, providing valuable insights into the latent factors and model structure in singular ARMA models. The results of our analysis demonstrate the same level of estimation efficiency in both the mean square and spectral density domains. Additionally, our methodology allows for consistent estimation of the singular values and eigenvectors in large systems of equations. A simulation study evaluates the performance of our methods against existing approaches, while a real-world application examining neurophysiological signals showcases our results in action.

The properties of the Moreau proximal mapping at stationary points are crucial for solving problems involving the proximal regularized problem of find $\bar{x} \in Q$ such that for all $x \in Q$, it solves $\left[ f(\bar{x}) - f(x) + \partial g(\bar{x}) \circ (\bar{x} - x) \right] \geq 0$. In this paper, we establish that under certain conditions, the fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping satisfy the equilibrium problems when the mapping represents a monotone time-invariant system. We also explore the complete characterization of the fixed points when the mapping is affine and demonstrate that under geometric or convex conditions, the fixed points satisfy the equilibrium problems. Furthermore, this result leads to a geometric characterization of the fixed points when the mapping represents a group action. We provide a numerical example to illustrate these findings.

Deep learning's widespread adoption can be attributed to its impressive empirical performance, but it lacks a theoretical foundation. To address this, we aim to develop more effective and robust models by restricting the set of possible functions that can be learned. Predictive models in deep learning typically employ maximum likelihood estimation, resulting in uncertain predictions and model criticisms due to their limited dataset. By incorporating Bayesian methods to constrain the model's functional capacity, we can quantify its limitations and guarantee certain predictions and model criticisms. Two Bayesian deep learning models are discussed in this study: the first involves learning a network's functional form, while the remaining involves sampling from a pre-trained network. We focus on applying these methods to classification, regression, model selection, and topological inference, and provide supporting numerical experiments.

Turbulent effects that involve magnetic cross-powers on short and long timescales have a crucial role in the geophysical and astrophysical context of dynamos. Notably, studying the geodynamo without considering these effects would lead to an incomplete understanding. In our investigation, we specifically analyzed the comparative efficiency of turbulent pumping forces related to magnetic cross-covariance and cross-powers generated by dynamos solving the mean-field induction equation in spherical coordinates. These dynamos were driven by velocity fields produced by two different numerical schemes - the local and non-local test-field method, with an additional double-adiabatic approximation variant. By adjusting certain parameters and introducing non-locality, we observed significant variations in the ratio of turbulent pumping coefficients, leading to interesting implications for turbulent dynamo theory and suggesting new approaches to modeling energy cycling in the geodynamo.

A study focusing on the molecular outflow in the center of the galaxy NGC4945 utilizing ALMA detected multiple kinematic features. The features revealed an ionized gas outflow with rates higher than 1000 M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$ and extended up to 200 pc. However, the mass outflow rate significantly decreased with increasing distance from the galaxy's center. The detected features extended to a much farther distance when using total molecular mass outflow rates, reaching up to 2700 M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$. The study found that the majority of the molecular gas outflow rates were powered by super-ejecta. The study also discovered two gas components, each exhibiting distinct velocity ranges. The study suggests these components may be two separate gas outflows, however further observations are needed for confirmation. Additionally, the study found that the elevated velocity components were closely linked to the galaxy's gas outflow. Furthermore, the study observed no significant change in the velocity properties of the gas as it moves via the galaxy's wind. The study found agreement between the observed outcomes and the simulated predictions for the gas outflow. However, the study was unable to identify the gas outflow head or gas headstart position, possibly due to the gas outflow not being oriented perpendicularly to the galaxy's plane.

In the quasilinear theory of weak turbulence, the evolution of wave energy is linked to its own average value. We re-examine this connection by considering turbulence in both magnetic and collisionless plasmas. By postulating that wave energy growth is linked to its particle probability distribution, we derive wave equations that are applicable in both cases. In magnetic turbulence, the growth rate of wave energy depends on the energy density of the parent distribution, leading to an exponential growth of wave energies. In collisionless turbulence, the growth rate is proportional to the gradient of the particle distribution function, causing waves to couple and couple at specific scales. Our revised wave equations result in reduced wave growth compared to predictions made by other theories, particularly in collisionless turbulence.

Weakly absolute monotone WAM) Runge-Kutta methods in the Generalized Lorenz System (SGLMs) have been popular due to their efficient error behavior on uniform domains. This study examines six stepsize-adaptive WAM R-K methods in the context of both uniform and non-uniform grids. The findings indicate that using non-uniform grids in WAM R-K methods may lead to reduced efficiency and increased inefficiency in certain situations. The research underlines the necessity for further efficiency improvements in WAM R-K methods.

Given a closed, symmetric operator $A$ within a complex Hilbert space, along with its self-adjoint extension $A_0$ within the domain of $A$, we derive a Lyapunov inequality. This inequality ties the boundedness of resolvent $\left(\lambda - A_0\right)^{-1}$, the existence of $A_0$'s inverse, and the boundedness of the $A_0$-resolvent to the inequality itself. Under certain conditions where $A$'s resolvent is bounded and the $A_0$-resolvent is left-invertible, we derive a uniform bound for the resolvent of $A_0$. This inequality involves $\lambda > 0$ and the norm of $\left(\lambda - A_0\right)^{-1}$. We then approach the theory of second-order hyperbolic equations within a bounded domain by utilizing the Lyapunov inequality to derive a comprehensive theory. This theory ties the properties of the Dirichlet series representing solutions, the regularity of the solutions, the growth of the solutions, the non-tangential boundedness of the solutions, and the uniqueness of the solutions to the inequality itself.

A new software package called MuMuPy has been created to compute the probabilities of electroweak transitions for dimuonium ($\mu^+\mu^-$) splitting up into other particles such as pions, neutrinos, and $J=\gamma, 3S, 1P$ states. Using these calculations, we can determine the impact of these transitions on searches for neutral currents in muonium experiments and also influence the final states of such transitions in muon colliders. MuMuPy allows users to run a variety of transitions simultaneously and includes functions for calculating radiative corrections that enable comparisons with more advanced methods, thereby producing highly accurate results. The package is available for free download on the GitHub platform with the address https://github.com/CNPMU MuMuPy.

We develop a utility function for modeling an investor's portfolio optimization strategy. By distinguishing between absolute and relative wealth, this function provides a comprehensive approach that can be tailored to fit various levels of wealth. Its incremental value lies in its dynamic responsiveness to both absolute and relative wealth, enabling it to pinpoint optimal investment portfolios that maximize the investor's net worth. Furthermore, this utility function captures the investor's desire for growth and stability, making it a versatile model. By comparing the results with standard utility functions, such as the Log utility function, we conduct a comprehensive analysis and find that our utility function's predictive ability exceeds that of the Log utility function. Lastly, we validate the feasibility of implementing this utility function using modern portfolio optimization techniques.

Green Pea galaxies in the EagleAccretion simulation exhibit analogous characteristics to compact, star-forming systems observed at redshifts above 6. To better comprehend early cosmic processes, researchers are intriguingly discovering similarities between these systems. An investigation into the characteristics of 48,333 simulated Green Pea galaxies across the Cosmic Evolution Survey (CES) domain reveals their correlations with larger cosmic structures. These correlations are consistent with observations from programs such as CANDELS and COSMOS. Key findings suggest that the sizes, star formation rates, and stellar masses of Green Pea galaxies vary according to their halo masses, while their gas metallicity is influenced by the mass of surrounding interhalo medium. An underlying relationship implies that the masses of halo haloes and interhalo medium grow in tandem with the masses of central haloes, influencing the masses of galaxies and their surrounding gas. Additionally, the study finds that the masses of central haloes and haloes within the redshift range of 4 account for the majority of the masses of galaxy-gas components. An underlying structural pattern reveals that the masses of halo-gas components, central haloes, and halo-halo filaments gradually develop across redshift ranges. An in-depth, three-dimensional analysis further indicates that the masses of halo-gas components, central haloes, and halo-halo filaments gradually develop in redshift ranges.

This research explores the application of a modified version of the boson-fermion model to understand the behavior of quasiparticles in systems with ferromagnetic spin fluctuations, particularly in the context of the mean-field boson-fermion theory. Within the fermion-boson exchange framework, the model describes interactions between fermions and bosons, with bosons acting as intermediate carriers of interactions between fermions. By assuming nearly degenerate fermion states, particularly relevant in the context of ferromagnetic spin fluctuations, the research develops a long-range bosonic self-energy. By analyzing the resulting self-energy, the behavior of quasiparticles can be comprehensively studied. Utilizing the Haldane-Popov approximation, the interactions between fermions can be expressed in terms of the bosonic degrees of freedom. A detailed examination of the obtained momentum-dependent interaction, in the context of the boson-fermion model, is conducted, with the information and insights gained applicable to the understanding of mean-field boson-fermion theories of high-temperature superconductors and other systems.

The braided Thompson's groups, denoted $F_b$, $T_b$, and $T_{bb}$, have been investigated within the framework of braided groups. Interestingly, these groups fail to satisfy the requirements for a locally compact Hausdorff topological group when equipped with the pointwise convergence topology. Consequently, the natural embedding of $F_b$ into $T_{bb}$ does not hold in the relative uniform topology. Nevertheless, the embedding of $F_b$ into $T_b$ retains its continuity under the relative uniform topology. Moreover, the embedding of $T_b$ into $T_{bb}$ is continuous in various topological structures but fails to be continuous in the relative uniform topology when $T_b$ and $T_{bb}$ are respectively equipped with the weak* and pointwise convergence topologies. Furthermore, the properties of linearly defined subgroups have been explored for the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and their braided counterparts $F_b$, $T_b$, and $T_{bb}$. Interestingly, the braided Thompson's groups fail to exhibit linearly defined divergence but display other forms of linearly defined anomalies.

This paper presents our approach to refining the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture by leveraging contrastive learning to enhance the capabilities of the dense retrieval table. During pre-training, RAG uses a self-supervised method that asks it to distinguish between actual pairs of passages and artificially created ones. However, our analysis reveals that the initial pairing method fails to effectively exploit the potential within the passage pool, leading to underutilized local and fine-grained similarities within the table. To address this limitation, our proposed framework 'PAIL' optimizes passage indexing by pairing real and artificial instances in both semantic and spatial contexts, while applying contrastive learning to improve within-table similarity. Experimental evaluations using GLUE benchmark tests demonstrate that our PAIL method outperforms the baseline RAG model on most tasks, particularly demonstrating enhanced adaptability on the SQuAD benchmark. The accompanying code can be accessed at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/zwang1998/self-supervised-pairing-for-RAG.

RH methods offer a unified approach to finding approximate solutions of initial value problems whose behavior changes suddenly due to the application of sudden forces. By transforming this problem into an integral equation, we can analyze its long-term behavior in the complex plane and apply a test function to isolate singular components. Typically, model problems like the Airy equation or the Schrodinger equation, allow us to approximate solutions near singularities, while general nonlinear problems are approximated using power series expansions in appropriate norms, allowing us to analyze the error at each term.

Automatic summarization, being a widely studied topic, poses significant challenges in ensuring the accuracy of ground truth annotations, particularly in resource-constrained settings. In our research, we tackle this issue by designing a data qualification pipeline to generate rigorous, gold-standard explanations. This pipeline leverages evaluations from human annotators to identify and address issues with existing annotations, ultimately refining the development dataset. By implementing this method, we notice substantial improvements in the dataset's consistency and reliability. The refinement also yields noticeable enhancements in the performance of summarization models evaluated on the qualified dataset, as marked by increased precision and recall in the leading evaluation benchmarks.

Recent text-video retrieval methods primarily focus on final output frames from pre-trained models like Giraffe-VAE, yet neglect their hidden states and temporal structure. Our proposed TS2-Net addresses this oversight by leveraging the capabilities of two complementary neural transformers - one for vision and one for fusion - to generate superior spatial-temporal video representations. TS2-Net's vision transformer processes a series of frames to capture intra-frame connections, while its vision-critical fusion transformer integrates channel and spatial attention to unify visual data, and our proposed efficient fusion method combines vision and language streams through cross and self-attention for final output generation. By doing so, TS2-Net outperforms state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets, particularly by a substantial 12.5% on MSRVTT Knuckle Benders with strong scalability on datasets like MSRVTT. Our source code is available at https://github.com/JohnnyWher/TS2-Net.

New transverse spin observables in rare top decays can uncover unique properties of polarized particles, including those involving the top quark. The Large Hadron Collider can detect these observables by producing the top quark in relation to the Z boson or b quark pairs. By analyzing the angular distributions in the t Z and t t-bar channels, researchers can determine the polarization of the top quark, offering insights into the Z boson and b quark production processes. These observables can reveal differences between standard model behaviors and those predicted by new physics scenarios, such as composite Higgs models. They may provide the earliest indication of new physics by appearing in rare occurrences at the LHC.

In our previous study (arXiv:2009.04437), we analyzed a hybrid random network model with preferential attachment and pair formation tendencies. To compare it with a purely preferential attachment network, we derived approximate power-law distributions for in- and out-degree in the hybrid model, assuming a large number of vertices. Now, we are verifying these predictions with simulations. Surprisingly, even though our model does not explicitly include preferential attachment, the in- and out-degree distributions of the hybrid network match those of a purely preferential attachment network. Moreover, when we censored the time-dependent simulation data according to the waiting times observed in a real network, the resulting degree distributions showed better agreement with our theoretical model predictions. Our findings suggest that approximate analytical degree distributions can be used to design network models, even without direct implementation of the corresponding attachment mechanisms. Additionally, we extended the degree distribution theory to capture power laws with exponents between 2 and 3, compared to the standard case of exponent 3. Finally, we have conducted experiments to estimate the uncertainty of this model by repeating the degree distribution fitting process many times and showing that these estimates are reliable even with a small number of vertices.

In the area of the Internet of Things (IoT), various devices operate on distinct frequencies and utilizes algorithms to identify incoming signals. To compare advanced signal processing algorithms, a unified dataset comprising samples from 11 different protocols operating on various frequencies (or using no frequency at all) was created. With 5 different interference signals, the algorithms were applied to a dataset containing 500 unique samples per class. When analyzing signals from the same technology or using cross-technology interference, the classification accuracy was found to be 99.2% and 33.3%, respectively. To the best experience, this study is the first to examine cross-technology interference, providing insights for accurately identifying interfering algorithms. Such research is crucial for accurately detecting noise from various sources.

This passage explores the interaction of a Klein-Gordon particle with backgrounds generated by a Dirichlet boundary in anti-de Sitter space, using a hyperbolic radial coordinate. We examine the implications of this interaction on asymptotic behavior and construct a hyperbolic boundary for the related asymptotic cone, leveraging aspects of hyperbolic manifold theory and discrete series of SL(n, R) to understand asymptotic behavior and develop a hyperbolic Radon transform. Furthermore, this analysis leads to the discovery of new generalized harmonic forms in the asymptotic region and a characterization of asymptically harmonic forms within the asymptotic cone. We investigate the uniqueness of such forms and their implications for understanding asymptotic behavior as well as developing transforms on asymptotic manifolds. We also explore the connection to Meromorphic series for SL(n, R), leveraging which we construct a hyperbolic boundary for the asymptotic cone of the tree of spaces associated with a Dirichlet boundary in anti-de Sitter space.

It's well-known that countable locally standard measure algebras can be parameterized via a real number $\lambda$. This parameter $\lambda$ takes the value of $\lambda\geq 1$ when constructing the algebra, and it's placed within a countable framework. This parameter $\lambda$ has the property that $\lambda^2$ represents the maximal number of pairs of disjoint sets in the algebra $\mathcal{A}$ such that their measures are less than $\lambda$. This parameter $\lambda$ is often referred to as the 'growth rate' of the algebra $\mathcal{A}$. This parameter $\lambda$ also determines the ergodic theory associated with it, particularly in the context of an array $\{f_n\}$ of functions. This parameter $\lambda$ is further linked to generalized Cantor schemes through the use of an integer parameter $k\geq 2$, which is defined as the number of groups that the sets $\{x_k^\wedge\}$ belongs to. This parameter $k$ is utilized in the construction of generalized Cantor schemes.

The twist-6 parton distribution, or generalized parton distribution, E, is difficult to measure in LHC experiments but can be more accessible in fixed target experiments at the ELISE and JPARC facilities. ELISE will have the capability to measure all components of the twist-6 parton distribution E, while providing the opportunity to reduce uncertainties associated with the gluon distribution G. In contrast, the twist-6 parton distribution E will be accessible in JPARC experiments but the measurements will be affected by uncertainties linked to the gluon distribution G. Our proposed research aims to conduct a series of pilot experiments at ELISE to accurately map the twist-6 parton distribution E and the distribution G, ultimately contributing to the understanding of QCD at the high parton momentum fraction x. These pilot experiments will not only enhance our knowledge but also help establish the effectiveness of the "jet tomography" method in detecting twist-6 parton distributions. Our research will not only focus on the statistical limitations of the pilot experiments but also analyze the potential of leveraging elastic and inelastic electron-pion scattering processes to extract the twist-6 parton distribution E. In the course of this research, target and beam polarization will be explored as additional variables to aid in extracting the twist-6 parton distribution E.

We investigate how easily learnable high-dimensional binary classification problems can be made free of errors. The scenario involves a multi-class problem where each class is distinguishable from others in high dimensions, and linear classifiers are considered. For such problems, both regression and classification techniques aim to precisely separate classes from one another by minimizing misclassification rate and mean squared error, respectively. It is found that regression tends to overfit while classification tends to underfit when working with linear classifiers in high dimensions. The study further examines ways to balance these fitting strategies using regularisation techniques, and assesses their effectiveness in real-world applications. The analysis reveals that commonly-used regularisation methods overcorrect in regression and undercorrect in classification, leading to underfit in regression and overfit in classification. The study offers an explanation for the inherent challenges in achieving error-free solutions in high-dimensional learning, and highlights the importance of choosing appropriate learning objectives and techniques to enhance results. The analysis demonstrates that underfitting is a necessary condition to avoid finding perfect solutions in high-dimensional binary classification problems, and suggests that robustness could be a means to achieve error-free learning in such scenarios. The study presents a Python implementation of the methods explored in the analysis, making them available for development purposes.

In systems with strongly interacting bosons, spin-orbit coupling, and inter-specie interactions on lattices, unique forms of superfluids and supersolid phases can occur, characterized by distinct symmetry properties. By applying a self-consistent Hartree-Fock approach, researchers have demonstrated the existence of various exotic superfluids, which are influenced by the interplay between spin-orbit coupling and interaction strength. In particular, they have shown that there are two types of superfluids with real spin-orbit mean-field polarization and other states with complex polarization. Additionally, they have found a new class of supersolid with a unique symmetry in honeycomb structures. Notably, they have observed that in certain regimes, multiple order parameters can coexist, leading to unique and complex phase diagrams. This research highlights potential avenues for experimentally observing these unusual phases in ultra-cold Bose systems.
This text explains how p-r groupings of a saturated chain of Young diagrams characterize the finite abelian p-r groups.

Surface and line defects within the AdS/CFT correspondence can be represented as non-relativistic singularities. This is demonstrated through the use of regular holographic vector fields and their projection onto the P^2 manifold, resulting in the creation of both surface and line defects. The interaction between these defects and various fields, including fermions and gauge fields, as well as the associated quantum effects, are addressed in this framework. Additionally, an extension of the mechanism transforming surface defects into line defects along specified paths is proposed.

An novel, straightforward approach to fitting target kernels for kernel-based learning and classification techniques is presented. This method leverages tree structures to model data attributes, effectively replicating the benefits of kernel kernels. Utilizing additive kernels, we develop k-means for unsupervised learning and develop classification and regression techniques for supervised learning. This method directly operates on additive kernels without requiring explicit access, bypassing the need for data representations. Consequently, we introduce a novel, efficient algorithm for unsupervised clustering and develop analysis tools to investigate the clustering's asymptotic performance. Furthermore, we develop a novel, analysis tool to evaluate the clustering's asymptotic performance. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify the efficacy of this method in real-world applications.

Future lepton colliders heavily depend on high-quality, well-measured muon beams, making their production and management crucial components of any muon collider project. One significant concern for these muon colliders is the effect of in-flight muon decays in their beam lines. To address this issue, we have been exploring the optimal design of muon colliders, incorporating features that minimize the impact of decays during the data collection period. Our study focuses on a range of muon colliders with energies between 1.5 and 5 TeV and a 100 fb^-1 data set, evaluating the decay loss at various stages of the accelerator. Our results demonstrate that in-flight decays can be minimized through a combination of low beam intensities, precise momentum selection, and efficient decay loss reduction methods. Additionally, we have identified design parameters for a muon collider that not only reduce decay-related losses but also comply with a 100 fb^-1 data requirement without significant radiation damage to the detector. Specifically, a precise momentum measurement of around 0.5 GeV is essential for most design scenarios. However, this constraint can be satisfied using a spectrometer design such as the one proposed for the muon collider using a new type of muon spectrometer.

A new approach called Spartan is introduced to train neural networks with significant reductions in parameter count, particularly convolutional networks where optimal structural arrangements remain unclear. Spartan employs a balance between exploring new network configurations and exploiting existing ones on the target training set using the Bayesian-Queried Neural Network (BQNN) framework. BQNN draws upon the strength of the top-performing network configurations encountered so far, while also sampling an auxiliary set of network configurations for parallel evaluation, with the latter being selected based on an approximate posterior probability calculation via Monte-Carlo estimation. This approach allows Spartan to strike a delicate equilibrium between overfitting and underfitting, thereby facilitating training without extensive data augmentation or a lengthy training period. Moreover, Spartan's adaptability enables easy integration into existing hyperparameter optimization and network architecture search pipelines. Spartan achieves state-of-the-art results on various applications, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, EMNIST, MINIST-MNIST, MNIST, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet-44, ImageNet-2012, and the Visual Question Answering task, while also achieving a notable reduction in parameter count.

In a study of a three-dimensional crossover between Bose-Einstein condensation and superfluidity, particularly in dilute ultracold bosons with zero-range interactions, our findings reveal how Pauli blocking affects the excitations of the Bose gas. Unlike in other cases of interactions having a specific range, the presence of Pauli blocking in this scenario leads to a unique modification in the RPA dispersion relation, resulting from the absence of a wave-like cutoff in the intermediate states. Consequently, it yields a suppression in the density of states in the region of low energy. Notably, in comparison to interactions involving a range other than zero, the presence of Pauli blocking here results in a divergence in the low-energy density of states, rather than an energy behavior of a power law. Instead, it exhibits a density of states proportional to $\sqrt{\mu-\epsilon}$ where $\mu$ is the chemical potential and $\epsilon$ is the energy value considered.

While researchers agree that test smells exist and should be eliminated, they debate the severity of the problem. To gather primary data from software developers, we devised an experiment involving two parts. First, we surveyed developers to gauge their perception of the severity of five test smells. We found that the majority of respondents considered test smells to be moderately detrimental, although some believed they had a significant impact on project maintainability. The consensus among our respondents was that eliminating test smells would slightly improve maintainability. The second part of our study explored how developers actually handle test smells in real test code by examining Novice and Expert tasks. Our results revealed that developers consistently identified test smells, but tended to fail to refactor the affected tests. The main reason cited for this failure was a lack of knowledge about the refactoring process. The outcomes of our study suggest that educating developers about the process of eliminating test smells may be an effective means of promoting smell elimination.

In the given study, the properties of solutions to integro-differential sweeping processes are investigated. Specifically, the research focuses on integro-differential processes defined within Euclidean spaces, with clamped boundaries described by semi-invariant manifolds. The study demonstrates the continuity of solutions with respect to initial conditions, using an example that highlights strict continuity, distinct from Lipschitz-continuity. Additionally, the research develops existence proofs for solutions under either monotonically increasing or Lipschitz-continuous conditions. Furthermore, the study provides unique well-posedness criteria for integro-differential processes within closed convex sets. The research also offers corrections to previously published findings in the field, specifically those found in [28].

Researcher's at CERN's LEP-L3 Collaboration have enhanced their Monte Carlo algorithm for computing exact electroweak effects in lepton and quark pair production, describing the updated program's features and assessing its enhancements. The upgraded algorithm, named KKMCee, exhibits enhanced efficiency and improved processing speed, with specific comparisons to its predecessor, CLOSES, showing reductions of 65% and 75% in computation time for $m_\mathrm{top}=175$ GeV and $m_\mathrm{top}=500$ GeV, respectively, as well as gains of 33% and 167% in processing speed for $m_\mathrm{H}=80$ GeV and $m_\mathrm{H}=500$ GeV, respectively. Additionally, enhancements to the Monte-Carlo event generator have allowed for enhanced treatment of finite width effects, with examples provided of applying these enhancements to L3's complete 1999 data set, encompassing productions of both lepton and quark pairs with various masses of the W boson, the top quark, and the Higgs boson.

Deep learning techniques have enhanced the extraction of inter-beat intervals from ECG signals, although remaining issues with signal noise have not been addressed through improved IBI extraction methods. Our study uses a traditional approach to beat detection and evaluates how different ECG signal denoising methods affect the interval measurements. Six different denoising methods utilizing deep learning techniques were utilized and performed differently based on two evaluation metrics. Meanwhile, an unsupervised method was able to effectively clean the ECG signals while having minimal impact on the accuracy of the interval measurements.

In recent times, there has been a significant surge of interest in functional compositeness within the context of distributed computing and the "papyri" papers by Leslie Valavanis. Valavanis' work involved an algorithm for the parallel computation of a permutative function that, when applied to a tensor of 'd' dimensions with 'k' values, results in a unique value. Valavanis demonstrated that any such permutative function Valavanis' work primarily focused on the development of this composite function for the tensor. Incorporating novel concepts such as randomization and a customized hash function, the present work offers a more efficient randomized algorithm for the computation of t-SVD across a distributed environment. Specifically, this new algorithm requires at least one pass over the data tensor, as opposed to at most 'd' passes in the Valavanis algorithm. Furthermore, this work explores the properties of the Lebesgue measure, providing a novel analysis that highlights the robustness of hash functions.

Although a range of static graph embedding methods exist, adapting these methods for dynamic graphs poses significant challenges. Changes in node and edge sets, as well as evolving relationships, make dynamic graphs far more complex and difficult to embed. To address this, we've developed Enhancer of Graph Embedding (EGE), a new framework for embedding dynamic graphs. EGE utilizes a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to capture and embed chronic changes and evolving relationships. In order to optimize space utilization, we've integrated a dustpan and brush method for managing memory cells. In our experimental evaluation, EGE demonstrates superior performance on three real-world datasets, outperforming FastRAG on node classification, and outperforming Neural-Allocation on edge prediction.

Theoretical calculations using the ABACUS software, based on a highly accurate many-body effective Hamiltonian, have been conducted to study the properties of $^7$H. An unbound state in the energy range corresponding to a $1s_{1/2}$ neutron hole and a proton in the $p_{3/2}$ orbit was observed, at an energy of approximately $2.2$ MeV above the threshold energy. Additionally, our theoretical findings are consistent with experimentally-derived bounds on the $^7$H resonances by N. I. Bogdanovich, thereby validating the employed model.

In this work, we investigate a problem analogous to the Nirenberg type on the North half sphere, which can be represented as finding the maximum of a function f(x,y,z) subject to constraints and a condition that a specific derivative is non-negative. Similar to a variant of the Nirenberg problem on a sphere, this issue has an infinitely many solutions, which can express a singularly blowing up function. However, these solutions exhibit a distinct characteristic where they concentrate at points near the axis of the half sphere, distinguishing them from the behavior seen in the equivalent issue on a full sphere.

While class covariance is beneficial for classification, present studies indicate that equal contributions from all classes to the embedding space are ideal. Consequently, a major challenge in current feature learning methods is how to effectively utilize class information. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we introduce the Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL), whose primary goal is to enhance the learning of discriminative embedding spaces by minimizing class disparities. DCDD guides the embedding of each class to be unique while maintaining equal importance, thereby breaking the traditional equal contribution model. Through comprehensive experimentation on large-scale datasets, including ImageNet Subsets and Res50, we find that incorporating DCDD into siamese distance metric learning methods results in significant performance improvements, e.g., a relative improvement of 1.38% and 0.65% in the intra-class accuracy for ImageNet Subsets and Res50, respectively.

The failure of England's COVID-19 Test and Trace programme can be attributed to the inefficient handling of local tracing efforts, a problem that can be solved by developing a more robust system for coordinating local tracing efforts. To address this issue, we evaluate the potential benefits of a more efficient local tracing programme and propose the implementation of local tracing partnerships, consisting of a core team of local experts responsible for coordinating the tracing program. We provide economic evidence that partnering can mitigate delays and keep contact tracing teams within budget, thus preventing the escalation of outbreaks and reducing the need for national interventions. In a national context where limited resources are critical for preventing overwhelming hospitalizations, local tracing partnerships represent an essential public health measure with substantial economic benefits. Specifically, partnerships have the potential to further reduce infection rates by 25% and hospitalizations by 30%, among other desirable outcomes. Moreover, partnerships can achieve this without exceeding the allocated budget for contact tracing, a feat also achieved through the implementation of tracing teams, a method that partners can further enhance by streamlining their services.

Located approximately 1,000 parsecs away, near the Galactic Center, is the open star cluster Melotte 72. M67 has been recognized since 1901, making it one of the oldest known star clusters at an age of roughly 3.6 billion years. Preliminary investigations by Van Dyke, Zeilik, and Thompson suggested it could be as old as 9 billion years, prompting further investigation. Through photometric analysis on a 25 arcminute by 25 arcminute field, aiming to understand the nature of the cluster's reddening and distance, as well as proper motion, our findings reveal key characteristics of the cluster.

The focus is on a model where the random field "Y_at x, conditioned on, has a Gaussian distribution with mean "mu_at x and covariance function "u_n"(x-x').
